inventory.summary: The weathering kit and the street work hold one complete, measured method for making a built place look lived in and worn, and most of it carries to a forest village. What carries unchanged: (1) one entry point (aw.apply(set, look, state)) with a master dial per layer where 0 means untouched; (2) a settings file per place and a look file per mood, with generic code guarded by a lint that fails on copied place words or numbers; (3) roles that say what each object is, with per-role dial multipliers written as object custom properties; (4) a fixed layer order (dirt and soot first, then wetness, then joints, then cracks, then painted moss, then rubbish last, with plants as separate 3D pieces); (5) where-pictures made from the real shape of the scene (lowness, wall foot, sheltered, dampness, footfall, keep-clear, crown, edge, seam) instead of random noise; (6) mark sizes counted in plate dots, with detail fading to the average tone and never to clean; (7) pale-first marks on dark surfaces, a grime budget of about a quarter of the area at about a third darker, and a rule that the darkest part of a mark stays at 0.10 or above; (8) a wetness layer that darkens, makes smoother, adds a film coat and puddles by depth, with the roughness map (not the specular map) doing the work and no shine on walls; (9) joints that read under every light; (10) a rubbish mask built from the scene's real shape and kept off the road crown; (11) data-driven plant scatter with calibrated cover and exact-zero gates; (12) tests that make the whole thing checkable: dial-zero, isolation, determinism, reuse smoke, reuse lint, made-up-picture tests of the measures, and fresh checkers who re-measure. The measured proof is on one pit-village street (21 of 22 lighting pictures keep their joints; nothing darkened beyond the walls' 25 percent line after the fix round; draw time 1.32 to 1.39 times) and a second place, the Japanese courtyard, ran the same code with a different settings file and different looks (7 kit gaps found, listed below). What does NOT carry as it stands: the mask pack (numpy, OpenCV, a 25-80 s reader run per scene) is heavy and tied to the painter pipeline; rubbish_layer.py, make_places_pictures.py, make_joint_pictures.py and the 1926 look are tied to one street and one photo; there is no ruts or hoof layer, no thatch, timber, straw-roof or mud-wall treatment, no horse droppings, no forest-floor leaf litter or fern/bramble species, and no preset for a dirt track. For the forest-village request, the portable parts are the ideas, the dial names, the numbers and a lighter route (a few ray casts for lowness, wall foot, sheltered, dampness, footfall; the same layer order; the same checks). Things never run on this kit: the painter on kit output, Cycles on kit output, a dirt-only road, a forest set.

techniques.name: One entry point, and amount 0 means untouched
techniques.what_it_is: The kit is used through one call, aw.apply(set_id, look_id, state), plus set_master, set_layer_master, set_dials, layer_off/layer_on, set_state, camera, report and remove. Behind it a DataSnapshot remembers every mesh's material slots and deletes the kit's leftovers on remove. Every layer has an Amount dial and every mix factor inside it is a product that contains the amount, so Amount 0 gives exactly the input. Values are clamped before any division so nothing is ever NaN.
techniques.why_it_matters: A smaller model given a plain request such as 'build a village' can call one door and get the whole treatment; and every layer can be switched off alone to see what it adds. It also means the model never splices nodes into a material by hand, which was the biggest source of failures in the first round (hook failure in study 11).
techniques.how_to_do_it: In Blender: import apply_weathering as aw; w = aw.apply('<place id>', '<look id>', 'dry'); w.report() (read the 'problems' and 'skipped' lists); w.set_state('wet'); w.remove(). Never edit a mesh or a material slot, never call an earlier script's own remove(); put a layer in with kit.apply and take it out with kit.remove. The hook (apply/hook.py) finds the Principled shader of each material, takes a six-port bundle (Colour, Roughness, Specular IOR Level, Coat Weight, Normal, Metallic, plus Wet Normal), runs it through the ordered chain of layer node groups and wires the result back. Each port uses a 'wire or constant' splice: if the port was wired the layer takes the wire, otherwise a constant. Materials made of shader groups get an adapter (apply/adapters.py). The chain is rebuilt from an ordered list every time, so apply twice and remove gives the same node counts.
techniques.measured_results: Integrated door test on three scenes (street, lockout, courtyard), 0 errors: remove() gives the scene back (0.000 to 0.001 percent of dots over one step apart); all master dials at 0 against the earlier layers alone 0.04, 0.08 and 0.52 percent of dots over one step (largest 0.0275, 0.0235, 0.0902); two draws of one state 0.00 percent apart; apply and remove twice gives the same node counts (1067/1067, 1349/1349, 1822/1822); no kit leftovers; the kit changes 32, 26 and 39 percent of the dots; each group off alone changes the picture (walls 17-20, ground 9-24, growth 0.4-1.4 percent of dots).
techniques.traps_and_failures: An Attribute node on an object that has no such custom property reads 0 (EEVEE and Cycles alike), so a missing wk_<layer>_amount silently switches the layer off for that object: run kit.report() to see which materials got which layer. Kit.materials_for first missed the copies of materials that the water layer makes. An unexplained coat change at amount 0 had to be found and fixed. The earlier layers are pinned as copies in integrate/legacy_pinned/ so the baseline cannot drift; nothing may point at the originals.

techniques.name: A settings file per place and a look file per mood
techniques.what_it_is: Everything about a place lives in sets/<id>.json (roles, what each layer applies to, ground and wall geometry hints, footfall shapes, keep-clear shapes, shade, dampness, habitat, growth, hook adapters, cameras, lighting rigs, test set). Everything about a mood lives in presets/<look>.json (dial values per layer plus tables of what must read, what the period allows and what is forbidden). Code contains neither. A look is only dial values: the three courtyard looks (kept, neglected, rough) differ from each other only in dial numbers.
techniques.why_it_matters: This is what lets one set of code build a town, a harbour, a mine, a farm or a forest village: the model writes one small settings file for the new place and picks or writes a look. It is also what a preflight can check (a settings file with every role filled, a look with every dial resolved).
techniques.how_to_do_it: Copy sets/japanese_courtyard.json (it is the shorter, newer example) and rename the roles with object-name regexes, collections, material-name regexes or custom properties. Fill: roles and the per-role dial multipliers (for example a thatch role with soot and moss multipliers, a timber role, an earth-track role), never-lists (objects that must never get a layer), ground and wall geometry, footfall shapes (band_along, lines_along, polyline, rect, auto_door_to_edge, auto_door_strip, around_role, from_footfall), keep_clear shapes, shade, dampness, habitat, growth species list, cameras and lighting for tests. Resolve dials with apply.dials.resolve(layer, look, settings, overrides). Per-object overrides are custom properties: wk_seed, wk_role_id, wk_zmin, wk_zmax, wk_<layer>_amount, wk_<layer>_<dial>; random numbers come from wk_seed, the Seed dial and position, never from a name.
techniques.measured_results: The street set was written first; the Japanese courtyard (a gravel court with moss, no roads, no soot) ran through the same code with its own set and three looks and passed 0 errors in the door test. Its own findings note lists 7 gaps the kit had (roof GN instances not handled, no wall front, role_dials only honoured by the soot layer, lichen's rough_stone_only flag not read, moss brighter than stone, plinth treated as ground, validate_look timing). Those gaps show where a third place will also stumble.
techniques.traps_and_failures: The lint (harness/lint_no_set_names.py) must report zero hits over apply/ masks/ harness/ walls/ ground/ growth/: it fails on any set word, name or number list copied from a set file. Ordinary words (kerb, flag, sett, gutter, step, pipe, wall, iron) are allowed. role_dials only worked in the soot layer on the courtyard, so a per-role multiplier written in a settings file may be silently ignored by other layers: check with report() or the isolation test. Roles must not overlap in ways that give two multipliers to one object.

techniques.name: Layer order in the chain: dirt before water, joints and cracks after, moss, rubbish last
techniques.what_it_is: Layers sit in fixed slots. Slot A (before the water): soot, rust, steps, ground dirt film; the water then sits on top of the dirt the way it sits on the stone. Then WETNESS, then JOINTS, then slot B (cracks, dullness, that stay dull under water), then slot C (painted moss and algae), then RUBBISH last. Plants and litter pieces are separate 3D objects scattered by geometry nodes. A layer placed after the water layer also gets Wet Mask and Puddle Mask inputs; in slot A they read 0.
techniques.why_it_matters: A model that stacks wear layers in the wrong order gets dirt that the puddles wash off, cracks that shine like wet glass, or joints that vanish. The order was decided by measurement: the ground film in slot A at first reduced joint contrast, so it was lowered from 0.6 to 0.4 and the order kept.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Register each layer with kit.register_layer('<key>', builder, slot='A'|'B'|'C'), and let the hook place it. In a new place, keep this order even if some layers are absent (a forest village has no setts, so JOINTS may be empty but the slot logic is the same).
techniques.measured_results: With everything on, 21 of 22 lighting pictures pass the joint test (street without the new parts: 20 of 22); largest joint contrast 0.62 (limit 0.75, a black net). Joint contrast after over before at the plate's three bands: dry near 1.014, mid 0.993, far 0.969; wet near 1.009, mid 1.029, far 1.057.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Without the order, joint contrast fell because the film darkened the sett colour before the joints were drawn. Layers that need wall sheets (runoff) draw nothing without them: they fail silently.

techniques.name: Where-pictures from the real shape of the scene (the mask bus)
techniques.what_it_is: Instead of random noise, each wear layer reads named masks measured from the actual geometry: ground height, slope, lowness (a low place collects water and dirt), crown (the high middle of a road), wall distance, prop distance, seam distance, water distance, inside corners, step feet and pipe feet, edge_dist, piece_gap, sheltered (under eaves and overhangs), openness, sun shade, dampness, footfall (how trodden), keepclear (hard 'no plants here'), entry_rand (one random number per door) and existing_growth. Wall sheets hold masks for the face of each wall. A layer declares the masks it wants by name (M <Name>); a mask the place did not make reads its default.
techniques.why_it_matters: This is what makes a weathered place read as built rather than sprayed: dirt gathers at the foot of walls and in low places, moss grows where it is damp and shaded and not trodden, runs of rain stain walls under sills and eaves, and doorsteps are worn. It is also the cause of most of the kit's weight.
techniques.how_to_do_it: The reader (masks/reader.py, a Blender run of 25 to 80 s) casts rays at the scene and writes a pack of pictures: ground plan masks at 4 cm per dot looked up by world x and y, wall sheets at 2 cm looked up by position in the wall's own frame, texture-space masks looked up by the material's own picture. masks/make_pack.py finishes the pack in plain Python. The habitat fields are plain formulas: moss_site = (0.45 dampness + 0.30 shade + 0.25 edge) x (1 - foot_gate) x (1 - keep_gate) x (1 - smother); weed, algae and lichen sites have their own weights and exact-zero gates (nothing grows on the trodden lane, in a keep-clear shape or under water). Footfall shapes come from the settings file. View a mask with kit.show_mask('moss_site') (up to three names a+b+c go to R, G, B) and kit.hide_mask().
techniques.measured_results: The mask packs for the street, lockout shot and courtyard were built and checked against the earlier layers' own masks (masks/check_against_earlier.py). The reader runs 25 to 80 s per scene. In the rubbish layer the same idea (the street's real wall and step positions measured into a 4 cm picture) gave a mask that is 0.000 over the whole road crown.
techniques.traps_and_failures: keepclear first covered the whole pavement because the trodden limits were too low. Image rows in Blender run bottom-up; the packs' PNGs are written top-first so use pack.read_png. A mask that looks the same from every view means the other materials stayed bright (the debug views black out every material but yours). Blender's own Python has no cv2: masks.ensure_cv2() appends the system one. The pack is heavy (numpy, OpenCV, BVH tree, one pack per scene, rebuilt when the scene changes). My judgment: a forest-village plugin should keep the mask names and formulas but compute a small subset (lowness, wall foot, sheltered, dampness, footfall, keepclear, crown) from a few ray casts or from object bounds, and write them as vertex colour attributes or small pictures; this lighter route is NOT tested.

techniques.name: Dirt roads driven by horse and carriage (what the street gives, and how to map it)
techniques.what_it_is: There is no ready 'dirt track' layer, but the street's knowledge maps onto it. The street's footfall rules are the model: a band for the crown and horse walk (x from -1.3 to 1.3, weight 0.9, feather 0.35 m) and two wheel-track lines (x at -0.8 and +0.8, so wheels about 1.6 m apart in the file's own note, width 0.45 m, weight 1.0, feather 0.2 m). Footfall then drives polish (worn lanes paler and smoother), keep-clear for plants (no weeds on trodden dots), dried puddle rings in the low places away from the lanes, and the rubbish mask's rule that the crown stays clear. The wetness layer's lowness-driven puddles put water in the low wheel ruts. Straw and leaves are already species of the rubbish scatter.
techniques.why_it_matters: This is the nearest proven recipe for the user's 'unkept dirt roads driven down by horse and carriage'. It shows which dials make a track look driven on: trodden lanes read pale and smooth, the middle between the wheel lines can grow grass, low places hold water and dried rings, edges gather litter and plants, and the surface is not a clean flat plane.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Use my reading of the street files (not tested on a dirt road): in the settings file give the track a ground role; set footfall to two lines_along wheel tracks, ideally with a narrower or lower-weight centre band so that grass can grow between the wheels (the street's band blocks plants along the whole crown); put keep_clear on the tracks; let lowness make the ruts hold puddles; use the dirt layer's polish (polish 0.4, polish_lift 0.05, polish_rough 0.3) for packed lanes, water_marks 0.3 for dried puddle rings, film 0.5 with film_max_share 0.25 for a broad dirt film; use the growth layer for weeds (weed_cover 0.01, wall_foot_share 0.035, gutter_tuft_share 0.05, dead_grass_share 0.15, flower_share 0.08); put the rubbish layer's straw and mud on. For real ruts a displacement or a sculpted mesh with real depth is needed (see gaps).
techniques.measured_results: Footfall rules and polish were measured on the street only (zones check P6 and the readable table). The measured pieces: polish and tide marks are part of the ground dirt layer; crown rubbish 0.000 (see the rubbish entry). Nothing was measured on a dirt road.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Cart wheel spacing in the street file is marked as 'a guess; the research step may move it'. The street's crown band marks the whole centre as trodden, which would keep grass out of the middle of a village lane: set it deliberately. Cobbles and tar patches in the street are a stone-road feature (tar_patches 0.3, tar_max_share 0.03); set tar_patches 0 on dirt.

techniques.name: Mark size in plate dots, and fading to the average tone
techniques.what_it_is: All sizes are counted in dots of the final picture (the 'plate dot') so a mark is visible at the size anyone will see it. A mark's width is max(real width, min_dots x dot), where dot = Dot Across or Dot Along at that point. An Inflate Limit caps how fat a mark may be made compared with its real size; beyond that the mark fades to the layer's average tone, never to clean. Fine detail also fades with Fade Near; 3D plant pieces hand over to a painted far band. Vertical marks survive slanted views.
techniques.why_it_matters: A crack drawn at its real 1 mm width vanishes at film size and a mark drawn bigger and bigger would look like a stripe. Fading to the average tone keeps the overall darkening the same at every distance so the far wall does not suddenly brighten ('clean') and give the look of a model.
techniques.how_to_do_it: masks/scale.py supplies two node groups, WK SCALE and WK MARK WIDTH. A layer reads Dot Across, Dot Along, Fade Near and Far Blend as inputs and uses them as the table in the plan: marks 5+ dots at 0.08 contrast, lines 3 dots at 0.11, patches 15+ dots at 0.04 (these numbers come from the painter test: see the painter entry). Dial names: crack_dots 3.5, crack_contrast 0.11, near_only 15 (metres), ribbon_dots 4, frame_dots 8.
techniques.measured_results: Far-fade ticks and speckle were found only at 100 percent crops by the fresh checkers; plate-size crops were needed to see them. The rule that cracks gained marks when made stronger (36 good on the main plate against 28 before; 110 against 71 on the notice plate) shows the size rule works, but most marks stay faint.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Do not check marks on a shrunk preview only: far-fade ticks hide there. A steep relief far away is seen as single white ticks, so the groove slope is faded with distance (full to 5 m, 10 percent at 20 m).

techniques.name: Pale-first on dark surfaces, and the grime budget
techniques.what_it_is: A layer that only darkens makes dark walls into mush. So marks on dark surfaces start pale: a floor of 0.30 of the clean colour (lift_to) so a mark never goes near black, a pale dust lip along the edge of a crack, warm-cream whitened steps, pale washed patches under sills. The darkest part of any mark stays at 0.10 to 0.12 or above, and the surround of a dark mark at 0.18 or above. Dirt budget: about a quarter of an area at about a third darker.
techniques.why_it_matters: A soot film that darkened walls by 23 percent was caught by a fresh checker. After pale-first the dry walls fell from 26.6 percent over the 'a third darker' line to 2.8 percent. Dark surfaces get lost when the stage (the film pipeline) crushes anything under 0.10 brightness.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Use lift_to(colour, floor) in walls/walls_common.py (it takes a colour made in the nodes); keep soot film_mult 0.8, sheltered_mult 0.6, washed_mult 0.95, floor_mult 0.4 and base_lift 0; use dirt film_darkness 0.25 with film_max_share 0.25. Whiten rather than darken at doorsteps and under sills.
techniques.measured_results: M1 (share of a class darkened by a third, line 25 percent): walls 0.12 to 0.23 in the first round, 2.8 percent dry after the fix round (was 26.6). M2 (share under plate brightness 0.10, line +3 points on walls and trims, +8 on the rest): walls and trims go down by 3.4 to 6.6 points; the largest rise is the colliery's, +5.4 (main) and +5.2 (lockout); walls +1.1 and +1.8. M3 (mean brightness at least 0.88): all above 0.966. Whole plate 0.984 to 1.003.
techniques.traps_and_failures: M5 (each class stays within 0.90 to 1.00 and the bands differ by under 0.08) is NOT met: pale marks lighten the mid-distance wall to 1.06-1.12 (walls 10 to 20 m), and trims reach 1.76 (few seen). This is the price of pale-first; lowering washed_pale or washed_share would reduce soot readability. The paint layer was switched off because it was the only one that failed M2 to M4.

techniques.name: Cracks, chips and broken edges (ground and wall)
techniques.what_it_is: Ground cracks (flags, kerbs, setts) and wall cracks (stepped cracks in brick, plaster cracks, corner chips, spall patches), each a dial family. Each crack is a pale dust lip plus a dark core, stays dull under water (slot B), and has a relief groove with a small slope.
techniques.why_it_matters: Cracks and chips are the damage that tells a viewer a place is old. They must be sized in plate dots and look dull and dusty or they read as clean decals.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Ground dials (names and defaults): flag_cracks 1.0, flag_fine_share 0.11, flag_broken_share 0.03, flag_tilt_share 0.04, tilt_lip 8, corner_chip_share 0.07, kerb_chips 1.0, kerb_chip_share 0.28, kerb_break_share 0.067, kerb_scuffs 0.3, kerb_joint_open 8, sett_disturb 0.7, sett_disturbed_share 0.04, open_joint_share 0.14, missing_share 0.003, sunken_patch 0.8, crack_dots 3.5, crack_contrast 0.11, near_only 15, max_contrast 0.75, dull 1. Wall dials: crack_amount 0.3, crack_dots 3.5, crack_contrast 0.11, stepped_cracks 0, corner_chips 0.3, chip_cm 5, plaster_cracks 0, spall_patches 0.15, near_only 15, slope_mm 1.5, dull 1. For timber and plaster cottages, raise plaster_cracks and spall_patches in the look and lower stepped_cracks only if the walls are not brick (this is my judgment; the street has brick and stone only).
techniques.measured_results: Readability at plate size (first round, 60 percent good line): cracks main 14 percent good, notice 46 percent, lockout 12 percent; they gained marks when made stronger (36 good main, 110 notice against 28 and 71). Cracks stay faint at film size; how many survive the painter is not known.
techniques.traps_and_failures: A crack that is dark only reads in some light; the pale lip makes it read under all light. Do not let cracks shine when wet (slot B and dull 1.0 mean they do not).

techniques.name: Wetness layer: dark, smooth, film, puddles
techniques.what_it_is: A single node group WETNESS (35 inputs, 11 outputs: Colour, Roughness, Specular IOR Level, Coat Weight, Coat Roughness, Normal, Height after water fills the puddles, Wet Mask, Puddle Mask, Streak Mask, Puddle Depth) plus WETNESS DRIP for streaks under sills and eaves. Wet surfaces get five things: porosity darkening (colour multiplied by the measured wet share), roughness slid toward the soaked value, a specular boost, a film coat, and a grain-fill normal (the Wet Normal) that fills small relief. Puddles are cut from a depth number built 40 percent from slow wobble, 40 percent from lowness and 20 percent from relief.
techniques.why_it_matters: Wet ground at dusk is the biggest single visual change in the street. The study found: colour alone is nearly invisible at dusk, smoothness is the big change, the film adds the lamp pools, puddles add the mirrors. A specularity map alone, without lower roughness, would not look wet.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Per material class, set wet colour ratio, soaked roughness, spec boost and film coat. Measured wet colour as a share of dry (wet 0.85, puddles 0.5): setts 0.72, pavement 0.78, kerb 0.76, gutter 0.69, brick walls 0.70, stone walls 0.72, colliery brick 0.86, dressed stone 0.88/0.82, slate 0.90, yard 0.56. Defaults: puddle threshold top 0.79, range 0.52, curve 1.25; depth shares 0.40/0.40/0.20; softness 0.10. Walls: wet band measured in the wall's own coordinates from the floor (slope 0, offset 0), 0.9 m tall with a wavering top; porosity 1.0, darkest 0.2; Specular Boost 0, no coat, wet roughness 0.9; streaks under sills and eaves at 0.9 of the wet value. Calibrate the puddle dial against the share of road under water with the calibration driver (a puddle sweep) on YOUR camera.
techniques.measured_results: The wet road reads 1.50 times today's dry road in EEVEE (aim 1.5; Cycles 2.0; EEVEE default shadows 1.67 because soft-shadow noise leaks light). Baked glb versus live layer, dressed stone 1.12 times live (first bake 1.41), roofs 1.03 (1.23), colliery brick 1.13 (1.70); a flat surface 'wet all over' shines more than a surface wet in places. Wet-over-dry on walls: first-round shine made the lamp-lit wall base brighter (1.04 at roughness 0.75), roughness 0.9 with extra darkening fixed it; foot strip 0.85 after the plinth was darkened.
techniques.traps_and_failures: The wall band measured from the pavement was hidden behind a stone plinth (each cottage floor stands 0.15 to 0.46 m above the pavement): measure in each object's own coordinates. A wet wall must NOT get shine, because a lamp a metre away then lights the lower wall at a slant and makes it brighter. The glb exporter puts a specular map into the alpha channel of the glTF specular picture and only reads a grey picture's alpha unless a Separate Color is in the path; a picture alone can only lower reflection (the factor 1.5 lets 1.0 mean wet shine). Live reflections move with the camera; baked or painted ones stay stuck on the road (about 0.9 m of drift at 12 m for a 1.4 m move: estimate, not tested).

techniques.name: EEVEE soft-shadow speckle on wet ground, and renderer choice
techniques.what_it_is: A white speckle on wet road at the scale of one dot was blamed on relief for five runs. The real cause was EEVEE's soft shadows; the fix is shadow rays 4, shadow steps 16 and 32 to 48 samples. The side-by-side of EEVEE and Cycles on the rented RTX 4090 showed Cycles wins on lit wet ground and reflections, EEVEE is far faster, and the colour mood differs. The user's rule: Cycles when lamps, windows or fires are lit, otherwise EEVEE.
techniques.why_it_matters: A model chasing speckle by changing materials wastes hours and breaks the look. The fix is a render setting. A forest village at dusk with lit windows and a lantern will need Cycles; daylight can use EEVEE.
techniques.how_to_do_it: EEVEE: scene.eevee.use_shadows on, shadow ray count 4, shadow step count 16, ray tracing on, taa samples 32 to 48. Cycles (street/eevee_vs_cycles/tools/pair_runner.py): OptiX denoise, adaptive threshold 0.01, light tree on. Choose samples from the measured noise table in the eevee_vs_cycles results.
techniques.measured_results: EEVEE grain on the road's left third: 16 samples 0.0119, 48 samples 0.0078; on the full-size plate 0.0049 with no dot-scale speckle. Draw times (4 shared cores): EEVEE at 540 x 960 38 to 80 s for the dry street, 85 to 108 s wet at 16 samples with rays 4 / steps 16, 357 s at 48 samples; the full-size lockout plate (1536 x 2730, 32 samples) 20 min 27 s and about 7 GB of memory.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Do not change a material to cure the speckle; do not judge at 16 samples only. The colour mood differs between EEVEE and Cycles, so calibrate colour ratios in the renderer you will use. Never read ~/.runpod; use the serverless render client.

techniques.name: Sett and stone joints that read under every light
techniques.what_it_is: A JOINTS node group (road only) that makes joints between stones read in every light, dry or wet, by three things together: a dark colour (darkness 0.30), dullness (roughness 0.9, specular cut 0.35, coat cut 0.45) and a rounded groove normal that water cannot smooth, faded with distance (relief fade 5 to 20 m). The joint picture is a full grid made by the picture tool: the dark-line search finds only half the joints, so the tool finds the grid of rows and columns and draws the missing joints.
techniques.why_it_matters: Wet roads flatten joints; the same joints that read dry at 0.24 contrast read at 0.07 wet, until the groove and dullness were added. A pavement, cobbled yard, stone path or a stone wall's mortar lines in a village needs the same treatment.
techniques.how_to_do_it: make_joint_pictures.py (plain Python, numpy and OpenCV) makes sett_joints_clean.png (red = cavity, green = groove profile, blue = halo), a 16-bit groove normal map 8 mm deep with a rounded 6 mm edge, joint_cores_new.png for measuring, and a check sheet. It works on a 3 x 3 tiling then crops the middle so joints join across tile edges. Steps: black top-hat finds thin dark lines; bridge gaps up to 6 cm (60 dots) along a joint; remove specks under 500 dots and holes under 6000; smooth outline (blur 1.5 dots, cut at half), at least 5 dots wide; then complete the grid from the 10 rows and each row's columns. Defaults: darkness 0.30, dullness 1, spec cut 0.35, coat cut 0.45, dull roughness 0.9, edge shade 0.15, puddle cover 0.8. Joint Shadow (light never reaching the joint) is off (default 0): 0.25 to 0.7 gives a black net.
techniques.measured_results: Lighting test set A-E, 22 pictures: before, 6 pass (all dry); after, 21 pass. Wet dusk contrast 0.07 -> 0.52; glare from behind 0.03 -> 0.53; near contrast before 0.01 to 0.33, after 0.25 to 0.62; the grid is visible in 22 of 22 after, 1 of 22 before. Relief 3 to 6 times stronger changed contrast only 0.11 to 0.13 (and made white ticks on stone corners). At plate size 1536 x 2730, 64 samples, all 9 plates pass (round 2 failed the six wet ones, near contrast 0.05 to 0.10).
techniques.traps_and_failures: First picture missed about half the joints (pale sand fill); the grid completion fixed it. The one failing picture (lockout, brazier glare, heavy rain, middle band, contrast -0.05 against minimum 0.07) fails because 46 percent of the road is puddle and the remaining island of 479 dots is under the blaze, where joints read as bright lit edges; my second measure (grid visible against grain) read 0.15 against 0.06. Stone joints are tied to one Poly Haven CC0 photo (square cobblestone, 2 m across, 1 mm per dot): another surface needs its own picture.

techniques.name: Rubbish mask built from the scene's real shape, plus painted muck plus scattered 3D pieces
techniques.what_it_is: A RUBBISH layer (last in the chain) paints coal dust, cinders, ash, mud, wet straw, sodden paper scraps and dead leaves as colour, roughness and relief, wet where the street is wet. A scatter puts 6000 to 7000 real small pieces (cinder and coal lumps, ash heaps, paper, leaves, straw, a pot, a stick; 1 to 20 cm, ragged, no printed matter) on the same mask. The mask comes from five places: the gutter, the wall foot, corners and doorsteps (step feet, pipe feet, lamp post feet, inside corners), around props, and smooth noise patches; and the crown of the road is excluded.
techniques.why_it_matters: Real lumps catch light and throw tiny shadows, so they read as litter even where the painted layer is faint. A rubbish mask built from where things really are looks placed by weather and people, not sprayed. For a forest village this is leaf litter, straw, dung and mud at the wall foot and in the gutter-like edge of the track.
techniques.how_to_do_it: make_places_pictures.py measures the real 3D street into a flat 4 cm picture (distance to nearest wall or step, to nearest prop, where doorsteps, rain-pipe feet and lamp feet are, inside corners). The layer's dials (all 0 to 2 with 0 off): Rubbish Amount, Gutter, Wall Foot, Corners And Doorsteps, Around Props, Seed, Patchiness 0.55, Gutter Width 0.45, Wall Foot Width 0.75, Props Width 0.8, Crown Clear 1 (nothing within 1.3 m of the middle line, full strength from 1.8 m), the kind dials Dust And Cinders, Ash, Mud, Straw, Paper, Leaves, Dust Darkness 0.75, Grit Size 1 (1.8 cm cells), Relief, Wet Look. The pieces' dials: Pieces Density, Pieces Distance 45 m, Piece Size, Pieces Wet. Scatter classes are densities per square metre (lumps 70, coal 45, ash 6, paper 16, leaves 16, straw 18) with minimum distances (0.05 to 0.12 m). Wet pieces fade from dry to wet colour with a value node WET.
techniques.measured_results: Crown (|x| under 1.3 m): 0.000 in the street copy and 0.000 in the lockout except the prop rings (mean 0.034, 4.7 percent over 0.3). The gutter is dirty along its whole length; about half the kerb and pavement and 40 percent of the wall strip carry clear rubbish; a tenth of the road (its outer strip). Joints measure the same with rubbish as without in all 16 street pictures (the contrast identical to two decimals; largest move 0.003). Clean road brightness change 0.00001. Dots left out of the joint measure: 3.8 percent of the road (main), 1.3 percent (close), 27 percent (lockout). Prop rings cover 11 percent of the lockout ground between 0 and 45 m.
techniques.traps_and_failures: rubbish_layer.py has street numbers in it (X0, X1, Y0, Y1 = -4.5, 4.5, -12, 72; gutter centre 2.35, half 0.15; crown from 1.3 to 1.8; a places picture value of 1.0 is 1.275 m) so it is tied to one street: carry the dials and the five-places idea, not the numbers. Pieces on the crown were not counted, only seen to be absent. The pieces are for the plate only (not in the glb). Nothing modern: no print on paper, no plastic.

techniques.name: Weeds, moss and algae: where they grow and how many
techniques.what_it_is: Growth is scattered as separate 3D pieces by Geometry Nodes from species.json (data-driven). pieces.py builds ragged plant meshes in code. scatter.py is a Poisson scatter with one node group per kind (for speed). A point is kept with probability = site x liking x gates x rubbish rule x existing-growth avoidance x distance fade. Calibration makes the cover dials mean what they say (weed_cover 0.01 means about 1 percent). A baked litter_dist picture and an above_water picture give the 5 cm litter clearance and the no-plants-in-puddles rule. Plants widen with distance up to 3 times to keep their screen size; a painted far band takes over beyond the 3D range (distance 18 m, fade 5 m).
techniques.why_it_matters: Weeds in the gutter, moss in the shade and algae in the wet are the strongest signs of an unkept place. Moss that is too bright or lime-green reads as fake; plants in puddles look like floating strings.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Growth dials: weeds_amount, cushions_amount, distance 18, distance_fade 5, piece_size, weed_cover 0.01, gutter_tuft_share 0.05, wall_foot_share 0.035, cushion_cover 0.008, min_spacing 0.15, toadflax_clumps, rubbish_thin_max 0.45, rubbish_heap_min 0.75, dead_grass_share 0.15, flower_share 0.08, max_pieces 2500, wet_dark 0.7, tilt_random 0.5. Painted moss (groundmoss): joint_share 0.08, shade_bias 0.6, ribbon_dots 4, ribbon_m 0.02, broken_len 0.3, algae_fan 0.6, algae_radius 0.55, liverwort 0, far_band 0.5, far_band_m 0.45, moss_value 0.36. Courtyard moss look extras: colour_gain 0.15, colour_sat 1.2, existing_avoid 0.7, piece_inflate_limit 3. Add species by editing species.json (pieces are built in code in pieces.py).
techniques.measured_results: Weed tufts and moss cushions were the only mark that passed the readability line in the first round (main 70 percent good, lockout 100 percent; notice 45 percent fails because the pavement is lit and the plants have no contrast). Moss ribbons and algae fans: main 9 percent, lockout 9 percent, FAIL. Plants stood in puddles: 36 percent (32 of 88) before the fix; after baking above_water, no root in a puddle (0 of 157 on the main plate), and the checkers' pixel count fell from 39 to 19 percent (the rest is leaves leaning over a puddle's edge and reflections). About 18 percent of the street's ground counts as puddle in above_water.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Lime-green weeds (fixed with colour_gain and saturation dials); moss at value 0.12 gave green bands (moss_value 0.36 now); cushions_amount lowered from 1.0 to 0.6 to stop flat moss strings that read as floating; lichen is exactly 0 in the street and lichen's rough_stone_only flag is not read (a courtyard gap). A mask that says 'puddle' in a dry plate too is the price of keeping dry and wet plates the same plants.

techniques.name: Rust and iron
techniques.what_it_is: The iron layer rusts iron objects (posts, pipes, drums, covers) by height and by collars where parts join, with chips in paint, a metallic drop (rust is less metallic), a heat tint on stacks and drums, a soot halo and a rust run down from the rust. Also in the ground dirt layer: a rust halo on the ground round the foot of iron posts and pipes (10 to 25 cm) and a rust bleed ring round standing objects (the fire drum); at a pipe foot it is a dark wet stain instead.
techniques.why_it_matters: Rust and rust stains are the quickest way to age metal. For a village, they apply to hinges, nails, bands on barrels, cart wheels' iron tyres, lantern brackets, pump and well fittings, and the stable's ironwork.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Iron dials: rust_cover 0.3, rust_height 0.55, chip_share 0.3, collar_spacing 1.9, collar_rust 0.5, metallic_drop 0.6, heat_scale 0.3, soot_halo 0.5, paint_keep 0.6, rust_run 0.12. Ground rust: rust_halo 0.5, rust_halo_m 0.18, drum_ring 0.5. Rust colour tints from the look file (RUST_TINT 160, 110, 80; DRUM_TINT 140, 75, 40).
techniques.measured_results: Rust readability in the first round was 0 marks in the main-camera zone and 3 in the notice zone (0 good): the rust marks were too small or not in view. It was not re-measured at plate size after the fix round in my reading.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Iron roles must be set in the settings file; the lint forbids a name. Zero rust marks read means 'unproven'.

techniques.name: Soot, run-off streaks, whitened steps and the wall foot band
techniques.what_it_is: Wall layers (walls/): soot (a film, sheltered sooting, washed pale streaks and mortar soot), runoff (rain streaks under sills and eaves, needs wall sheets), foot (splash band and tide mark at the wall foot), steps (whitened and scrubbed doorsteps with dished and chipped nosings), wallgrowth (moss and algae on walls), paint (off in the final look).
techniques.why_it_matters: Walls tell the age of cottages: a dirty splash band at the foot, streaks below sills, moss on the north face, a worn doorstep. For a forest village the soot role would be less (wood smoke on thatch and chimneys, not coal) but the same masks apply.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Steps dials: whitened_share 0.5, scrubbed_share 0.3, frame_m 0.06, frame_dots 8, boot_grey 0.3, dish_depth 0.004, nosing_chips 0.3, wear_polish 0.4. Soot dials: film_mult 0.8, sheltered_mult 0.6, washed_mult 0.95, washed_share 0.2, floor_mult 0.4, grey_pull 0.2, mortar_soot 0.3, mottle_size 1, mottle_contrast 0.4, edge_sharp 0.5, stack_mult 0.6, roof_mult 0.9, base_lift 0. Set role_dials in the settings file for per-role weights; warm the colours with the look's colour tables. In the courtyard run, runoff drew nothing (wall sheets missing).
techniques.measured_results: Readability first round (60 percent line): soot and dust patches 34 to 40 percent good (FAIL), run-off streaks main 0 marks, notice 10 percent, whitened steps main 0 marks, wall-foot band main 0 percent. The reason is that walls are dark and seen almost edge-on, so 41 to 48 percent of the soot patches and 63 percent of the notice run-off streaks are lost. Only weeds and moss cushions pass. So the wall stains read at plan view and in close views, not at film size on far walls: judged from the tables.
techniques.traps_and_failures: A soot film that darkens walls by a third reads as black: use pale-first. Run-off needs wall sheets (the pack), or nothing is drawn. The steps' random whitened or scrubbed choice uses entry_rand so the scrub strip on the flags uses the same random number (consistency).

techniques.name: Preflight, reuse lint, and made-up-picture tests of the measures
techniques.what_it_is: A set of checks that fail loudly. harness/lint_no_set_names.py fails when kit code contains set words, names or number lists copied from a set file. harness/selftests.py has dial_zero (at Amount 0 the picture is identical at 16 bit), isolation (a layer alone changes only the dots of its roles), determinism (two draws are identical) and reuse_smoke (every registered layer goes in and out without a crash and materials are restored exactly). harness/test_measures.py runs every measuring script against made-up pictures with known answers (28 checks). kit.report() lists 'problems' and 'skipped'.
techniques.why_it_matters: These are the checks the new plugin's preflight can turn into 'fails when a material or the scene lacks them'. They catch the silent failures (an object without wk_ properties reads 0, so the layer is silently off).
techniques.how_to_do_it: Preflight for a new place: (1) settings file loads and every role matches at least one object; (2) after aw.apply, report()['problems'] is empty and 'skipped' lists nothing that was meant to be applied; (3) every ground and wall material has the bundle chain (kit.report); (4) every layer reaches amount 0 = identical; (5) lint reports 0 hits; (6) a mask pack exists for the scene (or the lighter route's attributes exist). Run python3 -I harness/lint_no_set_names.py and blender -b --disable-autoexec SCENE --python harness/run_selftests.py -- SET SCENE OUT TESTS WxH (tests: hook, remove, nothing, legacy_nothing, dial_zero, isolation, determinism, reuse, lighting).
techniques.measured_results: Door test on street, lockout and courtyard, 0 errors (see the first entry). Measures were tested against made-up pictures (28 checks) so a bad measure is caught before it judges the scene.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Fresh checkers re-measured and found false claims in builders' own reports; far-fade ticks found only at 100 percent crops; decide up front whether covered dots count in a measure (puddle dots, rubbish dots, the kit's own dots): the joint count read 18 of 22 with the kit's own dots left out until a fix, and the line was 20. Budgets (runs, time) ran about double what was planned.

techniques.name: Lighting test set and the measures of a finished look
techniques.what_it_is: A fixed set of 22 pictures (street 16 and lockout 6) in lighting rigs A to E (dusk with lamps, glare from behind, heavy rain, close view and so on) and a family of measures on them. Joint contrast, delta and 'seen' share in near, middle and far bands; wet-to-dry ratios; not-dark-mush M1 to M5; readability GOOD/RISKY/LOST via painter_survival_fit; period caps and hue; zones; drawing time; and class and depth passes.
techniques.why_it_matters: It lets any model check a place under more than one light, and stops a look that only works in one picture. The same set can be built for a forest village (dawn, noon, dusk lantern, rain).
techniques.how_to_do_it: harness/lighting.py holds the rigs as data (in the set file: cameras, lighting, test_set). harness/measure_joints.py, measure_wet.py, measure_mush.py, measure_readable.py (needs plate_detail_check and painter_survival_fit.json), measure_zones.py, measure_time.py (best of three), measure_period.py and coverage.py. P1 to P10 pass lines in HOW TO USE.md section 5: P1 joints 21 of 22; P2 wet look kept; P3 readable at the painter's size; P4 nothing wrong for 1926; P5 not one dark mush; P6 no weeds or moss where they must not be; P7 time within +30 percent; P8 amount 0 changes nothing; P9 reuse; P10 deterministic.
techniques.measured_results: P7 drawing time (best of three, 1536 x 2730 at 48 samples): street 2.2 s earlier layers alone, 3.05 s everything = 1.39 times (before the fix round 2.06; line 1.3, NOT met); lockout 3.24 against 4.27 = 1.32 times (before 1.75). First picture after applying: 14.5 s look change + 16.1 s first draw (limit 40 s met; 1.5 times line not met). P2 street: 3 lines out after the fix round (before 6): light E wet road wet/dry 3.6151 against 3.7119, light E heavy 3.4883 against 3.5763, light C wet highlight share 0.0361 against 0.0425. P5 M5 not met by design.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Calibrations belong to a camera: re-fit puddle dial and colour ratios for each new camera. The street test set is tied to the street (camera names, rig letters, painter fit). I did not read measure_zones in detail; I read the headers only.

techniques.name: What the painter and the stage do to marks (film-pipeline facts)
techniques.what_it_is: When plates are painted over by the painter step and shown on the stage, marks are lost. Painter test measured: marks 5 or more dots at contrast 0.08 survive, lines 3 dots at 0.11, patches 15 or more dots at 0.04. The stage crushes painted values under 0.10. The painter weakens colour; far third of the road texture is invented by the painter; the painted picture behind must also be wet to match.
techniques.why_it_matters: For the film, wear that cannot survive the painter is wasted. This is where the plate-dot rule comes from. It is specific to the explainer film's pipeline.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Use the readable table in the look file; run measure_readable.py with painter_survival_fit.json on the plates. Keep the darkest part of a mark at 0.10 to 0.12 or more.
techniques.measured_results: First-round readability: only weeds and moss cushions pass the 60 percent line; soot patches 34 to 40 percent; cracks 12 to 46 percent. How many marks survive an actual paint pass of kit output is NOT known: no call to the painter was made.

techniques.name: Honest checking: fresh checkers and plain reporting
techniques.what_it_is: Each builder's work was re-measured by a fresh checker who had not seen the builder's claims, and the checker's own file (MY_RESULTS.json) was kept beside the builder's. The kit recipe prints every number including what fails.
techniques.why_it_matters: Fresh checkers found false fixer claims, far-fade ticks only visible at 100 percent crops, keepclear covering the whole pavement, and a coat change at amount 0. A model that checks only its own work will report success on failures.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Workflow: build a part, then a separate checker re-draws and re-measures with the same scripts, and lists problems in order of importance; the builder fixes; the checker redraws again. State up front whether covered dots (puddle, rubbish, the kit's own marks) count. Report measured versus judged. Budgets run about double: plan for it.
techniques.measured_results: Round 1 checker listed eight problems in the wetness work; fix round brought P1 count with the kit's own dots left out from 18 to 21 of 22, drawing time from 2.06 to 1.39 times (street), plants in puddles from 36 percent to 0 roots.

techniques.name: The second-place transfer test (Japanese courtyard)
techniques.what_it_is: After the street, the kit was used on the Japanese courtyard (gravel, moss, stone, rake lines, a pond, no roads or soot) with only a new settings file and three looks. It is the proof that the code is not tied to the street.
techniques.why_it_matters: It shows what a third place (a forest village) needs: roles, footfall shapes, keep-clear shapes, habitat, a look, not code. It also shows which parts of the kit still leaked: seven gaps.
techniques.how_to_do_it: The seven gaps listed in the courtyard set file: (1) roof geometry made by Geometry Nodes instances is not seen as ground or wall; (2) no 'wall front' role; (3) role_dials only honoured by the soot layer; (4) lichen's rough_stone_only flag is unread; (5) moss reads brighter than stone; (6) a plinth had to be treated as ground; (7) validate_look timing. Fix these in the plugin's copy of the kit before the village: roofs (thatch, shingle, slate) and plinths are in every village.
techniques.measured_results: Courtyard door test 0 errors: remove gives the scene back (0.001 percent over one step), all master dials at 0 give 0.52 percent over one step (largest 0.0902: the biggest of the three), no leftovers, kit changes 39 percent of dots; each group off alone changes the picture (walls 20, ground 24, growth 1.4 percent). Runoff on the courtyard cannot be tested (it draws nothing there).
techniques.traps_and_failures: The courtyard's 0.52 percent at amount 0 is the weakest dial-zero result: the contract is not exact there.

reusable_code.what: Second settings file as a pattern

techniques.name: Pinned earlier layers and the integrate folder
techniques.what_it_is: The earlier wetness, joint and rubbish layers are kept as hash-identical copies in integrate/legacy_pinned/ and legacy_round2/ and run through harness/legacy_stack.py so that the baseline cannot drift. integrate/tune_log.md records every tune decision.
techniques.why_it_matters: The kit as built depends on these copies for WETNESS, JOINTS and RUBBISH; a plugin that carries the kit must carry (or rewrite) these three layers.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Prefer a clean copy of wetness_layer.py, joint_layer.py and rubbish_layer.py inside the plugin with their licence notes, wired by legacy_stack.py. Do not carry the pinned folder wholesale (it holds street pictures, texture paths and results).
techniques.measured_results: Hash-identical to the street_wet originals.
techniques.traps_and_failures: The three legacy layers hold street numbers (see the rubbish entry) and street texture file names. Do not carry harness/baseline pictures.

reusable_code.what: Puts the earlier layers on the materials in the same hook

checks_and_measures: Amount 0 gives the input exactly (selftests.dial_zero, 16 bit); the courtyard result was 0.52 percent of dots over one step, the weakest.
Isolation: a layer alone changes only the dots of its roles (selftests.isolation).
Determinism: two draws of one state are identical (0.00 percent apart).
Reuse smoke: every registered layer goes in and out without a crash and the materials are restored exactly; apply twice and remove gives the same node count.
Reuse lint: python3 -I harness/lint_no_set_names.py must report 0 hits over apply, masks, harness, walls, ground, growth.
kit.report(): lists 'problems' and 'skipped'; use it to find objects missing wk_<layer>_amount (they read 0 and the layer is silently off).

Joint test over the lighting test set: near and middle bands must reach a minimum contrast, 'seen' share and brightness difference, and never exceed 0.75 contrast (black net). Line: at least 21 of 22 pictures, and nothing that passed before may fail.
Wet look (P2): wet over dry brightness per element and per light; the wet road reads 1.50 times the dry road in EEVEE (aim 1.5).

Not-dark-mush M1: no more than 25 percent of a class darkened by a third. M2: share under plate brightness 0.10 up by at most 3 points on walls and trims, 8 on the rest. M3: mean brightness at least 0.88 of base. M4: spread inside a class at least 0.85. M5: each class stays within 0.90 to 1.00 across distance bands (not met).
Readability at plate size (P3): GOOD / RISKY / LOST via painter_survival_fit (marks 5+ dots at 0.08 contrast, lines 3 dots at 0.11, patches 15+ dots at 0.04); a 60 percent good line per mark kind.
Period (P4): nothing modern in the look (no graffiti, road lines, wheelie bins, print on paper); hue allowed lists and forbidden lists in the look file; lichen exactly 0 on the street.
Zones (P6): no weeds or moss where they must not be (road crown, doorsteps, inside puddles); count plant roots in puddles (0 of 157 after the fix).
Drawing time (P7): kit on over kit off, best of three, within +30 percent (1.32 to 1.39 times measured: not met on the street); first picture after apply under 40 s.
Class and depth passes: a plain flat-number picture per role and a depth picture, used to cut measures by surface and by distance band.
Made-up-picture tests of every measure (test_measures.py, 28 checks) before the measures are trusted.
Calibration per camera: puddle dial against the share of road under water; colour ratios wet over dry per material (tools/23_calibration_driver.py, 23b_puddle_fit.py, 04b_colour_ratios.py).
Grain / speckle: EEVEE grain measured on a flat region (0.0078 at 48 samples; 0.0049 at full plate); look at 100 percent crops, not only shrunk previews.

Suggested preflight for the plugin (my design from these parts): settings file loads; every role matches an object; every ground and wall material has the chain; kit.report has no problems; amount-0 identity on the new scene; lint 0 hits; a mask pack (or the light attributes) exists; wet and dry states both draw; a per-material check that roughness, normal and colour all have a layer (the 'surface-and-wear pass').
gaps_or_unproven: No dirt-track, rut, hoof-print or horse-dropping layer exists. Real ruts need a displacement or sculpted depth; the kit only has footfall lines, polish, puddles in low places and dried rings. Not tested on a dirt road.

No thatch, timber, shingle, wattle-and-daub, cob or mud-wall preset exists: the kit's walls are brick, stone and dressed stone with coal soot. Roofs by geometry-nodes instances are an open gap (courtyard finding 1). The soot layer's coal flavour needs a wood-smoke look.
No forest-floor species: no ferns, brambles, nettles, fallen leaves cover, pine needles, mushrooms or tree roots; growth is low weeds, moss cushions, algae fans, dead grass and small flowers.
No stable, hay, straw-bedding, dung or trough rules; no wood grain weathering (silvering, splits, rot at the foot, woodworm).

The full mask pack is heavy (numpy, OpenCV, BVH tree, 25 to 80 s per scene, a pack folder per scene). A lighter mask route (ray casts into vertex attributes) is only my suggestion and not built or tested.

The painter was never run on kit output; how many marks survive painting is not known. Cycles was not run with the kit (the kit was tuned in EEVEE). The user's rule (Cycles when lit lamps, windows or fires) is untested with the kit.

Wall stain readability at film size fails the 60 percent line: soot, run-off, whitened steps, wall-foot band and rust were mostly lost on dark, edge-on walls in the first integration round; only weeds and moss cushions passed. Not re-measured after the fix round for every mark.

M5 (distance bands stay in range) is not met and cannot be without hurting soot readability; the draw-time line of 1.3 times is not met on the street (1.39) and the 1.5 times first-picture line is not met.
The wall foot / wet wall measurements were tuned on one set of walls; a different wall (timber, plaster) has no measured wet ratios.

rubbish_layer.py, make_places_pictures.py, make_joint_pictures.py, apply_*_to_set.py and the 1926 look carry street numbers and one photo; the generic parts have to be separated before carrying. I read the heads and key parts of rubbish_layer.py, rubbish_pieces.py and make_joint_pictures.py but not every line, and did not read 09 Research or the b02/b04/b09 helpers.

Third-party textures: the street's colour pictures come from Poly Haven (CC0 'square cobblestone', roughness and height pictures); if any are carried into the plugin, keep a note of the source. Code is the person's own; no third-party code found in the kit.
The cart wheel spacing (about 1.6 m between track lines) in the street set is a guess marked in the file; real cart gauge is about 1.4 m. The correct value for a village track is not measured.

Courtyard 7 kit gaps (roof GN instances, wall front, role_dials only in soot, lichen rough_stone_only unread, moss brighter than stone, plinth as ground, validate_look timing) are listed as found, not confirmed fixed.
harness/remote.py still points at the old cached render client and reads a state file; it must be changed to the serverless client. harness/.remote_state.json must not be carried.

inventory.summary:
I read the garden in full: the plan (30), story logs 30 and 31, the notes 32 to 34, the style note (with section 0), the direction note, all four briefs, normal_tools.py, every builder, fixer and checker report inside workflow_result.json (concept, direction, 4 builders, integration, first art check, 4 fixers, second integration, re-check; the second check, on construction, normal maps and money, was lost in a container restart and is null), the first-round test reports (shapes, life, surfaces, light and its lessons file), and the code of all stages. Most code was read in full (wood, roof marks, stones, moss, ground world and tufts, scatter, water material, ripples, maple crown, chain and conflict check, all checkers, measures, render job, regrade, surf_kit, weathering stage); the rest (r_tiles node-group editing, r_walls, wood_deck, wood_frame, stage_life, stage_light bodies, g6_moss remap, stage_fix) I read as docstrings and function lists only. I looked at the before and after sheets and the concept-next-to-final sheet.

What happened, in plain words. The person asked for a garden that keeps its art style but has character: real normal maps, real plank geometry, wear, moss, a bridge that makes sense. Four builders (wood, roof and stone, ground, pond and trees) worked side by side on one starting scene, each only touching its own objects, each with a priority-ordered brief and numbered acceptance tests. One integration step chained them and checked after every stage that nothing foreign changed. A fresh art checker then found: pale clean planks with almost no moss (a builder had claimed 9.8 percent, the checker measured 0.6), one knot stamped on most planks, a pond that only read up close, a darker heavier maple, moss cushions like bean bags, a hairy pine, a moss sticker on the lantern and green stripes on rocks. Four fixers, one per owner, fixed these; a fresh re-check said style kept, more character, bridge makes sense, all yes, with leftovers (smeared lawn colour, heaped moss banks, clean orange deck, 6 of 8 iron straps with a floating nail head). The squint test (0.92 target) was missed at 0.883 and 0.873 and got worse in the fix round.

The most reusable material for the plugin, ranked: (1) the numbers and recipes of the character round (plank, tile, tuft, moss, water, bridge, normal maps), (2) the checkers: structure/support graph, normal-map wiring and direction test light, UV hygiene, fingerprint and ownership diff, picture measures (value range, detail energy per region, flat windows, saturation, squint with a where-it-loses map, silhouette overlap, light-group sum), (3) the stage pattern (owner tags, copy-never-edit-shared, idempotent cleanup that restores what it changed, conflict check after every stage), (4) the workflow shape (concept, direction with briefs, builders in parallel, integrate, two fresh checkers, fixers per owner, integrate, re-check), (5) the render job and regrade scripts, (6) the traps. Almost every code file hard-codes this garden's object names (Rock n, Hall roof, Astra / varied planks) or scratch paths; the genuinely generic ones are normal_tools.py, wood_geo.py, wood_maps.py, r_maps.py, r_stones.py (ray-cast moss caps and cracks), r_moss.py cushion_mesh, g6_tufts.py primitives, g6_scatter.py, g6_common.py cleanup helpers, surf_kit.py, render_job.py, regrade.py, normal_dir_all.py, nm_struct.py, nm_dir.py, fp.py, squint_regions.py. Code that depends on the person's Astra add-on (r_tiles.py node-group editing of the CT roof, g6_moss.remap_astra_moss, stage_life.py scatter, pigment tool) must not be carried. The weakest parts of the evidence: the 12-of-16 reading test was never done blind; moss share on planks was never confirmed by an independent count after the fix; pay figures do not reconcile (ledgers add to about 14,300 card seconds, roughly US$4.4 at US$1.10 an hour, while the story quotes US$10.89 from RunPod's hourly bill); several builder tests were run only on their own stage, and the four fixed stages were never run twice in a row as a chain.

techniques.name: Scene inspection before and after building: floating parts, short posts, buried lights, faces fighting
techniques.what_it_is: Measured checks on the open Blender scene (no drawing needed) that find parts that hover, stop short of what should carry them, sit buried inside another solid, or lie on the same plane as a neighbour so the two surfaces flicker (z-fighting). Plus a flat-colour 'which group is this pixel' picture that counts how much of the frame each group fills, and flat-colour close-ups of the flagged spots.
techniques.why_it_matters: The garden's scene study found faults nobody had seen in the pictures, and they are exactly why the person later said 'the logic behind how the bridge is constructed makes no sense'. A model asked for a village will otherwise build floating cottages, posts that stop short of beams and lights buried in stone, and will not notice, because a picture hides it. The share-of-frame count also tells which things deserve the effort.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1. Open the scene read-only and dump every object (type, collection, evaluated face count, modifiers, materials, UV layers, size), every material (node types, images, how many Bump and Normal Map nodes), lights, world, camera and render settings as JSON. 2. Run the Scenario expert skill's delivery gate (bx_audit.deliverable, profile 'render') on logical GROUPS, not the whole scene: leave out the sky dome, far hills, hidden source objects and prototypes; set the three distances (z-fight, touch, float) to the same value (1 mm); realise instanced roofs on a throwaway copy inside memory; run scatter objects (leaves, moss, pebbles, needles) one by one and expect 'floating' from them because they are separate by design. 3. For every flagged item measure the real gap yourself: bounding box z of the part against a ray cast straight down onto the ground or onto what should carry it. Re-measure even if the plan quotes a number (two studies disagreed). 4. Draw flat-colour Workbench pictures of the flagged spots with every part in its own colour so a human can see the gap. 5. Draw an ID picture at the main camera (Workbench, flat light, no anti-alias, one colour per group of object-name prefixes) and count the pixel share per group; rank work by share times how wrong it looks. 6. After building, run it again and write before and after numbers per repair. Leftover 'floating' on scatters is allowed; anything else is a failure.
techniques.measured_results: Start scene (measured): veranda step floating 23 cm; bridge piers 2.2, 2.5, 5.0 and 4.4 cm short of the boards; wall caps 8.5 cm above the walls (the plan said 6.5); lantern cap and finial floating 14 cm, 7 mm gap at the post, glow box buried inside solid stone (flat white cut-out); 77 deck faces in the same plane as the plinth top (38+13+26); hall plaster against posts 8 coplanar faces; shoji bars 368 coplanar faces; roof carried by nothing (22 cm gap); deck-edge posts 4 cm short of the eave beam (found by the gate, not by the plan). After the shapes stage: main group 19 errors to 2; hall 6 to 0; lantern 2 to 0; bridge 0; roof plus timbers 6 to 1 (the add-on's own tile overlap). Share of the golden-hour frame by group (measured on a flat-colour map): sky and hills 22 percent, ground 16, maple 10, rocks 9, gravel 7, pond and bridge 12, roof 5, plaster and walls 4. On the street: 73 inside-out closed parts found nobody had noticed (69 headframe bars, both winding wheels, 2 trims).
techniques.traps_and_failures: The whole-street gate reported 908 errors because its distances scale with a 3.5 km sky dome; leave out sky and far hills and set 1 mm by hand. The gate skips floating checks above 5000 loose pieces, hence the groups. Scatters always read as floating (82 fragments of Fallen leaves, shrubs, pine pads): not faults, but the report must say why. Shoji rails shortened by 3 mm first made the whole lattice float (fix: keep rail ends on posts, move the outer uprights 2 mm). The lantern point light was inside the glow box, so in Cycles the box blocks it. 'Touching' is not 'carried': a part can touch and still be wrong, so test support and clearance separately. A pass is not art acceptance. Two studies gave different gap numbers (6.5 vs 8.5 cm cap gap), so re-measure first.

techniques.name: Real-world scale and setting facts written as numbers into the brief
techniques.what_it_is: Before building, research how big, what colour and how set the real things are, write each fact as a number with a source and a confidence mark (strong, weak, guess), and use those numbers in the briefs and in the checks.
techniques.why_it_matters: The garden's biggest 'wrong at a glance' faults were facts, not skills: gravel was dark pink-brown (real: pale grey-white granite), maple leaves 20 to 34 cm (real: 4 to 12 cm), rocks sunk only 22 percent (real: half buried, grouped in threes), pond opaque, rake lines too coarse. A small model has no way to know these unless the plugin forces a facts table for the place type.
techniques.how_to_do_it: For the place type, collect: sizes of the main parts, how things are built and set (burial depth, spacing, spans), colour of the real material (as value range), how it ages (where moss, mould, stains form), scale of the damage. Write a table: fact, number, source, confidence. Put the numbers in the brief as limits and in the acceptance tests. Give weak facts a note so builders do not treat them as law. Examples the garden used (from sources and measured on the scene): maple leaf 5 to 12 cm wide, seven lobes; gravel pale grey-white, 2 to 5 cm deep, 9 mm grains (survey of 341 gravel areas in 166 Kyoto temples), four raking patterns, raked 2 to 3 times a month; rake lines about 12 cm apart and about 1.5 cm high (sun 9 degrees above the horizon, so 1 cm already throws a 6 cm shadow; 2.5 to 3 cm looks ploughed); a rake line needs at least 4 mesh squares across (used 5, 2.4 cm cells); rocks buried about a third (reasoned) and never wider at the top than at the base; planks 9 to 17 cm wide, 4.5 to 7 cm thick, gap 5 to 14 mm, bow at most 6 mm, cup 4 mm, twist 1.5 degrees; top-edge wear radius 6 to 12 mm; bridge supports no more than 1.4 m apart; posts 14 cm square with 1.5 cm chamfer; pegs 14 mm; iron strap 3 x 12 cm, 4 mm thick; bollard posts 10 to 20 cm above the deck; roof tile 0.67 x 0.31 m; wall batter 3.5 degrees; cap overhang 10 cm; grass tufts 12 to 70 cm, flowers 1.2 to 2 cm; one readable feature per 5 to 10 cm on timber, 20 to 30 cm on ground, 50 cm on stone and walls.
techniques.measured_results: Sources read in full: Conder 1893 (about 400 KB of text) and a 2015 Kyoto gravel survey; the plan marks gravel colour, grain, stone setting, wall shape and maple and pine facts as strong; roof moss on Japanese tiles, lantern lichen, exact rake pitch and the one-third burial as weak or reasoned. Measured on the scene: buried share of rocks 22 percent before, 34 percent after; pond-edge stones already 55 percent; width ratio top over base 0.66 to 0.82 for all 23 stones.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Weak facts were presented to builders as numbers and got built as if certain (12 cm rake period; checker could not verify). The style note's palette hexes name colours of the RENDERED picture; the shader needs albedo values that give those colours under the scene's light, so they were calibrated on a crop (sunlit plank in the picture was rgb 146,121,107): putting rendered hexes straight into the shader gave pink planks and yellow-olive posts in the first wood round. A real-fact table can also fight the art style (real maple leaf size fine, but realistic grass detail broke the style): facts set size, the style note sets how much detail.

techniques.name: Scanned (photographed) surfaces done right, and why scans alone read as bland
techniques.what_it_is: Put photographed CC0 surfaces (Poly Haven colour, roughness, height) on every material, projected from world position because nothing has UVs, with the scene (not the photographer's sky) deciding overall colour.
techniques.why_it_matters: On the street the person said the scanned bricks 'look incredible'. On the garden the same stack was later judged 'bland and no character': scans give surface texture, not designed shapes, wear or construction. The plugin needs both: scans for base, designed marks and geometry on top.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1. Shortlist scans per role in a JSON (id, real size in metres, why, caution) and pick by DRAWING a test plate of each, not by thumbnail (Hinoki and Dark Planks showed hard board seams that read as cracks on a post; Old Wood Floor won). 2. Download 1k maps (colour sRGB, roughness and height Non-Color) with a generic agent name; keep a licence note (CC0, no credit needed). 3. Colour rule 'normalise': colour_out = target_mean * (scan / scan_mean) ^ contrast (linear), so the scene sets overall colour and the scan only adds small variation; contrast under 1 quiets it. Keep per-scan mean in scan_stats.json. 4. One shared node group per scan, built ONCE per run (rebuilding it cuts the wires of every material already using it: the first plate sheet had four black cubes). Two modes: 'planar' from above with a second look at another size, angle and shift mixed by low-frequency noise so no tile repeats, and 'tri' box projection weighted by the normal (power sharpness 5), with a grain axis so boards run the right way. 5. Per-object variation from the object's Random value (offset in metres and a brightness factor); per-board tint for plank tone materials. 6. Use the roughness map; use the scan's height only as a bump (rake lines stay real geometry). 7. Find objects by name pattern or by the custom property garden_role, map to a family, replace 'placeholder' materials. 8. Measure the plank direction in the scene instead of trusting the plan (it said along y; all 8 runs measured along x). 9. Pack the images into the .blend before the final save (about 62 pictures, a packed real file about 35 MB) and re-open to prove it draws the same.
techniques.measured_results: Preview brightness on a 0 to 255 display scale, before to after: roof band 44 to 64 (5th percentile 2 to 14), gravel 100 to 140, bridge boards 85 to 109, garden wall 143 to 113, whole picture 85 to 93; edge over centre brightness stayed 1.08 at that stage. 114 materials rebuilt (all tagged garden_owner=surfaces), 20 left alone (moss tones, bamboo, leaves, needles, water, hills, glow). Previews 960 x 640 took 3 to 4 s each on the card. A saved test file re-opened without re-running the stage drew the same hero picture.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Kit moss on scans came out pale lime on stones (four tuning rounds; the pale-mint blotches came from patch moss, not wall growth), then read as polka dots. Roof scan tile rows do not line up with the instanced tiles. Ground used from-above projection, steep sides could stretch (not seen). Scans are 1k, soft at 100 percent. Tiling is a danger on a 16 percent ground area (macro variation needed; the smeared lawn colour was still the worst leftover at the end). Do not mix the add-on's pigment tool with scans on the same object. After the character round the scan stack was the 'bland' part: they have no designed marks.

techniques.name: Real normal maps: UV first, soft height, right direction, wired in, checked
techniques.what_it_is: Turn designed height pictures (or blurred scan heights) into tangent-space normal maps in the OpenGL convention (green = up the picture), give every object a UV map, wire Image(Non-Color) to Normal Map(Tangent, uv_map set) to the shader, and prove with a test light that the lit side is the right side.
techniques.why_it_matters: The person asked 'are there any normal maps used?'. Answer found by opening the scene: none. 0 Normal Map nodes, 0 Displacement nodes, 175 Bump nodes (strength 0.5 to 0.55 on most timber, stone and ground), and none of the 132 mesh objects had a UV map, so a normal map in the usual way was not even possible. A small model will say 'bump is fine'; the plugin has to make it build and check real ones, and must not let a flipped map through (a flipped green channel makes every groove a ridge).
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1. UV first: write a UV layer named UVMap by script. Box UV per face (the two axes not along the face's dominant normal, divided by a tile size in metres, so 1 UV unit equals the real size of one map tile) for stones, walls, timber; planar (x,y)/tile for ground and water; planks: u along the length, v across, plus a random offset per plank; roof tiles: put the UV on the PROTOTYPE tile (instances inherit it: proven for 688 of 688 instances with a checker texture). Flip u on faces whose UV winding is clockwise so no island is mirrored. 2. Height picture, white = high: from a blurred scan height (blur 3 to 11 px at 1024) or drawn with numpy (periodic noise in Fourier space so it tiles; grooves as periodic functions). Keep it soft and large: nothing under about 5 mm, no micro pores. 3. Calibrate by slope, not by guess: scale so the steepest 1 percent of the slope tilts the normal about 26 to 34 degrees, or choose the strength for a target mean slope (0.065 glaze, 0.045 plaster, 0.11 stone, 0.28 moss pillows) or RMS slope. 4. height_to_normal(h, strength, tile=True) with wrap-around differences so it tiles. 5. Blender 5.2.2 gotcha: set colorspace_settings = 'Non-Color' right after images.new and BEFORE writing pixels; setting it afterwards wipes a generated image to black. 6. Material: UV Map to Mapping (scale to tile) to Image (Non-Color, Cubic, Repeat) to Normal Map (Tangent, uv_map = UVMap, strength 0.45 to 1.5, usually 0.8 to 1.0) to Principled Normal. Keep an old scan Bump only if it is capped at 0.3 and its Normal input is fed by the Normal Map node. Max 4 image maps per material. 7. For long grain maps use a 2 x 2 mirror tile with the red or green channel sign flipped on the mirrored copies (seamless, shows four different boards); each plank takes a random window and half are turned 180 degrees (rotation, never mirror). Knots go in a separate 16-bit height picture used with a Bump node on top (8-bit gave contour rings). 8. Pack the images before saving. 9. Test light (below in checks): flat plane, default UVs, orthographic camera straight down, sun 30 degrees up from +X then from +Y, Cycles CPU 32 samples; correlation between the fine luminance and the decoded normal (red for +X, green for +Y) must be at least +0.25; the same render with green flipped must give a NEGATIVE value on +Y so the test can fail; also run once on a bump: NORMAL_DIRECTION line.
techniques.measured_results: Self-test line: NORMAL_DIRECTION PASS (right/left under sun from +X 0.804 vs 0.158; top/bottom under sun from +Y 0.806 vs 0.156; flipped-green detected). After the round: 85 materials with a Normal Map from 17 pictures (wood 14 to 18, roof 39 to 41, ground 21, pond 6), mean blue 0.979 to 1.000, red and green 0.50, share of pixels with blue below 0.5 is 0, UV layer present on every user, 0 violations in the re-opened combined scene. Per-map correlations (+X / +Y): plank top +0.35/+0.91 (builder) , glaze 0.95/0.97, plaster 0.96/0.97, stone 0.97/0.97, moss 0.99/0.99, pebble 0.99/0.99, ripple 0.94/0.94 (rings brighter on the sun side in all 5 spots, 0.99), swell 0.39/0.40 (drawn at test strength x8). Integrating the plank normal map back to height gave +0.88 agreement with the groove picture (grooves are grooves, not ridges). Detail energy effect: first ground map too strong (lawn corrugated, grass-box energy 10.5), cut to 0.85 strength: 4.17 to 4.39.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Test plane size: for long thin maps (plank 4096 x 1024, post 1024 x 2048) a wrong plane aspect made the correlation read about 0; the integrator reported 'plank map fails in X (+0.061)', the re-check showed it was wrong (+0.55 with the right plane), but also that the plank map has almost no X slope because grain runs along the plank, so the X test carries little information for it. The flipped control did NOT fail for the water swell map (+0.87): its direction rests on the main test only. 'Leftover bumps above 0.3' counted by one script (60) were the weathering kit's inner nodes, not old scan bumps. Seven pond-edge stones kept 40 to 73 percent mirrored UV faces (cause not found; lighting looked right). Box UV seams on dense CT stone meshes were never inspected at 100 percent. The knot-through-blend-maths design broke the rule that the Normal Map node reads its picture directly; redo as mirror tile plus Bump knots. The builders' own direction tests were never re-run on the combined scene by the integrator (the re-check re-ran 8 maps).
