checks_and_measures: PREFLIGHT CANDIDATE, normal maps: every material of a visible mesh has a Normal Map node (space TANGENT, uv_map set) fed by an Image Texture whose colour space is Non-Color, image at least 1024 px, mean blue at least 0.85, mean red and green 0.50 +- 0.03, the Normal output reaches a Principled BSDF Normal input (checked forward through nodes), at most 4 image maps per material. Measured on the garden: 85 materials from 17 images, 0 violations (checker2/scripts/nm_struct.py).

PREFLIGHT CANDIDATE, UVs: every mesh object using a normal-mapped material has a UV layer with the named UV map; mirrored-face share per UV layer at most 2 percent (checker2/scripts/uv_check.py; 7 pond-edge stones failed at 40 to 73 percent).
PREFLIGHT CANDIDATE, bump leftovers: no old Bump node above strength 0.3 unless its Normal input is fed by the Normal Map node (kit-internal nodes excluded).

NORMAL DIRECTION: flat plane, default UVs, orthographic camera straight down, sun 30 degrees up from +X then from +Y, Cycles CPU 32 samples, float EXR; correlation of fine luminance (picture minus box blur) with the decoded normal red (sun +X) and green (sun +Y) at least +0.25, and the same render with green flipped must be negative (normal_tools.check_direction prints NORMAL_DIRECTION PASS; fix/final/normal_dir_all.py does every image of a saved scene). Use the right plane aspect for long thin maps. The flipped control did not fail for water swell, so it is weak for very small slopes.

STRUCTURE: contact graph from parts to ground (rest patch of at least 16 cm2 within 8 mm); every plank on at least 2 supports, every stringer on 2 bearers or a sill, every bearer on 2 posts, every post on a footing within 1 cm, no unsupported span over 1.4 m, no part floating (nearest support under 5 mm); pegs touch their plank within 1 mm; walkability rays every 5 cm hit a plank top, steps at most 2 cm, slope at most 1:20, deck width 1.05 +- 0.05, longest miss one gap (checker2/scripts/struct.py, seat.py).

FLOATING AND FIGHTING FACES: delivery gate at 1 mm on groups (hall, bridge, lantern, walls, stones, steps, ground and water, roof realised), scatters alone and explained; count coplanar overlapping faces (z-fighting), floating fragments, inside-out closed parts (signed volume negative).

PLANK CHARACTER (all planks): width std at least 1.0 cm and range at least 5 cm, thickness std at least 3 mm, gap 5 to 14 mm std at least 2 mm, at least 85 percent with bow, cup or twist over 2 mm or 0.5 degrees and none over 15 mm or 3 degrees, every top edge bevelled at least 5 mm, at least 10 percent chipped, 15 percent with end check, 6 to 9 percent replaced, no two planks identical in shape (hash after removing position and rotation), at least 25 pegs and 6 cramps on a bridge, at most 400 vertices a plank.
DECK: 14 or more rows, at least two board lengths, neighbouring joints at least 40 cm apart, visible thickness at least 4.5 cm, nosing, deck top within +-0.005 of target.

WEAR COVERAGE (to count in rendered pixels, not only in a mask picture): moss plus mould 4 to 12 percent of visible plank area, concentrated near posts, rocks, water and shade, at most half as much on the walking line; walking line lighter than the average plank by 0.02 to 0.06 luminance; roof moss 4 to 10 percent and lichen 1 to 3 percent of visible roof pixels; at least 6 drip stains, 3 slipped, 6 chipped and 1 broken or missing tile all seen from the main camera; walls per long wall at least 4 cracks, 2 plaster-loss patches, 3 chipped cap tiles; lantern at least 2 cracks and a chipped cap corner; at least 5 big rocks with one soft moss cap each; at least 6 rocks with collars.

GROUND: at least 8 different tuft meshes, scale range at least 3:1, at least 3 tints, seed heads on 15 percent or more, blades at least 6 mm at the base (fix used folded leaves 26 to 91 mm), tuft triangles at most 2 times the old count, flowers 20 to 60 covering under 0.3 percent, one bare worn path in each main view, soil lip and tufts at kerbs, every leaf within 1 cm of its surface and none on deck, bridge or water; lawn hue within 6 degrees and luminance within 0.03.

WATER: bed visible within 40 cm of the bank; edge-band luminance spread at least 1.5 times the middle band; middle darker than edge by at least 0.04 and within +0.03 of the old; at least 3 ripple spots, 5 notched pads of different sizes, 3 flowers, 3 iris stems; algae rim on every pond-edge stone that touches water; no turquoise or violet.

TREES: pads 5 to 8, at least 4 branches visible between pads at the main view (7 plus trunk in the fix), canopy area within 10 percent and overlap at least 0.75, leaf count within 20 percent, leaf colour distribution unchanged (rank-map to the old quantiles), maple box energy 7.7 to 9.5; pine 5 to 8 flat discs, thickness at most 0.35 of diameter, needle count within 20 percent, wall shadow unchanged.
VALUE RANGE: main view median within +-0.03 of the reference, 5 and 95 percent within +-0.03, 99 percent not above the cap, mean saturation within 0.36 to 0.44 (reference garden 0.399).

DETAIL ENERGY per region: between 0.9 times the reference and the smaller of 1.4 times and 10 (mean absolute difference of 8-bit luminance minus a 2 px Gaussian blur). Garden reference roof 8.0, bridge 5.4, grass 3.6, maple 8.4, sand 7.5, wall 3.4, rock 3.6. Use object-mask regions for a new place.
FLAT COLOUR: no 96 x 96 window (step 48) below the sky outside hills, paper and glow with luminance std under 0.010, under 2 percent under 0.014 (garden: 0 of 931).

PALETTE: at most 1 percent of pixels outside the accent colour with saturation above 0.70 (garden was already 1.45 before and ended 1.76), at most 0.3 percent turquoise outside sky and hills, no pure-white patch over 30 pixels outside the glowing parts.

SQUINT: SSIM of 12 px blurred luminance against the previous picture at least 0.92 (judgement, missed at 0.883 and 0.873); always report where it loses points per region with a heat map, and at 24 and 36 px.
SILHOUETTES: IoU and share-of-old-shape-covered per object group at each camera, at least 0.85 (decide which yardstick counts).
LIGHT GROUPS: sum of Combined_<group> layers within 2 percent of the picture (undenoised exact), main finals; render under 90 s on a 4090 with GPU in use and under 12 GB card memory.

OWNERSHIP AND IDEMPOTENCE: stage alone on the start scene changes nothing owned by others (vertex count and position hash, material node and link counts, light linking, collections); new objects carry garden_owner and garden_role and sit in G6 <owner>; nothing renamed or deleted; run twice gives the same object count and file size within 2 percent (but also test on an already staged scene); plain and reverse order both 0 violations.
READING TEST: at 50 percent scale a blind reviewer names at least 12 of 16 character features (never done blind; 7 to 11, then 9 to 13 by non-blind checkers).

DESIGNED-IN TEST: 100 percent crops of bridge, roof, grass and pond next to the old crops show the same picture language, few big clean marks, nothing finer, sharper or noisier than the big rocks and the lantern.

REAL-FACT CHECKS: maple leaves 5 to 12 cm; gravel pale (albedo near 0.46 to 0.6) 2 to 5 cm deep; rake lines about 12 cm with at least 4 mesh squares per line; rocks buried about a third and never wider at the top than the base; stepping stones 3 to 6 cm above ground with at least 10 cm gaps; planks and spans as listed in the plank technique.

PERSONAL DETAILS AND SECRETS: grep all new code, notes and requests for the person's e-mail, name parts, '.runpod', keys, tokens, endpoint ids, machine ids, volume ids; a price lookup once printed an account holder's name (not copied); the helper that sent an e-mail address to Wikipedia in the kit's download scripts is the earlier lesson (log 28).
MONEY: ledger row per paid call; Fal request history equals the ledger one to one; RunPod seconds from the job ledger; record balance before long jobs.

HOUSEKEEPING: free disk at least 0.4 GB; keep .blend and EXR on the store; JPG previews under 400 KB; pictures named '31 <Name> - <what it shows>.jpg'; no leftover preview cameras in the delivered scene (48 were left).
gaps_or_unproven: No blind reviewer ever ran the reading test (12 of 16 features); the checkers saw the list. The 'designed, not photographic' 100 percent crop review was by eye only, mostly by the same helper that built or measured.

Moss and mould share on planks after the fix (11.6 percent from a mask picture) was NOT independently confirmed: the checker's colour count cannot tell moss from greenish wood. The original claim (9.8 percent) was disproved (0.6 percent).

Squint test: 0.92 was a judgement; every fixer missed it and the fix round made it worse; nobody decided whether to follow the concept or the squint test. Silhouette IoU versus share-of-old-shape-covered not decided.

The second check (construction, normal maps, money) was lost in a container restart and re-ran only partly as the final re-check (supports, normal-map wiring and 8 maps, ownership, money); structure, walkability and ownership were not re-run by it.

The four fixed stages were chained once; running the whole chain twice on one scene (idempotence of the chain) and pictures from the reverse order were never done; order independence is not exact (a few thousand triangles).
Box UV seams on the dense CT stone meshes were never inspected at 100 percent; seven pond-edge stones kept mirrored UV faces (cause not found).

The flipped-green control did not fail for the water swell normal map, and the plank grain map has almost no X slope, so the X direction check is weak for those two; direction proof for them rests on the +Y test and on the groove-agreement check.

Painted look (flat-shaded planes, pigment tool, passages) was not carried into the character round; only the realistic look has the new geometry. Painted-stack code (painted_stack.py: passages with firm and lost edges, quiet_grain) is unmeasured against the person's rules beyond by-eye checks.

RunPod money does not reconcile: ledgers add to about 11,354 s plus about 2,900 s without ledger (about 4 hours, about US$4.4 at US$1.10 an hour); the story quotes US$10.89 by RunPod's hourly bill; whether cold starts are billed is unknown.

The stall cause is unclear: low balance (US$0.13) explained 07:31 to 08:30 for the helper, the integrator saw the same stall from 07:37 and recovered after purging and resubmitting (it did not know the balance); a unified rule 'check balance first' is a hypothesis proven by one case.
Tool/permission facts from the run (not from files): sub-agents could not write report .md files; the plugin must tell agents to return reports as structured text and save evidence as json or txt.

Judgements about those files come from docstrings, function lists and the reports.

Third-party and personal code: the delivery gate needs the Scenario expert skill's bx_audit (MIT; licence file and a source note must travel with it); r_tiles.py, g6_moss.remap_astra_moss, stage_life.py, life/ship/addon_copy and the pigment tool depend on the person's Astra add-on and must not be copied into the plugin (rules may be restated in own words).

Almost every code file hard-codes this garden's object names (Rock n, Hall roof, Astra / varied planks, Life / pond bed), hero-pixel boxes (700,300,1500,500 etc.), coordinates (bridge nodes, pond box, ground extents) or scratch paths under /tmp/claude-0/...; the files named as generic are generic in algorithm, but each needs a settings layer (names, regions, tile sizes, waterline z) before the plugin can use it for another place.

Not tested at all: another Blender version than 5.2.2, another card than RTX 4090, EEVEE with these materials, animated or moving cameras, any place other than the garden (no village, stable, cottage, cart rut or timber-framed medieval prop has been built with these tools; dirt-road wear, ruts, hoofprints, hay, barrels, weeds in cracks are NOT covered by anything in the garden except the worn bare-earth path mask and the generic tuft and moss methods).

inventory.summary: I read the surface-making work and the seven Scenario skills and changed no file. Read in full: the cookbook start page and the seamless, relief, baking and checking, geometry, painted look, shapers and pattern-maker guides; the new-surface checklist; the Reuse guide; the project story (all 31 logs, logs 1-17 closely); the layer contract (interface.md); the slate layers Lessons and wood-from-maps Lessons; the Scenario texturing, uv-baking, geometry-nodes, lighting and expert skill pages and the expert bpy checklist; the log 23 note; lib/ headers and function lists (recipe_tools, bake_harness, sweep_tools, make_strip, description_audit in full); and the door-bake JSON files in skills_test/22b. Only headers or guide text, not code: the layer files, the reuse-trial boxes (grime, cracks, knots, grain, rivets, edge light, ruts, stones, soil, facets), the research experiment scripts, the export and previs skills. Not opened: wood_from_displacement 08 Recipe, mask_test notes, reuse_trials 00 Inventory, the uv-baking, lighting and geometry-nodes procedures.md files, blender-5.2-deltas.md, third-party/, and the code of kits/weathering and street_wet (I know them only from story-log summaries). Nothing was run by me, so every number is one I read from a file; each entry says MEASURED (a file records a run) or JUDGED (a person or checker looked, or I reasoned). Main ideas for a place builder: (1) make every tile repeat at the source and prove it with several tests, because each test has blind spots; (2) sizes in tile units, big areas by tile count, never by copying the position; (3) know what the height map means before building relief; (4) colour maps on Standard view and data maps on Raw, 16-bit heights; (5) Bevel, AO and Pointiness wear shows only in Cycles, so bake it or use a curvature attribute before EEVEE; (6) split a surface into layers with a fixed bundle, own seeds, and an Amount of 0 that means exactly nothing; (7) never trust one score, because the references' own tools reward flat pictures and tuned settings; use a fresh-eyes checker with a numbered fault list; (8) check wear at the size and under the lights a viewer sees. Gaps that matter most for a forest village: no layered recipe exists for thatch, cobbles or a dirt road with two wheel tracks and a hoof-path (mud's ruts came out as narrow winding lines, not broad braided bands); every layered tile was tuned to painted references and reads cleaner, flatter and more regular than them up close; nobody has used these tile recipes on a real 3D mesh at world scale; and the EEVEE behaviour of the layered tile recipes was never measured.

techniques.name: Seamless patterns at the source: donut trick, whole counts, wrapped piece numbers, seamless warp
techniques.what_it_is: Blender's own Noise, Voronoi, Wave, Magic, Gabor and Gradient do not repeat at a tile edge, even at whole-number Scale. A tile repeats only if it is built to. Four ways work. (a) The donut trick: turn u and v into two circles and read 4D Noise or 4D Voronoi on them, so walking off the right edge lands on the left edge. (b) Whole-number layouts: bricks, rows, planks, bands counted so they fill the tile exactly. (c) A piece number that wraps, so a half brick on the right edge gets the same random shade as its other half on the left. (d) A warp made of seamless noise only.
techniques.why_it_matters: Roads, walls, roofs and boards are one small tile laid over a big area. A seam shows as a straight line every few metres. Example: plain 3D Noise at Scale 5 has a seam number of 20.5 where 1.0 means no seam; the donut version has 0.87.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) Noise or cells: Texture Coordinate UV -> Separate XYZ -> multiply u and v by 2 pi -> cos and sin of each -> Combine XYZ(cos u, sin u, cos v) into Vector, sin v into W -> multiply by Scale / (2 pi) -> add Seed to W -> Noise or Voronoi set to 4D. Scale then means features across one tile. rt.tileable_noise_group() and rt.tileable_voronoi_group() build this. 2) To stretch a pattern give it two counts (builder.tnoise(across, up), tvoronoi(across, up)); never scale the position first. Example from the metal build: rust 44 features across and 30 up; thin upright streaks 260 across and 6 up. 3) Voronoi: use 4 or more cells across, better 6 or more. 4) Bricks or planks: Scale / Brick Width whole, Scale / Row Height whole, rows even when staggered; wrap the piece number (Floored Modulo by pieces across and rows) before White Noise (tileable_bricks_group, builder.rows_and_columns). 5) Wave bands: Scale = k x pi/10; Magic: k x 2 pi/5; Checker: even Scale only; Wave rings, straight Gradient and Gabor never tile. 6) Warp: seamless noise -> Subtract 0.5 -> Scale 0.05 to 0.3 -> Add to the position -> the pattern maker. Never use Wave's own Distortion. 7) Shapes drawn from a list: fold each shape's middle into the tile first, then draw a copy one tile over wherever it touches an edge (up to 9 copies), and let traced patches join across the edge. 8) For anything baked use UV coordinates; Generated on the bake square is (u, v, 0.5) and an unconnected Vector input is Generated. 9) Stretch noise with Map Range before cutting it: raw noise only spans about 0.25 to 0.73.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED (cookbook seamless guide, research tables): seam numbers on 512-dot pictures: Noise 20.5, Voronoi 34.6, Wave bands 24.4, Magic 72, Gabor 13.9, Gradient 470; donut Noise 0.87 and donut Voronoi 1.07, identical after moving one whole tile (difference 0.00000). Cost about 30 percent more render time (1254 dots, Detail 8: 2.5 / 8.7 / 34.9 s plain at 4 / 16 / 64 samples; 3.2 / 12.1 / 46.5 s donut). Mapping Scale (1, 4, 1) before the donut draws the same strip four times (quarters differ by 0.85 steps against 45.63 for a real tile); Scale (1, 2.5, 1) gives a seam (wrap jump 39.77, biggest ordinary row jump 7.34). Brick Scale 4, width 0.5, row height 0.25 gives 8 across and 16 rows, seam 0.03; Scale 4.3 gives 13 to 17. Brick colour output with whole numbers still seams (2.43, peak 5.2); with wrapped numbers 0.03. Wave Scale 3 x pi/10 seam 0.08. Warp with plain noise: wrap jump 19.66 against biggest ordinary jump 2.52; with donut noise it stays inside the ordinary range. Wave Distortion: seam 6.7, peak 52. Cell-count shortfall by arithmetic: 1 percent at 12 cells across, 4.5 percent at 6, 36 percent at 2. JUDGED: 2 and 3 cells across look curved and uneven; 8 and up look like normal Voronoi.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Scaling position before the donut repeats or seams the tile. Few cells distort. Typing numbers into an unconnected Vector input does nothing (identical pictures). A different random pattern than plain noise, so ramps and cuts tuned on plain noise must be retuned. Brick node's Colour output still seams with whole numbers. Wave Distortion and plain-noise warps break the tile. Slate shapes running past the tile made 18 percent of dots differ in the half-tile test until each shape's middle was folded in first. Wood's traced patches left a colour seam (edge jump 12 times normal) until patches merged across the edge. Brick's slow waves (110, 170, 260 dots) do not divide 1254; the fix (lengths that divide the tile) was proposed but NOT TESTED. Repairs after the fact (cross-fades, mirrors, patching a finished picture) all had side effects: ghost doubles, symmetry, ghost bricks. The donut on a non-square tile and Voronoi features other than F1 on the donut are NOT TESTED (wood's Distance to Edge on a stretched donut drew diagonal criss-cross lines).

techniques.name: Proving a tile or area repeats: five tests and their blind spots
techniques.what_it_is: A set of checks for 'no seam and no copies'. The half-tile test (bake once, bake again slid half a tile, compare with the first rolled by half, with a wrong-roll control); the wrap jump compared with every ordinary jump in the same direction; first column against last column; a 2 x 2 look and a zoom on the crossing; and the exact test that moves the recipe by whole tiles.
techniques.why_it_matters: Each test alone passed real faults in this project. Example: the brick area bug (a hard-coded 1254 made the 2508 bake show a quarter of the picture) passed the half-tile test because both bakes had the bug; only first-versus-last column (correlation 0.23 against 0.9 for neighbours) found it.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) Half-tile test: bake with a shift of (0.5, 0.5), compare with the first bake rolled by half; always run the same comparison rolled a few dots wrong as a control. 2) Wrap jump: take the jump across the wrap edge and set it beside the jumps of every ordinary pair of neighbouring columns (and rows), in the same direction; a seamless tile has the wrap jump inside that range. 3) First against last column and row, compared with neighbouring pairs. 4) Make a 2 x 2 copy and zoom on the crossing, and roll by half and look at the cross. 5) For a shader recipe, the exact test: photograph it moved by +1 whole tile, up, both, and by (-3, +2); it must not change. 6) Turn grain off or make it slide with the shapes, and turn off the 8-bit dither when you want exact zeros. 7) For an area, compare its quarters with each other at every shift: a copy gives 1.0, new content 0.04 to 0.37. 8) For a recipe built of layers, also run each layer alone through the same test.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED half-tile results (mean difference in steps of 255 / dots over 40 steps / wrong-roll control): brick 0.36 / 0.0 percent / 35.9 percent; slate 0.67 / 0.0 / 13.2; wood 0.74 / 0.00 / 14.7; metal 0.56 / 0.0 / 5.4 (mean 16.2); gravel at 1254 dots 0.78 / 0; mud 0.76 with 0.98 percent over 8 steps (a different cut). Plain 3D noise fails the exact test (average difference 0.060 colour, 0.084 height). Six builds' 2 x 2 areas: wrap jump 0.75 to 1.06 of an ordinary jump; quarter match 0.04 to 0.37 (a copy gives 1.0); tile repeated 2 x 2 gives quarters differing 0.48 to 0.49, tile count 2 gives 32.5 to 41.4. The slate layers' half-tile numbers: 1.6 steps raw, 0.31 after a 2-dot blur, 15 for the control. The 1.6 was found by the honesty check to be Blender's default 8-bit dither on about 57 percent of dots, not the recipe.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Seam number false alarms: a perfect Checker with Scale 8 scores 72.98 and a perfect saw-tooth Wave 92 (a real edge sits on the tile border); false pass: a Checker with Scale 7 scores 0.17. References themselves score 1.69 to 2.49. Grain hides seams (brick traced L fell from 2.11 to 1.0 with grain 0.14, no change at the seam). Mixing sideways and up-down jumps gave 3.71 for upright wood bands that were really 0.91 when compared in the same direction. One line against a whole-picture average reads 1.38 to 1.65 on seamless warped bands. A crop of a bigger area is not a tile (tiling score 0). The half-tile test cannot see content made before the slide, and it passes a copied seam (wood L2w passed at 0.47 while its edge jump was 3.72). Grain fixed in space (not slid) gave a false 10 steps for wood, 3.28 for slate, 3.2 for metal (0.71 with grain 0). Compare like with like: gravel's numbers were measured at 512 dots though the text said 1254; mud counted dots over 8 steps, others over 40. A control that does not reach 1.0 flatters the result (wood's was 0.972 because the shrunk tile was 313.5 dots; with whole dots it is 1.000). Wood: a recipe with 5 rows and a rule needing an even row count gave 2 of 3 touching boards the same source row across the tile edge; found only by counting.

techniques.name: Bigger areas without copies: tile count, sizes in tile units, any picture size
techniques.what_it_is: To cover a bigger area with new content, multiply every feature count and layout count by k; never multiply the position (that copies the tile). Measure every size as a share of the tile, so the same recipe draws the same shapes at 512, 1254 or 2508 dots.
techniques.why_it_matters: A village road, wall or roof is much bigger than one tile. Copies show the same dark spot every few metres; the eye finds a repeated knot or crack at once.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) Write the tile size into the settings and read it everywhere; never type 1254 in code. 2) For an area of k x k tiles multiply: donut feature counts, brick or slate rows and pieces per row, planks, stones, clods, knots, rivets. 3) Keep colour tables and size spreads unchanged. 4) Divide warp amounts by k (my reasoning; NOT TESTED). 5) Settings counted in dots of the picture (normal strength, height blur, pixel-filter width, per-dot grain) must be scaled by hand with the picture size; Bump Distance, donut counts and Brick Scale are already in tile units. 6) For a place, pick a tile size in metres per surface (example: 2 m for cobbles), compute Tile Count = area width / tile size and write it in the settings (my reasoning for a place; the cookbook proved the idea on 2 x 2 areas of six surfaces and a 4 x 4 slate area).
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED: slate 2508-dot area (16 rows of 12 slates) wrap jump 0.75 and 0.58 of an ordinary jump, strongest quarter match 0.371, bake 131 s. Brick 24 courses of 8: 1.04 and 0.99, 144 s. Wood 10 planks 232.6 s. Metal 298 s. Mud 114,875 shapes 228 s. Gravel 252.6 s. Brick at 1254 against 2508 shrunk: SSIM 0.994 (mean difference 0.7 steps); 512 enlarged 0.754. Bake times at 512 / 1254 / 2508: brick 25.3 / 33.7 / 76.3 s; slate 13.6 / 31.6 / 100.7 s. Gravel's slope stayed 0.374 / 0.367 / 0.352 when strength scaled with size. Slate pixel filter: width 2 = 0.5-dot blur, width 4 about 0.9, so ask for about 4 x the blur. NOT TESTED: a 4 x 4 area on any surface except slate; shader-only whole surface at tile count 2.
techniques.traps_and_failures: A hidden constant (the brick generator divided by 1254) photographed only a quarter of a 2508 description. A bigger picture adds crisper edges, not detail. Stones keep their dot size in a bigger area, so they look half as big at a 1254 preview. A slow whole-picture measure written per column took hours at 5016 dots; compute whole-picture numbers once. Disk: a 2508-dot 16-bit height is 14 MB, a 5016-dot colour picture 31 MB. A preview at 384 dots blurs about 3.3 times more of the tile than the same pixel-filter width at 1254.

techniques.name: Non-repeating big surfaces from one source map (pieces and windows)
techniques.what_it_is: When a map (a scan or a painted picture) is the raw material, cut it into pieces along its own separators and let nodes pick a random piece for every board or brick, with flips, small zoom, tone changes and painted-out landmarks. One switch gives an exactly repeating tile or a big area.
techniques.why_it_matters: Scanned photo surfaces are the realistic route (Scenario: scanned set plus masks for realism). A big road or wall made from one scan repeats unless this is done. The street already used photo surfaces from Poly Haven.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) Measure where separators, rare features (knots) and stains are, and whether the map wraps. 2) Cut from the middle of one gap to the middle of the next, never gap-top to gap-top. 3) List the landmarks (about twelve) and find clean grain to show instead; check each by eye. 4) Make every random number from the position with White Noise 4D as a hash; the same node tree gives a tile (numbers repeat) or an area (salted differently). 5) Make neighbours take different source rows on purpose and count it; with a wrapping tile the number of rows must be even. 6) Hide every cut with a made-on-purpose joint in the material's own style (a stepped crack, not a straight line). 7) Read colour and height at the same position; make the normal from the arranged height, not from a re-arranged normal map (a flipped piece would point the slopes wrong). 8) Bend each window a little but cap the shift (8 dots) and measure source dots per picture dot.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED (wood): same-kind 0.839 against 0.665 for the best new tile of the earlier pure-node wood (partly because the tile is built from the reference's own dots). Twin test: 0 to 2 percent of pieces have a twin in the 4 x 4 area, against 14 to 18 percent in round 1 and 100 percent for a plain repeat. Each used dot of the map appears about 30.7 times in 16 tiles; 12 landmarks shown about 64 times. Touching pairs sharing a source row: 19 percent in round 1, 1.1 percent after the fix. Magnified blocks after capping the shift: 1.6 percent down to 0.0009. Seam measure of the result 1.08 and 1.12; the uploaded map 2.76 and 3.97. JUDGED by the look checker: still reads as stacked stone, not long boards (boards about 2.5 times longer than high, straight full-height joints), with a soft dark dash and a few hard round tone patches where landmarks were painted out.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Straight joints and short boards read as a brick wall. Boards cannot be longer than the source row. Stain stamps cut from the map can contain the knot. A soft cross-fade paint-out left smudges; a hard ragged edge with a well matched ring worked. 'At most one knot per row' means one per 4 tiles of row in an area. A written rule is a claim: count it (19 percent against 'never'). Eight-bit debug pictures carry dither that splits board numbers into hundreds of pieces; read exact numbers from the 16-bit height. A big sideways shift fading out at an edge squeezes the picture up to 2 times. Stronger variation lowers the same-kind score.

techniques.name: Relief: bump, normal map and displacement, with the numbers that matter
techniques.what_it_is: Height map: grey picture, white high. Normal map: picture of which way each dot tilts. Bump node: turns a height into a tilt at render time (shading only). Displacement: really moves the surface so outlines and shadows change.
techniques.why_it_matters: Dirt roads, cobbles, planks and thatch all need relief that survives raking light. Blender's default Bump Distance (0.001) is nearly flat, so a plain 'add bump' looks smooth.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) Strength = how many dots tall white stands above black; Bump Distance = strength / dots across (units: tile widths on a 1 x 1 tile). On a real object Distance is the real height of the 0..1 range in scene units (Scenario's rule: lower Distance, not Strength). For a 1 x 1 tile use 0.02 to 0.1 for clear relief; the six references work out at 0.004 to 0.008. 2) Hard steps (mortar, joints): Filter Width 1 to 4; smooth heights: 0.1. 3) A height reused in a Bump node needs Image extension Repeat. 4) Displacement: Height -> Displacement node (Midlevel 0.5, Scale = true depth) -> Material Output Displacement; set material.displacement_method to DISPLACEMENT or BOTH (default is Bump Only and the node then does nothing); mesh must be fine: a dense grid or Subdivision Surface with Adaptive Subdivision and Dicing Rate 1 to 2. Distance moved = (Height - Midlevel) x Scale. 5) Normal map: Non-Color, OpenGL (green up) for Blender; tell the convention apart from the map alone (the correlation of the sideways slope's change down the rows against the up-down slope's change along columns is -1.00 for OpenGL and +1.00 for DirectX) or against the height slope (+0.94 OpenGL, -0.94 DirectX). 6) Height in 16 bits, Non-Color, Raw. 7) Normal from height by plain slope: red = -strength x (right - left)/2, green = +strength x (below - above)/2, blue 1, length 1, times 0.5 plus 0.5. 8) Use ONE source of relief per scale (Scenario: normal map OR displacement, never both): displacement for large forms, normal or bump for fine grain.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED: Bump Distance d on N dots equals slope strength d x N within 4 to 8 percent (best fit 5.46 for 5.12). On a hard step Filter Width 0.1 shows mean tilt 4.1 degrees, 1.0 gives a 24-dot bevel (17.8 degrees mean), 2.0 gives 29.5. Displacement formula: Height 0 and 1, Midlevel 0.5, Scale 0.1 moved -0.0498 and +0.0502. Far outline bumpiness: Bump Only 0.16 dots (straight), Displacement Only 3.1, both 3.1; render time 3.6 / 2.1 / 3.6 s. Mesh fineness (shading spread kept): grid 16 x 16 0.038; 256 x 256 0.160; adaptive Dicing 2 0.1615, 1 0.1635, 0.5 0.1627 at twice the time. A baked height in Bump: normal seam 0.46 Repeat, 1.43 Extend or Mirror, 105.9 Clip. 8-bit ramp: 54 levels against 3,957 in 16 bits; 53 percent of dots with zero tilt from 8 bits against 0.9 percent from 16. Bump Distance does not depend on picture size (0.0007 difference). Bump equals Cycles Bake Normal within 0.00008. Brick reference normals: OpenGL correlates +0.972 with its height slope, the DirectX upload -0.972. A normal map read with the wrong convention lights with render correlation -0.02 against 0.85 for the right one.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Old tutorials (Bump Strength 0.3) assume the old large default Distance. AO cannot see a Bump node (all-white bake). Bump never changes the silhouette. A mirrored normal map needs red or green flipped in the mirrored copy (error 0.12 and 0.11 if forgotten). Both red and green flipped (dents instead of bumps) reads as OpenGL in the map-alone test; keep the height to check. Normal maps saved in 8 bits are not exactly length 1; skipping the length-1 step added about 5 degrees to metal's ceiling. NOT TESTED: displacement of the baked heights on a real object; Material.max_vertex_displacement (the API warns larger movements may show gaps); the Normal Map node Base setting; Vector Displacement. Cookbook measured 'both' (displacement plus bump on the same height) with no doubling (shading spread 0.100 against 0.098) while Scenario says never both: unresolved, see gaps.

techniques.name: Decide what height means before building relief (sign of height, colour-made versus real)
techniques.what_it_is: A height map made from colour brightness and a height of real raised shapes can point opposite ways. In the six references the height IS the brightness of the colour picture.
techniques.why_it_matters: For a dirt road or stone wall the stones must be high and the joints low. Example: on brick, bright mortar became HIGH and the bricks LOW, the reverse of a real wall; real raised bricks correlated -0.15 with the reference height. Cobbles copied from brick kept 'bright = high' and the sandy joints came out higher than the stones.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) Decide first whether height comes from colour or from real shapes; give real relief the larger share unless you must match a colour-made height. 2) If from colour: fit a stretch (1st and 99th percentile of the new tile's own brightness stretched to about 10 and 245), blur first (0.5 to 0.7 dot) then the curve, keep it 16-bit. 3) Where a layered recipe makes height, wire real layer heights in and treat paint brightness as a share (the slate's combine.tone_blend). 4) Check the sign on every new surface (stones and clods high, joints, ruts and cracks low).
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED: grey = 0.299 R + 0.587 G + 0.114 B reproduces the six reference heights to 3 to 5 steps of 255 (correlation 0.989 to 0.997); the six normal maps are the slope of the 8-bit height at strengths 6, 7, 8, 5, 9, 10 (brick, slate, wood, metal, mud, gravel). Slate's tone_blend 0.4 gives height group 0.505, 0.7 gives 0.654, 1.0 gives 0.629. Real-geometry heights against the reference: brick -0.15, metal 0.07, gravel about 0, slate 0.52; 50/50 mixes did not help in any build (metal 20/40/60 percent mixes 16.69, 16.87, 17.46 against 16.62). Real geometry rebuilds were quick (metal 1.3 s, gravel 9 s against 65 to 100 s) but scored lower on the same-kind tool. COMBINE's slate rule cut off 6.9 percent of brick's dots at the top of the height range (height group 0.299 against 0.597 with a 13-node box).
techniques.traps_and_failures: Slate's stretch left cedar all white; the gravel stretch left 62 percent of pebble heights white; re-find the stretch per surface. A dead setting: raising real lip height and chip depth changed nothing because the finished height was 70 percent paint brightness. A 4-point curve was off by 17.9 steps (8 points 7.9) because it cannot bend flat at the ends. Heights fitted once to a reference add score (brick +0.116, metal +0.083) and must be quoted beside the plain score. A mesh made from nothing in Geometry Nodes renders black until Set Material is added.

techniques.name: Getting maps out of Blender: photograph or Bake button, colour management, bit depth, filter, samples
techniques.what_it_is: Two routes. The photograph: a flat 1 x 1 square under an orthographic camera, glowing with one channel (Emission), no lights, so each dot is the channel's exact value. The Bake button: Cycles writes what a material does on a real object's UV map into an Image Texture node.
techniques.why_it_matters: Wrong colour management quietly ruins every map. Example: a height of 0.5 comes out as 0.500 with view transform Raw, 0.737 with Standard, 0.667 with AgX (a fresh scene's default).
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) Flat tile: photograph. Cycles, CPU, samples 8 to 16, adaptive sampling and denoising off, max bounces 0, pixel filter Box 1.0, black world, orthographic camera at ortho scale 1, 5 units above, clip 0.01 to 100. 2) Colour: view transform Standard, 8-bit, hex palette colours converted to linear first (rt.srgb_hex_to_linear); height, roughness, metallic, normal: Raw, 16-bit for height, loaded back as Non-Color. 3) Real object: Bake button with a UV map, an Image Texture node selected AND active, samples 8 to 16 (default 4096), colour through the emission trick (Bake type Emit) into an sRGB picture, data into a Non-Color picture, normal Tangent +X +Y +Z (OpenGL); Selected to Active: Extrusion above the tallest bump and Max Ray Distance 0 or larger than extrusion plus bump. Blender 5.2 has no Bake type for metallic or height; use the emission trick into a Non-Color picture (not tested). 4) A Gaussian pixel filter can act as the height blur: ask for width = about 4 x the blur. 5) EEVEE cannot bake.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED: photograph against Bake: colour within 0.0011 (emission trick) and roughness within 0.00001. Diffuse bake of a metal material comes out black (0.0069 against 0.5917). View transform on a brick recipe: AgX colour difference 7.17 Delta E, Filmic 7.99, Raw 26.84 (colour strength 28.49 right, 23.25 AgX). Roughness baked into an sRGB picture: 0.7422 instead of 0.5113; colour baked into Non-Color: error 0.2686. Edge error on a hard diagonal: Box 1 dot at 1 / 4 / 16 / 64 samples 0.516 / 0.171 / 0.062 / 0.027; Blackman-Harris 1.5 blurs 63 dots away from the edge, Gaussian 1.5 blurs 259. A bake ignores the pixel filter. Harness at 256 dots ran in 1.7 s (project notes give about 20 s at 1254; NOT TESTED by me). Selected to Active with Extrusion 0 left 50 percent of dots flat; Extrusion 0.1 with Max Ray 0.05 left 100 percent flat. AO on a displaced surface min 0.84, mean 0.988.
techniques.traps_and_failures: A new scene uses AgX: set the view transform in every script that renders. image.save_render applies the view transform to an sRGB image (0.5 became 0.2157 with Raw) but not to Non-Color. A fixed old bug: save_array_png wrote only the red channel for grey arrays. Camera height: thousands of stacked flat shapes must stay between the camera and its clip range. Palette colours typed as hex come out about 73 steps too bright. The harness's --normal-reference option matches a spread of tilts, not a look (on smooth noise it chose strength 38.59 against brick's own 6). NOT TESTED in a build: the Bake button on any layered recipe, metallic or height by emission trick, metal's pixel-filter 0.01 setting.

techniques.name: Wear and dirt that follow a real object's shape, then bake it for EEVEE
techniques.what_it_is: Edge chips and cavity dirt driven by Bevel, Ambient Occlusion or Pointiness nodes (what Scenario's M.add_wear does), or by a curvature value stored on the mesh. Bevel, AO and Pointiness work only in Cycles and are stochastic, so in EEVEE the wear is missing unless baked.
techniques.why_it_matters: Cottage doors, stable posts, barrels and carts need chips on real mouldings, which tile recipes cannot do. On the wet street door the live wear was invisible in EEVEE.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) Build the wear with M.add_wear(mat, edge_color, edge_roughness, edge_metallic, dirt_color, wear_amount, cavity_dirt, radius 0.04 on a 1 m crate). 2) For an EEVEE plate either bake it to pictures (colour, roughness) or use a vertex curvature attribute (M.curvature_attribute) and threshold that. 3) Bake route: copy the object (the copy is the 'low', the worn original the 'high'), give it a new UV map (seams angle 60 with unwrap method BEST on the door; the door's own UV was a tiling 0..3 map), equal texel density, pack, bake DIFFUSE and ROUGHNESS at 1024, rebuild a plain material from the pictures (no Bevel, no AO), copy the UV map back. 4) Check each map with the skill's sanity numbers and the value report. 5) Give each object its own seed or object offset (see traps).
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED on one cottage door (EEVEE, 1,126 pictures not counted; door leaf 113,094 pixels). Live add_wear in EEVEE: mean change 1.0 of 255, warm chip share 0.0; same in Cycles: mean change 5.92, warm chips 12.17 percent. Wear mask means EEVEE against Cycles: Wear 0.0035 / 0.0567, Edges 0.0121 / 0.1375, Dirt 0.0437 / 0.1211. Baked colour and roughness in EEVEE: correlation with Cycles wear change 0.498 at 512 dots, 0.668 at 1024; warm chip share 6.0 to 6.3 percent; the whole route took about 5.8 s at 1024 on the rented card. Curvature-attribute route: first try changed 23.52 steps with 41.95 percent warm chips (far too much); calmer try 5.01 with 9.02 percent; both correlated with Cycles wear -0.08 and -0.16, so they place wear in different spots. Layer mute on the door (difference from all layers, 3.792 from nothing): without edge wear 3.27, without cavity dirt 0.691, without grunge spots 0.494. UV trials: seam angle 60 gave 78 seams and coverage 0.286; angle 30 gave 1,194 seams and 611 islands (coverage 0.037); sharp-edge seams at 30 gave 1,276 seams and a bake that correlated 0.062. Value report of the baked door: metal pixels below sRGB 180 flagged in both engines.
techniques.traps_and_failures: The baked normal failed its own check: 20.685 percent inverted normals (blue < 0.5) and 3.11 percent of rays hit another part first, so no normal map was used (normal_used false). UV checks also failed: coverage 29 percent (needs 70), 221 flipped faces, 36 zero-area faces, angle error p95 58 degrees, 406 hard edges inside islands. Automatic seams from sharp edges produced over 1,000 islands. Scenario's node groups have no seed (read from code, NOT drawn), so every door would wear the same way; linked duplicates share Object-space coordinates (my reasoning, NOT TESTED). Live Bevel or AO wear thresholded into metallic gives 17 to 18 percent fractional metallic at any sample count. Wear shows only in Cycles unless baked. Judged by the person: 'The third door looks photorealistic. Lol.' and realistic-looking textures are fine in the plate (the painter restyles it).

techniques.name: Layered material: painter's order, a fixed 11-number layout bundle, own seeds, Amount 0 means nothing
techniques.what_it_is: One recipe split into boxes, each answering one question: LAYOUT (which piece is this dot on and where), COLOUR AND FADE (bare material colour on every dot), OUTLINE AND SHADOW (dark gaps, edge light), MOSS or growth, DAMAGE, COMBINE (stack order and the four maps). LAYOUT hands every layer the same 11 numbers per dot: piece_id, row, local_x, local_y (0 at the TOP of the piece), piece_width, piece_height, edge_distance, top_edge_distance, gap_mask, piece_mask, base_height. Every layer returns exactly four outputs: Mask, Colour, Height (0 = no change), Roughness (0 = no change).
techniques.why_it_matters: Cottages share bricks, planks and slate looks but need different weather. Layers let one model switch a layer off, re-seed it or reuse it, and let a checker prove nothing else moved.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) Write the bundle first (names, units, ranges, which way local_y runs) and freeze it. 2) Each layer: its own seed (piece_id x big number + seed), Amount 0 gives exactly 0 mask, height and roughness (one shared finish_layer does it), no peeking at another layer except a declared link (one line in the file, a row in the contract and the guide; the recipe refuses circles). 3) Two coordinate kinds: whole-surface patterns on the seamless noise with scale = features per tile x Tile Count; per-piece patterns on local_x x piece_width and local_y x piece_height with offsets from piece_id. 4) Sizes in tile units. 5) Settings are named layer.control, strength order default < settings.json < bake parameters. 6) Stack order bottom first (slate: colour_and_fade, moss, damage, outline_and_shadow); colour = mix(colour so far, layer colour, layer mask); height = base_height + gain x sum of heights; roughness = base 0.8 + sum. 7) Prove independence with a table: bake once whole, then per layer with Amount 0 and with Seed + 1, count dots changed outside that layer's mask (must be 0 except the declared link). 8) Re-run a layer's row whenever its file changes. 9) Keep a ladder (what each layer adds) and bake three seed sets before adopting a setting.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED (slate, same-kind score at 1254 dots): ladder colour group 0.410 (joints and flat slates) -> 0.728 (+ colour and fade) -> 0.792 (+ moss) -> 0.822 (+ damage); overall 0.459, 0.735, 0.774, 0.789; without outline and shadow 0.601. Added to a part-built picture colour and fade gives +0.318, moss +0.064, damage +0.030; taking outline and shadow out costs 0.146 colour and 0.332 height. Independence: every row exactly 0.0 percent outside; only declared-link moss moved when damage changed (0.92 and 1.57 percent, all inside the damage mask). 176 controls (49 to 73 set). The skeleton took about 13 s at 1254 dots and 4 samples. Layers tuned alone do not add up: first stacked bake 0.615, 13 hand rounds to 0.695 like for like. Five seed sets 0.792 to 0.824 after the look fixes (spread 0.032; before: 0.701 to 0.769, spread 0.068).
techniques.traps_and_failures: local_y runs down the piece while the picture's y runs up. In the gap the piece numbers are still defined: use gap_mask or piece_mask. The bundle has no distance to the nearest corner, so corner effects need local_x, local_y and sizes. A slate-specific habit (weather from the top of a piece) becomes tongues on brick; a per-layer direction setting is proposed, not built. Edge masks decided per dot show a one-dot staircase unless samples are 16. A default change moves every dependent result (ladder, variations, seed spread, area, tests, guides): keep a list and one command each. Variations written as fixed numbers go wrong when the default moves; write them as multiples. One score measure (feature size) gave three quarters of the colour gain; report a score with its biggest part. The honesty check found first versions of guides saying 'outline is worth the most' (wrong for colour) and 'identical' (1 to 2 step dither differences).

techniques.name: Which layers carry to a new surface, and the new parts each surface needed
techniques.what_it_is: The Reuse trials built brick, wood, metal, mud and gravel from the slate's layers, changing settings and adding only the smallest new boxes. They show what to expect for a new surface.
techniques.why_it_matters: For the village: a dirt road is nearest to the mud and gravel trials; cottage walls to brick; boards, doors and stable to wood; hinges and nails to metal; roofs to slate.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) Reuse as is: layer interface, COLOUR AND FADE (by settings), COMBINE stacking, baking and scoring tools. 2) Expect to write a new LAYOUT for pieces other than staggered rows (4 of 5 needed one; wood needed a 5-node turn so streaks run along the grain). 3) Expect one to three new layers: brick GRIME, wood CRACKS, KNOTS, GRAIN, metal EDGE LIGHT, RIVETS, mud RUTS, STONES, gravel SOIL, FACETS. 4) Use MOSS and DAMAGE only where their rules fit; switch off otherwise (brick MOSS, gravel MOSS, mud DAMAGE and OUTLINE were switched off). 5) Replace COMBINE's height rule on 3 surfaces. 6) Put weather start-points where the real weather comes from.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED (independent check): share of nodes from shared parts: brick 83.5 percent, wood 86.9, metal 77.5, gravel 56.2, mud 54.8 (43.2 counting only boxes that work). Same-kind score, layered mean of 3 seed sets against own earlier recipe: brick 0.615 against 0.725 (behind), wood 0.667 against 0.606, metal 0.648 against 0.579, mud 0.507 against 0.391, gravel 0.622 against 0.380. New boxes (nodes): brick GRIME 161, height box 13, optional layout 118; wood TURN 5, CRACKS 95, KNOTS 78, GRAIN 31 plus 39 borrowed; metal LAYOUT 191, EDGE LIGHT 98, RIVETS 125, height 19; mud LAYOUT 295, RUTS 212, STONES 637 (498 borrowed); gravel LAYOUT 564, SOIL 170, FACETS 109, height 12. Shared slate layout by settings on brick 0.646 against 0.654. Shared layers alone on a gravel layout 0.21. 31 to 34 of 51 tools fit each surface as is or by settings. The new boxes were 1.2 to 4 times bigger than the inventory guessed.
techniques.traps_and_failures: JUDGED by eye: every layered tile is cleaner, flatter and more regular than its reference (ruler-straight edges, identical rivets, uniform black gaps, a butt joint in every board). Mud is the least finished (flat mosaic, no lit and shadowed clods, narrow winding ruts instead of broad braided bands, stones 8 percent of dots against 18, cartoon tan stones, plastic grey ones). Ruts first came out as hairlines; MOSS first painted hundreds of tiny bits; local numbers froze beyond one patch width and drew straight blocks (found only at true dot size; fixed by a box two patch widths wide); lichen discs and pits used as stones looked like polka dots. MOSS as puddle water works only because the new layout hands over basins. Gravel: three upright grids made a plaid (each grid turned by its own whole-number step); straight-edged stones scored 0.472, ragged 0.641; round 7 went backwards to 0.566. Brick: first GRIME hard black blobs; round 3 overshot (37 percent dark against 24). Metal: 31 and 34 percent rust on sets 2 and 3 against 22 in the reference; an unlucky bar count stops with 'two bars overlap'. Wood: Grain Stretch multiplied instead of divided. Seed set 1 (the tuned one) flatters; the seed alone moves score 0.02 to 0.09. Eleven ranked gaps: wiring tied to slate, layout per piece kind, settable height rule, light direction, whole-surface paint across gaps, stamps, soft-height bake option, audit of numbers in code, pieces running across the tile, cracks starting anywhere, metallic per dot.

techniques.name: Flat painted look (and how it was made, so it can be switched off for realism)
techniques.what_it_is: The references are hand-painted: flat patches of one colour, dark outlines, a one-to-two-dot staircase at edges. The nodes make it by stretch, cut into flat steps, colour, mix.
techniques.why_it_matters: The film repaints plates in the series style, so realism is allowed in the plate (log 23). But when a painted result is wanted the same rules apply. For a village most realistic effects (soft stains, grime) need the opposite settings, and no realistic preset of the layered recipes exists.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) Chain: noise -> Map Range (stretch) -> Math Multiply Add (more or less) -> Color Ramp with Constant steps (one flat colour per step) -> Mix over the base. 2) Work out a tone step per dot from small pieces (piece tone, streaks, patches, specks, big areas), ROUND it, look it up in a palette of 9 to 12 colours; rounding is what makes hard edges (hardness setting 0 to 1, keep at 1). 3) Brightness only, not red, green and blue separately (grey stones turned purple and green). 4) Tall shapes, not round blobs; growth that starts at an edge and runs down; shadows in 2 flat steps with a ragged border. 5) Hard masks (0 or 1 nearly everywhere). 6) Patches that stop part way. 7) Outlines: measure their width. 8) Convert hex colours to linear before typing them in. 9) Grain is a separate switch. 10) Compositor filters (Kuwahara) break the wrap: wrap-pad, filter, cut the middle out. 11) Map Range Stepped with Steps N gives N + 1 levels; Math Snap rounds down.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED (slate demo, same-kind): plain soft tiles 0.372; patches of the wrong size 0.270 (worse); ragged edges 0.278; outlines 0.486; stains 0.506; height blur 0.8 dot 0.555; drip size from measurements 0.574; Kuwahara 0.534 (0.506 to 0.482 on an already flat picture). On the six references 85 to 94 percent of strong edges change colour within 2 dots; patches 20 to 50 dots across; 8 colours reproduce each to a colour difference of 3.1 to 4.5; dark outlines about 5 (brick), 12 (slate), 8 (wood), 6 (metal), 3 (stones) dots wide; edges have a 1 to 2 dot staircase. A cut on raw noise at 0.6 covers 6.7 percent of the tile, at 0.65 1.1 percent, at 0.55 22 percent. Wrap padding for filters: seam 2.61 -> 1.05. A multiply by a dark colour darkens twice (soot 29, 5, 2 instead of 58, 45, 39).
techniques.traps_and_failures: Independent random colours per patch make camouflage confetti; colour a patch as the colour beneath plus a small change. The compositor's Posterize works per channel and turns brown into red, olive and black: posterise a grey value then colour it. Measure patch size before judging the look (metal's first wear made 4 to 5 dot patches against 9 to 13: leopard print). A colour layer covering everything hides layers below it (rust share 0.156 -> 0.010); use Multiply for brightness-only layers. Set noise cuts from the noise's own sorted values (same cut covered 5 or 30 percent). Slate look checker found 'flame tongues' in paint, flat khaki moss with teeth, tan L-shaped chips, rippled-plastic relief under low light, black drips under rows, and (round 2) straight-edged glass-like facets on about 14 slates that needed a code change (not made).

techniques.name: Real geometry detail through Geometry Nodes
techniques.what_it_is: Build raised parts (stones, bricks, rivets, grooves, weeds) as real 3D shapes, then use them directly in the scene or photograph them from above as height, colour and normal.
techniques.why_it_matters: A cart rut, a stone step or a wall course must stand out in silhouette and shadow. Real geometry is the right tool when a surface must really stick out in 3D; it lost every comparison against painted references only because their height is brightness.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) End every Geometry Nodes group with a Set Material node. 2) Photograph with an orthographic camera, height as 16-bit. 3) Geometry does not wrap: make 9 copies (shifted -1, 0, +1 in x and y) and use seamless noise; store per-piece numbers BEFORE Realize Instances. 4) Distribute Points with Poisson Disk only separates inside the tile; relax points 40 times in a Repeat zone using 9 shifted copies. 5) A curve with no profile is only edges: good for 'distance to the curve' (grooves, ruts, cracks) but invisible to the camera. 6) Mesh Bevel needs its four offsets set. 7) Cut holes with ONE cutter and the Manifold or Float solver. 8) Rigid Body piles do not wrap: move the pile half a tile and settle again twice. 9) Use at least one mesh vertex per dot and let the mesh reach a little past the tile edge.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED (geometry guide): brick wall tile of 48 bricks took 110.5 s at 1254 and scored same-kind 0.171 (0.407 for the painter; not like for like because the tool changed minutes apart). Seam number without and with 9 copies: brick 10.37 -> 0.62, slate 40.19 -> 0.27. Two Poisson points sat 0.0048 apart where 0.064 was asked; 40 relax steps cured it. 144 holes: 12.7 s with 144 Boolean modifiers, 0.19 s with one cutter and Manifold. Rigid body: 69 stone pairs pushed into each other across the edge, 14 after two re-settles. AO gives free crevices but colour took 87 s against 6.8 s. A Set Material-less group rendered black (0.0003 against 0.3253). Height error 0.0000076 of range in 16-bit. Normal error 0.00077 when the mesh goes past the tile edge against 0.0013 when it stops. Metal bars and rivets 1.3 s; gravel columns 9 s against 65 to 100 s.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Blender's tessellate_polygon silently mis-filled 396 of 8,687 traced outlines (one lost 44 percent of its area). Real-geometry 50/50 mixes did not help in any build. Gravel's real-geometry route lowered same-kind from 0.362 to 0.173. Geometry colour came out soft and blobby (slate AO colour alone took 76 s). relax_tools and layout_tools were judged not useful for the layered route (it needs 11 numbers for every dot, not points). Scenario's GN skill adds: same Seed on two Random Value nodes moves scale and rotation together (correlation 1.0); Random Value implicit ID inside a for-each zone gives silent wrong output; wire simulation state through; a Set Position tree must be object-local (world directions need Self Object -> Object Info -> Invert Matrix).

techniques.name: Scattering weeds, litter and props, with counting checks
techniques.what_it_is: Instances placed by a density mask on a surface. Scenario's scatter_tree takes density x mask, a world-space slope limit, upright or aligned, picked from an object or collection. The weathering kit and the street rubbish mask used the same idea (cross-reference: logs 22 and 25, outside my main scope).
techniques.why_it_matters: Weeds along road edges, straw in a stable, litter by walls and fallen leaves are what make a place read as lived in. Example: the street's scatter placed about 6,400 to 7,200 small 3D pieces from a mask built from its real shape.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) Make the mask from the place's real shape: gutters, wall feet, doorsteps, pipe and post feet, inside corners, rings round props; never the middle of the road (street rubbish). 2) Offset seeds per use. 3) Prove with counts: scatter count within about 12 percent of density x mask x eligible area; rotate the object 90 degrees and double the input resolution (trait selections scale, index ones jump). 4) Look: nothing floats or sinks. 5) Cap the size of pieces near the camera. 6) Keep weeds off puddles and the road middle.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED (Scenario try-out 23d): the scatter builder gave a correct litter scatter first time and its counting checks proved it. JUDGED: scattered litter was too small to read in the film's main camera. Street (logs 22, 25): rubbish gathered about 8 to 1 at the kerb against the pavement after a fix (was 5 to 1); weathering kit: lime-bright weeds standing in puddles, about 50 weeds mid-slab on the notice pavement, moss pieces like cut-outs were found by checkers and calmed in a fix round; at film size the kit then added little a viewer could see except rust and a few weeds.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Near-camera coal chips looked like faceted gems and straw like matchsticks (fixed: flat irregular lumps, shorter thinner curved straw, size cap). The painter dropped hairline cracks and tiny tufts but kept big weed clumps. Scenario web export lost scattered litter unless realised. NOT TESTED: the weeds and litter at village scale by me.

techniques.name: Scoring, yardsticks and why a score is not a look
techniques.what_it_is: Two scoring tools with different questions: lib/texture_compare.py ('same kind of surface?', 14 measures in 4 groups) and lib/pixel_compare.py ('same picture dot for dot?', tiers none, layout, close, exact).
techniques.why_it_matters: A new place has no reference picture, so these tools cannot score it. But their lessons say how to judge a tile.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) Decide what you check: same kind (new tile) or same picture (copy). 2) Know the yardsticks first: flat normal error and flat height error of the reference, what other surfaces score. 3) Bake at the same size and seed, bake three seed sets, and do not chase differences under 0.01 to 0.05. 4) Run a self-test with known answers (the reference itself, a moved copy, a blurred copy, a flat picture, other surfaces). 5) Report a score with its biggest single part. 6) Look at the sheet. 7) Never tune on the score you report.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED self-test (brick): reference itself same-kind 0.953 (tiling group 0.392 because the reference has its own seam 2.22); slid copy 0.992 and tier none; blurred 6 dots 0.241; other real surfaces 0.164 to 0.324 against brick and 0.179 to 0.498 against mud (gravel reference scores 0.498 against mud, above the new mud tiles' 0.383). Flat normal error: brick 16.72, slate 11.27, wood 24.11, metal 13.26, mud 23.5, gravel 24.46 degrees. Seed alone moves the score 0.01 to 0.03 (0.03 to 0.05 for gravel and mud). Smoothing the height 0.8 dot costs 0.992 -> 0.830. A 768-dot bake scores 0.632 against 0.701 at 1254 (scorer enlarges). Metal S 0.373 at 512 against 0.523 at 1254.
techniques.traps_and_failures: SSIM and the normal error reward flat pictures (flat brick 0.515 against slid copy 0.324; a normal error above the flat number is worse than no relief). The score cannot see 'cleaner and more regular than the reference', blocky stones or hue errors. A score tuned on is optimistic (wood 0.626). Two tools pull opposite ways at the finest scale (grain). The score fails (NaN) on a perfectly flat picture. The tier limits are the same for every surface. A colour-only reference makes the tier read only colour. A new reference name needs adding to ALL_REFERENCES and the anchors rebuilt (changes all scores slightly). description_audit counts bytes and list lengths only, so it cannot see tracing (slate L fine passes at 512 KB with 9,383 traced patches) and gave a false alarm on a list of polygons. 17 blind spots listed in the baking guide.

techniques.name: Fresh-eyes look checker and honesty checker loop
techniques.what_it_is: A helper who only looks (the look checker) judges the finished tile at full size, against the reference if there is one, and keeps a numbered fault list; a second helper (the honesty checker) re-runs every number and every claim in the notes.
techniques.why_it_matters: The numbers said the slate was good for many rounds; the eye found 11 faults in one look. Example: after the settings round the checker found rows of moss teeth, tan L-shapes at corners, a lone crack, black drips under rows and 'liquified' paint.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) Look at 1:1 crops, at a contrast-boosted copy (shows flat facets), at a 3 x 3 tiling (shows repeating landmarks) and under a raking light (shows relief). 2) Number every fault and keep the same list when looking again; each ends fixed, better, same or worse. 3) Fix by settings first; when 3 or 4 settings-only tries fail write a small code change with a new control that starts at the old behaviour and prove 'no change at the starting value'. 4) After each round measure about ten old measures again (before, after, reference) and look again. 5) Test the variations again whenever the default changed. 6) The honesty checker reproduces numbers, counts claims (for example twins, touching pairs, knots per area), and checks that a lesson in notes is used by the final tile. 7) Keep 'before' copies and show before and after in every table.
techniques.measured_results: JUDGED by the look checker (slate, round 1): 11 faults: flame tongues in the paint, too much flat khaki moss (10.8 percent against 6.6 percent) with sharp teeth, tan L-shaped chips, near-square corners and ruler-straight rows, rippled-plastic relief under low light, drippy shadow under rows, pale outlier slates, one hair-like crack, round lichen dots, 'dark and wet' reads as noise, 'fresh and clean' loses the painted look. After settings-only round 1: 4 fixed, 4 better, 3 unchanged, none worse, 5 new problems. After round 2: 5 fixed, 5 better, one new (straight-edged facets on about 14 slates). MEASURED by the honesty checker: like-for-like default 0.695 (0.705 in another file); 'outline worth the most' wrong for the colour score; normal-map credit reversed; 176 controls not 49; guides had 11 wording and number errors; wood round 1 claimed 'never the same strip as its neighbour' (really 19 percent).
techniques.traps_and_failures: Fixing one fault makes a new one (broader paint bands removed the ripple and brought glass facets). A better measure is not a better picture. A setting can be dead because of wiring (tone_blend). Two measuring rules for the same thing can disagree (slate grey spread 5.6 and 6.9 against 5.5 and 5.1); report both. Moving one setting can undo another. A message sent to a concept helper woke a second copy (8 extra paid calls, about US$0.70) in the garden job.

techniques.name: Scenario Blender skill rules that apply to any place
techniques.what_it_is: Seven MIT-licensed skills installed in /home/user/Music/.claude/skills (expert, texturing-shading, uv-baking, geometry-nodes, lighting-rendering, export, previs-storyboard) with 83 local edits: no installs, headless only, Blender run with xvfb-run -a and --disable-autoexec, scratch output only, EEVEE as the plate renderer.
techniques.why_it_matters: They hold the expert loop and numbers a smaller model should apply to any set: build big to small, measure, look, fix before adding detail.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) Expert loop: brief in numbers; plan stages; one stage at a time; gate with bx_audit and a review sheet; fix before advancing; deliver with evidence. 2) Texturing stance: data maps Non-Color; normal OR displacement; masks not painted colour (contrast through Color Ramp stops or Map Range); realistic = scanned set plus masks, stylised = procedural; micro detail in roughness not bump for skin and hair; judge in Standard view, with grazing light for relief; Noise Detail 5 or less. 3) Blend modes: Multiply darkens (grime, mould), Screen lightens (efflorescence; Add exceeds 1), Subtract on the height chain for spalling, Color Burn masks along bricks or into grout; chain order sets age (a decal before grime reads old). 4) Mask frequency against vertex density: vertex colours for broad soft masks, images for fine detail. 5) Real units, scale applied, box projection for rigid parts without UVs, Object coordinates for procedurals (UV on deforming meshes). 6) UVs: seams follow the method; unwrap method is a measurement (pass method=, 5.2 defaults to CONFORMAL); texel density first (FPS 10.24 px/cm, third person 5.12, top-down 2.56); pad by res/128; bake test at 512 then final.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED (Scenario's own numbers, cited in the skills, not re-measured here except where noted): dielectric albedo sRGB about 30 to 240, metal 180 to 255, metallic 0 or 1; brick wall roughness about 0.7; hue tweak 0.5 plus or minus 0.04; Edge-wear Bevel radius 0.04 on a 1 m crate (measured by Scenario); Bump Distance about 0.001, strength 0.1 to 0.2 for fabric; displacement Scale 0.2, Midlevel 0.5, Cubic, 16-bit source; bake samples 30 or more; paint bleed 8 to 12 px. UV: coverage above 70 percent, gap res/128, samples 16 for normals and 128 for AO, AO distance about 0.2 x bounding diagonal. Seven skills tried on the street (log 23): delivery check found 73 inside-out parts (69 headframe bars, both winding wheels, 2 trims) that looked fine; on the whole street it reports 908 errors because of the 3.5 km sky dome unless sky and far hills are left out and 1 mm set by hand.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Data map left sRGB bends bump; node wrangler's normal plus displacement doubles relief; displacement without geometry does nothing; pre-4.5 Bump Distance of 1.0 is stepped and plastic; Emission Strength 0 gives no glow; Bevel wear or Pointiness in EEVEE is missing; stroke right after setup paints partially; box projection or Generated coordinates on a rig swim. Skills tell Claude to use scenario's add-on and an MCP bridge: both are removed or marked 'not used here'. The local rules are instructions, not locks. Many tools were not tried: window-only ones, most light rigs, most export presets, moving mannequins, the animatic. Scenario's one-lamp-at-a-time shares mislead on a street full of glowing windows; its subject verdicts are built for faces.
