techniques.name: Check wear at the size and under the lights the viewer sees (cross-reference from logs 22 and 25)
techniques.what_it_is: Test that relief, joints, weeds and wear survive the real shot, not only a flattering close-up. Example: the road's joints only showed because they were dark in the photo; under 22 lightings only 6 passed.
techniques.why_it_matters: A dirt road with ruts, cobbles or planks can vanish under wet or flat light. A weathering kit that looked rich up close added almost nothing at film size.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) List the lightings the film will use (dry, wet, brazier-lit, heavy rain) and count how many show the relief. 2) Measure at the viewer's picture size and count every dot (including puddle and rubbish dots). 3) Spend effort by screen share (the street: road a third of the main view, walls a sixth, roofs 1 percent). 4) For relief that must survive any light, add a real height or a darkening and roughness change inside the grooves rather than a relief picture (a relief picture tells light which way a dot faces, not how deep it is). 5) Judge on a plate size picture, then in the stage. 6) Compare EEVEE and Cycles; a light cut-off setting can make EEVEE cold blue and Cycles warm gold.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED (street logs): joints read as grooves in 21 of 22 lightings after the JOINTS layer (18 of 22 counting every dot), before 6 of 22; walls got 0.84 times as bright when wet (foot 0.66); specularity map changed the road by 0.006 while roughness made it wet (0.28); plate brightness moved 1 to 1.6 percent with the kit on; EEVEE against Cycles on the main street wet picture 3.7 s against 14.1 s, road brightness 0.183 against 0.336 in Cycles; Cycles leaves 6 to 7 percent crushed black against about 1.5. Real 8 mm grooves cut into the road looked worse in the middle distance, so they were switched off.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Black pictures from a stale picture on the rented machine; a plan picture turned round; four wrong explanations of one failure; walls nearly black and seen edge-on hid soot, run-off streaks and damp bands; the painter repainted dry once when the brief said matte and no puddles. NOT TESTED by me; these come from story-log summaries.

techniques.name: What did not work (so nobody repeats it)
techniques.what_it_is: A list of dead ends, each with its evidence.
techniques.why_it_matters: Each of these looked reasonable and cost hours.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Avoid: (1) Real geometry to match a painted height; 50/50 mixes. (2) Repairs after the fact: cross-fades (ghost doubles), mirror tiling (symmetry, flipped normals), patching finished pictures (ghost bricks). (3) Hex and Wang tiling for structured surfaces (rejected in the big-surface research; not rebuilt). (4) Mapping before the donut. (5) Tracing a reference (copies its seam and faults). (6) Using a score to tune and then reporting it. (7) AI-generated stamp masks for moss and chips. (8) MOSS reused where its rules do not fit (brick soot, gravel rust). (9) Kuwahara on an already flat picture. (10) Random grain to chase 'close' (made the normal worse on wood).
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED: generated stamps (fal, six sheets, US$0.354 by the price list; the checker confirmed exactly six calls): same-kind 0.778 node-made, 0.783 moss stamps, 0.770 chip stamps, 0.775 both: all within noise. Only two of six sheets were usable after cleaning; fal gave black backgrounds four times of six, fluffy balls and square paper pieces when asked for drips. JUDGED: stamp moss a hazy see-through wash, rubber-stamped on every second slate. Gravel real-geometry route 0.362 -> 0.173. Brick real slabs correlate -0.15. Metal mix 20/40/60 percent 16.69, 16.87, 17.46 against 16.62. Invented clods made mud's normal error 28 against 23.5 for flat.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Same-kind score reached 0.80 on default seeds by one round-14 change but gained only 0.005 and 0.011 on two other seed sets and was not kept. Brick via layers with a quick layout scored 0.194. Grain lifts the same-kind score but lowers the dot-for-dot scores. Lowering the strength of a wrong normal map only moves it toward flat.
sources: /home/user/Music/procedural-textures/cookbook/06 Guide - relief - height, bump, displacement and normal maps.md

techniques.name: Working habits that saved or cost time
techniques.what_it_is: Lessons about running many heavy Blender jobs on a shared machine and reporting honestly.
techniques.why_it_matters: A place has many parts and many bakes; mistakes in process cost as much as mistakes in nodes.
techniques.how_to_do_it: 1) Run long bakes as a chain, one after another, each writing a log and a .done file, and keep every number in a .json beside its pictures; after a machine restart the half-finished items were found from these files in minutes. 2) Count bakes, not minutes (with another job running, a 2508-dot area took 22 minutes instead of 9 and a 512-dot bake three times as long). 3) Never run two of your own at once. 4) Use absolute paths and resolve them against the recipe folder, never start cleanup from a relative path. 5) Blender is not on the search path: give the full path. 6) Never stop processes by name on a shared machine. 7) Quote the size a test was run at. 8) Re-bake after the last change and compare only bakes made by the same code. 9) Check each 'why' by switching the suspect off. 10) Keep proof of what you changed. 11) Say which folders lost pictures to save disk. 12) Name files by what they hold. 13) A lesson in a builder's notes is not proven until the final tile uses it.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED: disk fell to 1.1 GB once; the slate folder was trimmed from 436 MB to under the 400 MB limit; the machine restarted during the slate layers and a second helper resumed without loss. Copy slips cost runs in the Reuse trials (an empty list, a missing seed in STONES, a wrong folder level). Metal used 13 Blender starts against a limit of 12.
techniques.traps_and_failures: The first metal helper could not find Blender. Slate's S0 pictures were made before its last description rewrite (1.3 steps apart). Wood's classes were called 20k to 480k but weigh 23.8 to 462.4 KB. KB means 1024 bytes in the audit; mud's 513,735-byte L passes the '512 KB' limit. Writing a person's email into a script's identity line to a website happened once (log 28): never put the person's name or email into requests.
sources: /home/user/Music/procedural-textures/cookbook/06 How to start a new surface - checklist.md (H)
/home/user/Music/procedural-textures/recipes/slate_layers/05 Lessons - slate in layers - what carries over to other surfaces.md (section 7)

checks_and_measures: Seam check, five parts, each with its blind spot: (1) half-tile test with a wrong-roll control (pass: mean difference under about 1 step of 255 and 0 percent of dots over 40; the control must be 5 to 36 percent); (2) wrap jump set beside every ordinary jump in the same direction (pass: inside that range; plain noise was 32.5 against 6.0); (3) first against last column and row (a bug gave 0.23 against 0.9); (4) a 2 x 2 look and a corner zoom; (5) the exact whole-tile move test (recipe_tiling_test.py). Run on a grain-free bake and with dither off.
Copy check for areas: compare the quarters of an area at every shift; new content gives 0.04 to 0.37, a copy gives 1.0. Make the control exact (whole dots).

Independence table for layered recipes: bake whole, then each layer at Amount 0 and Seed + 1, count dots changed outside that layer's own mask (must be exactly 0.0 percent except declared links; slate moss moved 0.92 and 1.57 percent inside the damage mask).

Colour-management check: photograph a grey ramp; 0.5 must come back as 0.5000 with Raw (Standard 0.737, AgX 0.667 are wrong for data); load data maps as Non-Color; check 16-bit with a level count (a 20 percent ramp holds 54 levels in 8 bits, 3,957 in 16).

Normal-map convention check: correlate the map's green with the height's slope down the rows (+0.94 OpenGL, -0.94 DirectX), and the map-alone test (-1.00 OpenGL, +1.00 DirectX); keep the height to catch both channels flipped.
Bump Distance check: Distance d on N dots should match slope strength d x N within 4 to 8 percent; the default 0.001 is nearly flat.

Displacement check: edge-on render; outline bumpiness (Bump Only 0.16 dots, Displacement 3.1 dots) and (Height - Midlevel) x Scale distances; material.displacement_method must not be BUMP; Dicing Rate 1 to 2.
Yardsticks before any score: flat normal error, flat height error, other-surface level, derivation ceiling (checklist A1 and A3); a normal error above the flat number is worse than no relief.
Seed discipline: bake three seed sets (a fourth never looked at), same size, same seed; do not chase gaps under 0.01 to 0.05; quote a score with its biggest single part.

Counting claims: count touching pairs that share a source row, twins in a 4 x 4 area, knots per area, visible stamp share, scatter count within about 12 percent of density x mask x area; rotate the object 90 degrees and double the resolution for scatter.
Local scale check for squeezed or magnified reads: measure source dots per picture dot from exact position pictures (block count magnified 1.6 percent fell to 0.0009 after capping the shift).

UV quality gates (Scenario uv_qa and uv_verdict): unsolved faces 0, no folding islands, angle error p95 at most 15 degrees (3 flat), coverage at least 70 percent, gap at least res/128, overlaps 0; bake sanity: inverted texels under 2 percent, projection miss under 2 percent, wrong-part rays under 1 percent (the door's 20.685 percent inverted and 3.11 percent wrong-part failed).

Texturing gates (Scenario): M.audit_material (colour spaces by role, explicit UV maps, Bump Distance at most 0.05, no normal map with displacement, Noise Detail at most 6, Emission Strength set) and M.value_report (dielectric albedo sRGB 30 to 243 with under 2 percent outside, metal above 180, fractional metallic under 5 percent, roughness std above 0.01).

Delivery gate: bx_audit.deliverable (floating parts, inside-out parts, negative scale, z-fighting, unapplied scale, missing UVs) per prop; leave out sky and far hills on a whole street and set 1 mm by hand (908 false errors from a 3.5 km dome); engines cull back faces so render with show_backface_culling on and off to see what they draw.

Lighting gates: value study with the subject owning a value group, clip at most 0.5 percent outside emitters, color_audit empty (it found data pictures set to colour in the wetness layer), EEVEE within about 30 percent of Cycles on the subject.

Look check procedure: 1:1 crops, contrast-boosted copy, 3 x 3 tiling, raking light, numbered fault list kept across rounds; measure about ten old measures again before and after each round; look at the variations again after any default changes.
Half-tile style test for every wear or dirt layer baked to pictures: slide, compare, and wrap-pad before any compositor filter (seam 2.61 to 1.05).
Test relief under every lighting the film uses and at the viewer's picture size, counting every dot (street joints: 6 of 22 before, 21 of 22 after; 18 of 22 counting every dot).
Re-bake before quoting; compare only bakes made by the same code; state the picture size and the unit (KB is 1024 bytes in the audit) with every number.
gaps_or_unproven: Nobody has used these tile recipes on a real 3D village. Every layered tile reads cleaner, flatter and more regular than its reference up close, and all were tuned to painted references. No realistic preset exists: the cookbook folder holds 'LATER - realistic moss and damage over the painted colour and weathering - NOT STARTED'.

No recipe exists for thatch, cobbles, a dirt road with two wheel tracks and a hoof path, a stable floor with straw, or timber framing. The nearest is mud (same-kind 0.507, partly reads as mud) and gravel (0.622). Mud's weaknesses are exactly the request: narrow winding ruts instead of broad braided bands, no lit and shadowed clods, sparse cartoon stones.

The checklist has never been followed on a brand-new surface from scratch; every transfer reused an existing generator (cobblestones, cedar shingles, fish-scale tiles, deck boards, hull plates, snow, pebbles were judged by eye only).

The layered recipes read UV 0..1 per tile. How to map them onto real meshes at world scale (tile size in metres, Tile Count, Object or box coordinates on cottage walls) was reasoned here, not tested. A 4 x 4 area was made only for slate; only 2 x 2 for the rest.

EEVEE: the cookbook says every tile test ran in Cycles on a CPU and EEVEE was NOT TESTED; later logs ran EEVEE on rented cards. The layered tile recipes are plain nodes and should work in EEVEE but nobody measured it. Bevel, AO and Pointiness wear is proven invisible in EEVEE only on one door.

Door bake: one door, one result. The baked normal map failed (20.685 percent inverted, 3.11 percent wrong-part rays) and was not used; the coverage was 29 percent against 70 required. Whether another seam setting or a cage fixes it is unknown. Whether linked duplicates share the same wear (no per-object seed) was read from code, not drawn.

Conflict not resolved: the cookbook measured displacement plus bump on the same height as no extra relief (spread 0.100 against 0.098), while Scenario says 'normal map OR displacement, never both' (Price and Brecht). Garden log 31 put real normal maps on 85 materials (I did not inspect how). Units also differ: Scenario's Bump Distance of about 0.001 is real metres on a prop; the cookbook's 0.004 to 0.008 and 0.02 to 0.1 are tile widths on a 1 x 1 tile.

Not tested in the cookbook: the donut trick on a non-square tile; Voronoi features other than F1 on the donut; dividing warp amounts by the tile count; wave lengths that divide the tile (brick); World and Camera coordinates; Vector Rotate; Material.max_vertex_displacement; the Normal Map node's Base setting; Vector Displacement; displacement of the baked heights on a real object; metallic or height by the emission trick; the harness at 1254 dots; the Bake button on any layered recipe; the node-only height-from-colour chain against the references' rule; roughness and metallic maps (baked but compared with nothing).

The scoring tools need a reference folder, so a new place cannot be scored; texture_compare.py also needs the new name added to ALL_REFERENCES and its anchors rebuilt (which shifts every score a little). Only the eye, counts and the checkers can judge a place.

A new reader of the plugin has no tool that places wheel ruts, hoof prints, weeds along a road edge, or straw in a stable by rule; the weathering kit (kits/weathering) and street rubbish mask exist but I read them only through the story logs.

Scenario's local rules are instructions, not locks; whether a smaller model follows them was never tested. It was later seen that a session picks the seven skills up, but not a session started in a sub-folder. Most Scenario tools were never tried (window-only tools, most light rigs, most export presets, moving mannequins, the animatic). The web export squeezes shapes by up to 52 mm and needs one added line in the stage.

Eleven ranked toolkit gaps from the Reuse guide remain unbuilt: recipe wiring not tied to slate, a layout library, a settable height rule, a light direction in OUTLINE AND SHADOW, a whole-surface paint layer across gaps, a stamp layer, a soft-height bake option, an audit that sees numbers in code, wrapped piece coordinates for pieces running across the tile, cracks that start anywhere, metallic per dot. Wood still has a butt joint in every board per tile.

Scores have caveats: height boxes fitted to the reference add +0.116 (brick) and +0.083 (metal); wood's earlier sampler was tuned on the same score; the colour-group gain after the slate look fixes came mostly (about three quarters) from one jumpy measure.

Third-party tools (Ucupaint, Material Maker, MCP Blender Agent) are in third-party/ and were found not to beat Blender nodes (borrow ideas only; MCP Blender Agent has no password, skip). I did not read their licence files; any code copied into the plugin must keep its licence and a note of where it came from. Scenario skills carry an MIT licence file in each skill folder.

Files I did not open that may carry more detail: wood_from_displacement 08 Recipe, mask_test notes, reuse_trials 00 Inventory, the uv-baking, lighting and geometry-nodes procedures.md files (tested code per stage), blender-5.2-deltas.md, the export and previs skill references, research/03 files, and the per-surface 04 Recipe guides. Their lessons files were read, so I expect most of their content is covered.
The research notes elsewhere give a different figure for the other-surface score ('about 0.1', 'blurred about 0.17'); the baking guide re-measured 0.16 to 0.50 and 0.241. Use the re-measured numbers.

I also read /home/user/Music/mine-scene (not on your list, but it is the closest thing to a cart-rutted dirt yard and a six-part build). I changed no file in the project or plugin (checked: nothing under /home/user/Music changed). My scratch is /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Music/02fc5154-76f5-5aac-a505-860164e7e921/scratchpad/plugin-work/inventory-plugin-and-rendering/.

WHAT I TESTED HERE (measured, not judged): (1) the plugin's own tests, python3 kit/calculators/tests/run_all.py: 25 files, 22 passed, 1 failed, 2 skipped; 728 checks passed, 2 failed, 11 skipped; 2 min 15 s. Both failures are the same cause: the film stage wants 4 GB of free disk and this computer has about 2.4 GB left after the filming it plans. (2) I reproduced the project's normal-direction test light on this machine: NORMAL_DIRECTION PASS, 0.804 vs 0.158 and 0.806 vs 0.156, the same numbers the project printed. (3) I measured the plugin's own tiling textures: all 8 normal maps are OpenGL (red-versus-green consistency -0.95 to -0.99); planks has only an X part (gaps, no grain); mean tilt is 3.6 to 14.8 degrees. (4) I built a deliberately flat hut (plain colours, no normal maps, no wear) with the plugin's own model kit and ran the plugin's model_lint: Verdict PASS, exit 0. So today nothing in the plugin can fail a scene for lacking surfaces or wear. (5) The weathering kit imports in Blender 5.2.2 here, both set files validate (0 errors, 0 warnings) and its no-place-names lint says CLEAN (0 hits). (6) Blender's own Python has no Pillow, so model_kit.py (which imports textures.py) fails inside the Blender program with ModuleNotFoundError: PIL; the skill's pip bpy environment is a second, different Python. (7) I asked Poly Haven's free list once with a generic agent name and no personal data: 869 textures and 521 models exist; the textures cover mud, forest ground, thatch and reed roofs, plaster and castle walls, but only a handful of models fit a medieval village (barrels, wooden buckets and crates, baskets, ladders, stumps, lanterns, a jug, a spinning wheel; no cart, hay, trough or stable fittings).

HEADLINE FINDINGS. (a) The plugin says almost nothing about surfaces and wear (A1), its first-read skills would lead a model to flat boxes that pass the lint (A2), it has no rented-card or Cycles text, and its painter template tells the painter to remove puddles and reflections (A6). (b) The project learned a great deal by building and checking: real normal maps that point the right way and are tested, UVs when objects have none, displacement at a believable depth, roughness (not specular) as what makes a surface wet, joints that hold under all light, wear placed from the set's own shape, weeds and moss with exact keep-out zones, designed wear in the picture's own art style with measured guard numbers, bridge-style construction logic with contact checks, building in parts with owners and fresh checkers that re-measure the builders' claims, and cheap pay-per-second Cycles on rented cards. (c) Honest limit: the shader-layer weathering kit, once calmed, added little a viewer could see at film size except rust and a few weeds; the garden's designed geometry plus real normal maps gave the visible character. Carry both, lead with the designed route. (d) Code worth carrying is listed per technique, with whether each file is generic or tied to a place and what it needs.

SUGGESTED ORDER OF WORK FOR THE NEXT STEPS: routing words first (descriptions and first lines), then one entry point per job (surface preset, aging, growth, construction check, render), a preflight stage fed by a Blender-written JSON (A3), a build-in-parts workflow with fresh checkers (B15, B16), and the generic rendering guide (A5). Every number here carries its kind: measured, judged or invented.

techniques.what_it_is: A route trace for a plain request such as 'build a village in the forest in Blender: dirt roads, an empty stable, cottages, scattered props'.

techniques.how_to_do_it: SKIP POINTS. techniques.name: A3. INVENTORY: how the preflight stages are built, and how to add a new stage the same way
techniques.what_it_is: kit/calculators/preflight.py (1,959 lines) is one runner for eight stages (script, record, shots, plates, paint, pages, film, finish). Each stage is a small function that asks for input files, runs calculators as separate programs, or makes findings itself; the runner hashes inputs, applies the signed accepted list, writes a plain report and a JSON report, and answers --gate.
techniques.why_it_matters: The request needs a preflight check that fails when a material or the scene lacks surfaces, wear or construction. The same shape works.
techniques.how_to_do_it: EDITS FOR A NEW STAGE (names are line numbers in preflight.py). (1) STAGES (84), STAGE_WORDS (85), GUARDED (96; the step it guards and 'paid', 'long' or None). (2) INPUTS (108-174): one entry per new input key, (what it is, which tool makes it); keys are turned into --options; PATH_KEYS (175) follows INPUTS; list inputs go in LIST_KEYS (184), plain values in ITEM_VALUE_KEYS (764). (3) STAGE_INPUTS (187): 'r' required or 'o' optional. (4) Write stage_NAME(run, item, where) after the pattern of stage_plates (1085), stage_paint (1161) or stage_pages (1183): run.need(item, key, needed_by, required, why) returns the path or records the exact file to make and the tool that makes it (exit 2); run.run_tool(title, 'calculators/x.py' or 'paper-film/blender/x.py', args, kind='python' or 'node') runs the tool with -I -B, adds --out and --settings and reads findings from its JSON verdicts or plain lines starting FAIL, LOOK, PASS (PLAIN_FAIL, PLAIN_WARN, PLAIN_PASS at 331-333); run.add_check(title, findings) records a check the stage made itself (finding = {verdict: fail|warn|known|info|pass, check, where, text, fix}); also run.read_json, run.show_known, run.cost, run.step_time, run.notes.append, run.house_number(key, default). (5) Add it to STAGE_RUNNERS (1541). (6) Add its options in build_parser (1803; dest with underscores; choices=STAGES follows). (7) Add an entry to EXAMPLE_PLAN (1775). (8) Put every threshold in kit/film-settings.json as an entry with value, unit, kind (measured, judged, invented) and source, in a new section with an 'about' line (settings.py check enforces it; test_settings.py compares code literals with the table). (9) The tool follows the calculator rules: first lines 'What this does', --help, --json, --out, --report, --settings via calculator_output.add_output_options and finish, exit 0 pass, 1 fail, 2 input missing; test_house_rules.py enforces the note and --help for every .py in kit/calculators and its tests. (10) Words in README.md (53-58), make-explainer-film/SKILL.md (57-66), tips guide (24-33), the preflight docstring and the header of bin/explainer-film-preflight. There is no 'blender' kind in run_tool: a check on a .blend works as two steps, a Blender script writes a JSON next to the place and the stage reads and judges it (as make_check_file.py writes check files and stage_shots reads them in check_file_findings, line 959), or the checker reads the .glb in plain Python (as model_lint does). Accepted problems need stage, check or text, reason, who and a real date (entry_problem, 405). --gate (1718) works for any stage because register_item_inputs hashes every named input and every tool's version.
techniques.measured_results: Measured by reading and by the test run (A4). model_lint already extracts per-triangle areas and Blender material facts (blender_material_facts, line 271: base picture linked or not, alpha, glow), so a 'share of the scene's area whose material has no normal map, no roughness variation or no wear' check can reuse parts_from_blender (207) and the glb reader.
techniques.traps_and_failures: bin/explainer-film-setup's check that every kit file the skills name exists only looks at names starting paper-film/, narration-tools/, examples/, docs/: a new kit folder (rendering/, weathering/, calculators/) is not checked unless its regex (near the end of the script) is extended. The preflight test counts at least 40 'made by:' lines in --list; adding inputs raises it.

techniques.name: A4. INVENTORY: how the plugin's tests run, and what they did here
techniques.what_it_is: python3 kit/calculators/tests/run_all.py runs every tests/test_*.py as its own Python process (python -I -B), prints one line per file, and exits 1 if any failed. A test passes by exit 0, fails by any other code, is skipped by exit 77 (with a line starting SKIP). Each test builds a Checker (tests/checks.py) with close(), within(), true(), equal(), note(), finish(), which print each check with 'recorded in' and 'proves'.
techniques.why_it_matters: New checks and kit code need tests that run on any machine with the plugin alone.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Run: python3 kit/calculators/tests/run_all.py [words] [--show] [--list] [--timeout S]. Paths outside the plugin come from environment variables (FILM_PROJECT, FILM_KIT, FILM_WORKING_FILES, BLENDER, VIEWS_AND_MODELS_NO_BLENDER=1 skips Blender parts) and a test skips a part with a plain reason, never fails it. A new test: file tests/test_NAME.py, 'What this does' note, Checker, fixtures under tests/fixtures/. test_model_lint.py writes tiny .glb files by hand with numpy (write_glb) so it needs no Blender: copy that trick. The Blender-side checker test (paper-film/blender/tests/run-checker-tests.sh) needs the pit village street file, which is not shipped (about 170 MB of models). test_house_rules.py only covers kit/calculators and its tests, not paper-film/blender. A kit_orig style regression is also covered: test_preflight.py runs the real wrapper (bin/explainer-film-preflight --list).
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED here, with TMPDIR and bytecode writing sent to my scratch folder: 25 test files, 22 passed, 1 failed (test_preflight.py), 2 skipped (test_after_painting.py and test_sound_gates.py need the project's pictures and audio); checks 728 passed, 2 failed, 11 skipped; 2 min 15 s. I re-ran test_preflight.py with the full text of its failing step printed (a debug copy executed from memory, nothing written to the plugin): both failing checks are the film stage, and the one finding is 'disk: filming needs about 0.54 GB and would leave 2.37 GB free (keep 4 GB) (plan_budget.py)'. So the plugin's own suite fails on a machine with under 4.5 GB free; plan_budget.py filming takes --free-disk-gb, which the test does not pass.
techniques.traps_and_failures: The background-job notice came before the suite had finished; I relied on the run's own last lines ('25 test files ... exit 1'). Skipped parts are reported, not failed, so a green run can still hide much (11 parts and 2 whole files skipped here).

reusable_code.what: The Checker used by every test.

techniques.name: A5. INVENTORY: what a generic rented-card rendering guide needs (no key, no id)
techniques.what_it_is: The plugin has nothing on rented cards. The working route is a RunPod pay-per-second 'serverless endpoint': a card (worker) starts only when a job waits and stops about 5 s after, so idle time costs nothing. Today's client, job taker and notes live in a scratch folder outside the repository and read the person's key and endpoint id from the person's own files.
techniques.why_it_matters: Cycles for lit scenes is only affordable this way: street pictures 3 to 25 s, garden finals about 40 s instead of minutes to hours on this shared computer.
techniques.how_to_do_it: THE GUIDE NEEDS: (1) WHEN: the person's renderer rule (verbatim): 'Cycles looks absolutely incredible. But it could be expensive. You know what? I think it's worth it. But only for scenes where the lights are on. When they're off, eeve is fine.' Cycles where lamps, windows, lanterns or fires are lit; EEVEE when they are off. (2) ONE-TIME SET-UP the person does, in plain steps: an account and a key that may create endpoints; one network store (30 GB) in one data centre holding Blender 5.2.2 and uploaded files; one endpoint with a plain Ubuntu image, the start command from start.sh, workers up to 3, idle timeout 5 s, job timeout about 1 h, cards RTX 4090 first then 5090 then 24 GB cards, the store mounted; run copy_libraries.sh once on a machine with the store to copy about 60 system libraries so Blender runs on the plain image. The plugin carries handler.py (job taker: put, get, info, run, ping; files in 7 MB pieces; runs shell commands) and start.sh (runs the job taker with the Python inside Blender, so no custom image is needed). (3) SETTINGS AT RUN TIME: the client reads the key and endpoint id from the person's own settings (environment variables first, or a path in one non-secret variable), never prints them, never writes them into a note, prompt, log or repository. Today's client reads ~/.runpod/auth_header and cached_machine.json; the generic one should not name that folder in code the helpers read. (4) DAILY USE: actions status, upload LOCAL [--remote], run 'COMMAND' [--cwd] [--timeout], job ID, wait ID [--limit], download REMOTE [--local]; folders go as one tar bundle, files skip when the checksum matches; Blender there: /workspace/blender/blender -b --disable-autoexec ... (no xvfb, no -t); one run command per batch of pictures (one wake-up); each job at most about 55 min; send a client name in the User-Agent (RunPod refused Python's default); write outputs into the store; clear the remote output folder before a run (stale pictures once came back as black roads); download only small JPG previews and JSON, keep PNG and EXR on the store. (5) BEFORE A LONG JOB: check the account balance (GraphQL myself.clientBalance); prove the GPU with one tiny Cycles picture (cycles_check.py: OptiX, print devices) or render_job.py --require-gpu; if jobs wait more than 5 minutes while workers show idle, stop and tell the person (cause once found: balance US$0.13); never purge the queue or change the endpoint. (6) COST: a 4090 is about US$1.10 an hour, 0.03 US cents a second (read the live price). (7) END: the person decides to set workers to 0 to switch it off; it must be switched back on before the next render.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED (project logs): cold worker wakes in 20-22 s, warm under 1 s; EEVEE wet street 540x960 5.8 s and 31.6 s billed (about one US cent); Cycles OptiX 540x960 at 128 samples 5.2 s; main street wet EEVEE 3.68 s vs Cycles 14.08 s, lockout plate 2.81 vs 25.3 s, cottage 1.55 vs 15.36 s; garden finals 2400x1600 at 512 samples with denoiser 44.3 s (hero) and 39.7 s (veranda), previews 1200x800 at 96 samples 6-10 s. The first always-on machine ran 13 hours (about US$11.60) mostly waiting. Garden character job: RunPod's hourly bill US$10.89 for about 4 hours of card time; the ledger of job seconds adds to 11,354 s (3.15 h, about US$3.5-4.4 at US$1.10) so the bill was about 2.5 times the work seconds: NOT explained.
techniques.traps_and_failures: FAILURES SEEN: RunPod's newer interface answered 'authentication failed' mid-setup (older interface worked); the job library pulled 2 GB of extras onto the store; a stale picture left on the machine gave black road pictures; sending 135 files one by one took 9 minutes (bundle: 8 s); the web address refused Python's default name; community cards vanish between asking and starting and on one host Cycles could not use the card; credit ran out (balance US$0.13) from 07:31 to 08:30 and jobs waited with idle workers, restarting workers did nothing, adding credit fixed it; the cloud container restarted twice (about 02:48 and 09:40) and one checker's work was lost, so jobs must write progress to the store; a plan picture was turned the wrong way. DO NOT CARRY: direct_to_machine.py and render_job_server*.py (read machine ids and tokens), render_client_cached.py (always-on, bills 30 minutes idle), diagnose/*.py (read the key folder and carry endpoint settings), harness/remote.py's fixed client path (CLIENT = 'scratchpad/runpod/render_client_cached.py'). The handler runs any shell command sent to it: the key is the only lock. The plugin's push guard (plan_budget.py SECRET_PATTERNS, lines 73-80) has no RunPod key or endpoint pattern; add one after checking the key format on the person's own account (not by reading ~/.runpod).

techniques.name: A6. INVENTORY: places where today's plugin text conflicts with what was learned (to settle in one place)
techniques.what_it_is: Eight conflicts a model would hit.
techniques.why_it_matters: Two rules saying opposite things make a small model follow whichever it read first.
techniques.how_to_do_it: (1) blender-mcp-notes.md:269-279 'glTF and three.js have no displacement': true for the old card route, false for plates drawn in Blender (displacement works in Cycles and EEVEE); say which route each rule is for. (2) make-3d-models/SKILL.md:13 'Cycles ... 35 to 90 s a frame, so Blender only BUILDS': out of date once cards are rented (Cycles 3-25 s a picture). (3) Texture size cap 1024 (notes D13) is a glb budget; the garden used 2048 normal maps and Poly Haven 2k near the camera. (4) kit/calculators/templates/paint-prompt.txt:7 'simplified painterly textures on brick, stone, slate and wood, and matte painted finish' and :33 never 'puddles or reflections': log 19 showed these words made a wet ground come back dry; the wet test removed them and asked to keep the sheen, joints and gutter puddles. (5) model_kit.py:111-112 bevel with harden_normals=False, although the notes call it wrong (127-130) and build_street.py soften() does it right. (6) The Scenario texturing skill (project .claude/skills, not in the plugin) says 'Normal map OR displacement, never both' and 'EEVEE finals' by default; the project used normal and displacement together with the normal's strength cut to 0.6 (mine_common.py) and a bump of at most 0.3 fed by the normal map (garden), and the person's rule is Cycles where lights are on. (7) Two Python environments: model_kit.py needs the pip bpy and pillow venv, the place route uses the Blender program. (8) The plugin's LLM tips say compute rather than search; the weathering kit says the plate renderer shows 'only in Cycles unless baked' for Bevel, AO and Pointiness: both agree edges must come from masks or baking.
techniques.measured_results: Judged by reading; (4) is backed by the measured wet-street test (road 0.72 times as bright as the dry painting, reflections overlap 0.60-0.63 with the plate against 0.04-0.10 for the dry painting).
techniques.traps_and_failures: Do not fix a conflict in one file only: the same words sit in the skill, the notes file, the tips guide and the template.

techniques.name: B1. Designed detail in the picture's own art style, not photographic noise
techniques.what_it_is: The person's rule (said twice, verbatim in the style note): 'These things need to be integrated into the style. So it's just part of design.' Wear, moss, cracks, joinery, tufts, flowers and stains are drawn elements in the same chunky, clean language as the rest, never a layer of scan-like detail.
techniques.why_it_matters: It is why the garden got visible character without turning photographic, and why the weathering shader layers (fine, scan-like) added little at film size.
techniques.how_to_do_it: (1) Before any building, measure the current picture and write a style note: brightness percentiles, mean saturation, the ten commonest colours, detail energy per region, what the style does NOT have. (2) Give every builder and checker the note and one test sentence: could this sit in a hand-painted game level next to the biggest, simplest thing without looking like it came from a more photographic picture? (3) Marks are few and big: a moss patch is one soft rounded shape with a lighter top edge, a crack one clean dark line, a peg one small round shape, a grass tuft 5 to 9 simple blades; about one readable feature per 5-10 cm on timber, 20-30 cm on ground, 50 cm on stone and wall ('one small story per hand-span, never a hundred tiny details of equal weight'). (4) Forms: corners bevelled 1-3 cm (6-12 mm on planks), no film grain, no micro-pores, normal maps soft and large (blur 1-2 px at 2048). (5) New colours from the existing palette family (moss olive to #2a2d24 in shade, mould dark grey-green, iron rust #5a3a2a, lichen #c4af8a, water stain cooler darker brown); the single hot accent stays the only strongly saturated area. (6) Run the guard numbers on every render (B17). For a new place with no reference picture, render the first honest version, measure it, and set the guard from that.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED on the garden hero: percentiles 1/5/25/50/75/95/99 % = 0.047/0.067/0.177/0.318/0.474/0.627/0.882; saturation 0.399; detail energy (mean absolute difference from a 2-pixel blur, 0-255 scale): roof 8.0, bridge 5.4, grass 3.6, maple 8.4, sand 7.5, wall 3.4, rock 3.6; photographs of the same things sit above 12 (judged). Guard (invented, one step's judgement): new detail energy not below 0.9 times or above the smaller of 1.4 times and 10. Result after the fixes (checker re-measure): bridge 5.34 to 5.30 (no extra fine contrast, the character is shape and colour), rock 3.61 to 4.58 (cap 5.0), roof 7.88 to 8.33, flat 96x96 windows 0 of 931.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Painters that broke the rule: Nano Banana Pro and prompts without the rule sentence gave photographic moss, hair-fine grass (grass energy 6.9-7.5, double) and leafy hedges. The first built planks came out pale cream with 0.6 percent moss (builder claimed 9.8); a scan-like lichen speckle remained on the roof close-up; the palette limit (saturation above 0.70 outside the accent at most 1 percent) was missed (1.76 to 2.25 percent) because of green domes, lily pads and an orange deck.

techniques.name: B2. Real normal maps that point the right way, and are proven to
techniques.what_it_is: The garden had no normal maps (0 Normal Map nodes, 175 Bump nodes, no object had a UV map). After the character job, 85 materials carry real tangent-space normal maps from 17 pictures, each checked to point the right way.
techniques.why_it_matters: Light needs a direction for every dot; flipped green makes grooves read as ridges and makes a place look wrong in a way people feel but cannot name.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Example first: a plank map is 2048x512 for a 1.0 x 0.25 m tile: 17 wavy grain grooves, 2 round knots, 2 thin checks. Steps: (1) every object that uses a map has a UV layer, and the Normal Map node names it (uv_map). (2) Make a height picture (white = high), soft: blur 1-2 px at 2048, no micro-pores. (3) normal_tools.height_to_normal(h, strength 1.5-3.0, tile=True): OpenGL, green = up the picture; 2.0 is soft and painterly, 6.0 strong; strength is counted in dots, so scale it with picture size. (4) Wire: UV Map -> Mapping -> Image Texture (Non-Color, Repeat, Cubic) -> Normal Map (Tangent) -> Principled Normal; add_normal_map_nodes does it. Keep an old Bump only below 0.3 and fed by the Normal Map. (5) Strengths used: moss 0.45, stone 0.8-1.0, roof tile 0.9, bark 0.9, plaster 1.0, ground 1.0, planks 1.5; with real displacement on, cut to 0.6 of that. (6) Test light on every shipped map: a plane with default UVs under a 30-degree sun from +X and from +Y; the lit side must be brighter, and a deliberately flipped copy must fail. (7) Wiring check on every material in the scene (nm_struct.py): space Tangent, image behind Color, Non-Color, mean red and green 0.5, mean blue at least 0.85, reaches the Principled Normal, a UV layer on every user, image at least 1024 px. (8) A map alone can be told OpenGL from DirectX: correlate the change of red down the rows with the change of green along the columns (-1.00 OpenGL, +1.00 DirectX); blind to maps with both red and green flipped, so keep the height. Flip a file with green = 1 - green; name files _nor_gl or _nor_dx. (9) glTF allows one normalTexture per material; export tangents; baked normals as PNG, JPEG q94 is fine under grain.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED. normal_tools check_direction here: NORMAL_DIRECTION PASS (0.804 vs 0.158 sun from +X, 0.806 vs 0.156 sun from +Y, flipped-green control fails as it should). Garden final: 85 materials, 17 images, all Tangent, all Non-Color, red and green means 0.50, blue 0.979-1.000, 0 problems; checker's own sun test +0.55 to +0.99 on 8 maps (post map +0.28, just over the +0.25 limit); plank map integrated back to a height agrees with the groove picture at +0.88. Plugin textures.py maps: all OpenGL-consistent (-0.95 to -0.99); planks map has only an X part and mean tilt 4.0 degrees (cinders 4.2, brick 8.5, setts 14.8).
techniques.traps_and_failures: (a) In Blender 5.2.2, setting colorspace_settings.name = 'Non-Color' after writing the pixels of a generated image wipes it to black; set it right after images.new. (b) One checker's test said the plank map fails in X (+0.061 against +0.25): it used the wrong plane size; with the right plane +0.55. A test needs its own control. (c) The swell map was so soft that picture noise hid it (+0.05): fix the test (16-bit, higher test strength), not the map. (d) First ground map was far too strong (lawn corrugated, grass energy 10.5, then 4.17). (e) The pond pebble, bark and swell maps came from blurred scan heights; Poly Haven's displacement picture blurred 2-5 px makes a soft painted normal. (f) A mirrored copy of a tile needs red or green flipped. (g) Normal and displacement together: see B4.

techniques.name: B3. UV maps when objects have none (box UV, planks, instances)
techniques.what_it_is: None of the garden's 132 mesh objects had a UV map; materials found their place from position, so a normal map could not even be used until UVs were written by script.
techniques.why_it_matters: Without UVs a normal map is impossible, and wrong UVs paint stripes or mirrored grain.
techniques.how_to_do_it: (1) Planar top UV (x, y)/tile for ground and water. (2) Box UV per face: drop the axis the face points along, use the other two coordinates divided by tile size in metres (1 UV unit = real tile size). (3) Planks: u along the length, v across, plus a random UV offset per plank, and randomly mirror or rotate some planks and switch a knot off on about half, or the same knot appears on every plank. (4) Roof tiles that are instances: put the UV on the prototype mesh (instances inherit it). (5) Flip any mirrored island (where the UV area is negative) so grain is not mirrored. (6) UV hygiene check: no UV layer missing, 0 mirrored faces, UV range inside the intended tile.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED by checkers: hygiene check on the wood stage passes (0 mirrored faces); roof stage left 7 pond-edge stones with 40-73 percent mirrored faces (cause not found); one checker found the same two spiral knots on 10 of 13 planks.
techniques.traps_and_failures: The plugin's own box_map (model_kit.py:233) uses location and scale but not rotation, so rotated parts smear texture (notes D14: map before rotating). Stripes from squashed UVs are the plugin's model_lint 'stripes' check; keep it.

techniques.name: B4. Real displacement where it matters, at a believable depth
techniques.what_it_is: Displacement moves the surface (outline and shadows change); bump and normal only change shading. The coal-mine yard used height maps as real displacement on mud, gravel, brick and slate.
techniques.why_it_matters: Roads, thatch, brick and roofs seen at a low angle need true outlines; normal maps cannot give that.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Example first: mud yard, relief 6 cm, terrain mesh fine near the camera. Steps: (1) Material Settings > Displacement set to Displacement (material.displacement_method = 'DISPLACEMENT' or 'BOTH'); without it the node does nothing. (2) Displacement node: Height from a 16-bit Non-Color picture, Midlevel 0.5, Scale = true depth in metres; set material.max_vertex_displacement = depth. (3) Enough mesh: a Subdivision Surface modifier set to Simple with adaptive subdivision (Cycles; no longer experimental in 5.x), pixel size 1-2; or a graded grid (0.12 m squares near the camera, each next square 1.09 times bigger, largest 5 m). (4) Depth by surface: mud 6 cm, gravel 4 cm, slate 4 cm, brick 3 cm, wood 3 cm, metal 1.6 cm; terrain mud 5 cm. (5) With displacement on, normal strength times 0.6. (6) Smooth 16-bit heights with a wrap-around blur (0.8 px) and stretch the 0.5 and 99.5 percentiles to 0..1 (prepare_textures.py); 8-bit heights band. (7) Use it on big close surfaces only; keep normal maps for the rest.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED: render of a rough surface seen low: Bump Only 3.6 s, Displacement Only 2.1 s, both 3.6 s (far outline bumpiness 0.16 vs 3.1 dots). Adaptive dicing 1 px 2.9 s, 0.5 px 5.2 s with no gain. A gentle ramp has 54 levels in 8 bits; its normal map has 53 percent flat dots from 8-bit and 0.9 percent from 16-bit. Mine photo 1080x1920 at 128 samples took 8 min 11 s on this machine's processor.
techniques.traps_and_failures: First mud test read as grass spikes: the relief was 30 cm; cut to 6 cm (mud) and 4 cm (gravel). A flat panel set at exactly the floor's height rendered pure black (coplanar): lift 2 cm. A mesh made in Geometry Nodes ignores the object's material until a Set Material node is added. The Scenario skill says normal map or displacement, never both (conflict A6). Real grooves cut into a road looked worse in the middle distance than a normal-map slope and were switched off (street). glTF has no displacement.

techniques.name: B5. Roughness, not specular, makes a surface wet; joints that hold under all light
techniques.what_it_is: A wetness layer sits between any material's dry look and its shader. Joints between stones are kept visible in every light by making the joint darker, duller and slightly sloped.
techniques.why_it_matters: Wet earth, wet stone and puddles are what make a village road and thatch read as lived in; and the person said the geometry must still show 'under all conditions'.
techniques.how_to_do_it: (1) Water gathers in low spots (from the road's camber to the gutter) and becomes puddles that flatten the stones and mirror sky and lamps. (2) Wet stone is darker and glossier with drier tops; walls get a darker wet foot and streaks under sills; a dial for wetness and one for puddles. (3) The roughness map carries wet: dry about 0.9, wet about 0.3. (4) A joint is dark because it is narrow, dirty and dull: darker (colour times 0.70 at the middle, 0.85 at the stone edge), duller (roughness back to 0.9, shine cut 35 percent, water film 45 percent) and with a rounded groove slope (8 mm deep, edge 6 mm wide) added after the water layer; under a puddle the dulling fades but the dark stays; far away fade the slope (full to 5 m, 10 percent at 20 m) because a steep far slope shows as white ticks. (5) Test under a fixed lighting set: 3 cameras x 5 lightings (dusk lamps, glare, low side light, flat overhead, light from behind) x dry, wet, heavy rain = 22 pictures; measure joint contrast (how much darker a joint is than the stone beside it) near, middle and far. (6) Draw EEVEE wet pictures with a smoothed copy of the relief (cure for white grit).
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED (street): the specular map changed the road by only 0.006, the roughness map by 0.28. Joints: 6 of 22 lightings passed before, 21 of 22 after (18 of 22 counting every dot); wet street joint contrast 0.07 to 0.52. Walls wet were 0.84 of dry, foot 0.66; road 1.5 times today's brightness. Painter kept the wet look when the brief allowed it (road 0.72 of the dry painting, reflections overlap with the plate 0.60-0.63 against 0.04-0.10 for dry).
techniques.traps_and_failures: A relief picture adds no depth (a groove floor leans only 9 degrees); stronger relief 3-6 times only made white ticks; the shine laid equally over stones and joints; the photo's joints were only dark moss, half were pale sand (completed the grid from row and column statistics); stale pictures on the rented machine gave black roads; four wrong explanations of the one remaining failure; a wet ground was once repainted dry by 'matte painted finish' and the ban on reflections (A6).

techniques.name: B6. Surface sources and hiding repeats (scans, procedural, per-object variation)
techniques.what_it_is: Poly Haven textures (free, CC0) with maps Diffuse, Rough, nor_gl (OpenGL), nor_dx, Displacement, AO and arm (AO, roughness, metal packed); or procedural recipes. Repeats are hidden by variation.
techniques.why_it_matters: A village needs many surfaces (mud, forest ground, thatch, timber, plaster, stone); repeats and stickers spoil them.
techniques.how_to_do_it: (1) URL pattern: https://dl.polyhaven.org/file/ph-assets/Textures/jpg/<1k|2k|4k>/<id>/<id>_<diff|rough|nor_gl|disp|ao|arm>_<1k|2k>.jpg; 1k set about 1.5 MB, 2k 7-13 MB; take 1k unless near the camera; send a generic agent name only. (2) Pick a surface by drawing a small test plate of it, not from a thumbnail; open every picture full size and look for stickers, brands and digits. (3) Colour sRGB; roughness, normal, displacement Non-Color; use the roughness map; box projection when there are no UVs, height only as bump on gravel so rake lines stay real. (4) Hide repeats: look every picture up twice (second at 0.79 scale, offset 0.37 and 0.58) and blend by slow noise (scale 0.17), never rotate (bumps stay lit); multiply by slow patches (noise scale 0.35, 'variation' 0.25); give each object its own tint and mapping offset; per plank random offset, mirror and knot switch-off; per roof tile a tone attribute (standard deviation at least 0.02). (5) Procedural route: Blender's noise does not tile (use the donut trick, 4D noise on a torus, in recipe_tools.py); photograph a flat tile with an emission shader for exact maps (bake_harness.py, view transform Standard for colour and Raw for data, 16-bit heights, box filter 1.0, at least 16 samples). (6) Surfaces on a forest village (Poly Haven names seen on 22 Oct 2026): brown_mud, brown_mud_02, brown_mud_03, brown_mud_dry, brown_mud_leaves_01, brown_mud_rocks_01, forrest_ground_01, forrest_ground_03, forest_ground_05, forest_leaves_02, grass_path_2, leafy_grass, thatch_roof_angled, reed_roof_03, reed_roof_04, riet_01, clay_plaster, clay_roof_tiles, castle_wall_slates, cobblestone_01 to 05, bark_brown_01, bark_brown_02, brick_moss_001.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED: Poly Haven list 22 Oct 2026: 869 textures and 521 models. The street's scanned bricks 'look incredible' close up (person's words). Plank map reuse: the same two knots on 10 of 13 planks.
techniques.traps_and_failures: At garden distance (16 percent of the picture) tiling is the danger, so a macro variation is needed; AI swatches: one had a blurred reflection of the whole scene in its lower 15 percent, one read as dragon scales, one roof swatch was too blue and flat; seam-test every swatch (half-shift test); one shared 'stone' material used by three objects of two builders was edited by nobody (copy on use); the plugin's fetch lists are the pit village's.

techniques.name: B7. A dirt road driven by carts: ruts, wet ruts, puddles, mounds, a graded mesh
techniques.what_it_is: The mine yard's ground (modules/ground_and_yard.py) is the closest thing in the sources to an unkept road driven by horse and carriage.
techniques.why_it_matters: The request asks for exactly this; a flat textured plane would fail the 'driven down' read.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Example first: two lines (the wheel tracks) a gauge apart follow each cart road; each wobbles (a soft noise along the road, about 9 cm) and varies in depth (depth times 0.85 to 1.25) and width; depth eases to 0 over the first and last 3 m. Height = base ground - depth x exp(-(distance/half width)^2) + a raised edge (0.30 depth) beside the rut + lumpy churned ground (broad swell, finer clods that get rougher near ruts, smoothed in the rut bottom by running water). Wetness = Gaussian along the ruts (0.9) + slow wet patches (0.45); the colour attribute marks wetness, far distance and coal dust per vertex and the material reads it (wet places darker and glossier). Puddles are flat sheets of glossy water lying 1.5 cm above the lowest ground they cover, in hollows dug 4 cm below the sheet; round pools flatten the slope across themselves (85 percent). Earth mounds and heaps are part of the ground mesh. Keep the ground exactly as the shared ground_height says right next to buildings and the track (a clear factor from distance to buildings, so things sit cleanly). Mesh: graded grid, 0.12 m near the camera growing 1.09 times each step to 5 m far, real displacement with dicing 2 px. Add the surface through the repeat breaker (B6). Seat everything on the ground with the shared ground_height(x, y). Add scattered stones and lumps (about 2,000 lumps in ONE object) and a handcart, barrels, timber rack, fence. For a village: add hoof dimples and straw with the rubbish mask logic (B10), keep plants off the crown and wheel lanes (B8).
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED/RECORDED: the mine photo 1080x1920 at 128 samples took 8 min 11 s on this machine's processor; the mine's six parts were built in 2 h 41 min by six helpers at once; first assembly 45 s at small size.
techniques.traps_and_failures: The first assembly showed smoke like giant black balloons, the headframe hiding the engine house, a foreground field of coal rubble, a doorway onto nothing (nobody built a floor); the engine house inside is nearly black; coal lumps a little sharp-cornered up close; a first test camera script used the same camera three times (settings typed the wrong way), caught by looking.

techniques.name: B8. Where wear goes: masks made from the set's own shape, and the weathering kit as one entry point
techniques.what_it_is: The weathering kit (kits/weathering) ages any Blender set: soot, run-off streaks, wall-foot damp, steps, wall cracks, wall growth, worn paint (off in the street), ground film, ground cracks, ground moss, iron rust, and small 3D weeds and moss. One call puts it on; remove() leaves every material exactly as it was.
techniques.why_it_matters: It is the project's model of 'one entry point per job, one settings file per place, looks as presets', and its masks say where dirt, damp and plants may be.
techniques.how_to_do_it: USE: import apply_weathering as aw; w = aw.apply('<set id>', '<look id>', state='wet'); w.set_master(0.8); w.set_layer_master('soot', 0.5); w.remove(). A NEW PLACE (recipe note section 6): copy sets/japanese_courtyard.json (id, scenes, plate size, roles by name patterns, never list, per-layer roles, geometry: ground roles, solid walls, step finder, wall sheets, ledges, entrances, water level; footfall shapes; keep_clear; shade; dampness; habitat weights), make a look in presets/ (dial values, any readable, period and forbidden tables), make the mask pack once per scene file (blender -b scene.blend --python masks/reader.py -- set scene pack_folder raw_folder; 25-80 s), run the lint (must say 0 hits) and the self-tests, then tune dials in the look, never the code. THE WHERE-MASKS (CONTRACT.md): ground height, slope, lowness (where water gathers), crown, wall_dist, prop_dist, inside_corner, step_foot, vertical_foot, step_top, step_edge, edge_dist, piece_gap, seam_dist, water_dist, above_water, litter_dist, sheltered (rain cannot reach), drip (run-off below sills, ledges, eaves, pipe joints), drip_dist, corner, reveal, openness, shade, dampness (wall foot, drips, water, low ground, shelter), footfall, keepclear, existing_growth, rubbish_heap, moss_site, weed_site, algae_site, lichen_site. Habitat fields are a product with a gate, never a threshold on noise: moss_site, weed_site and lichen_site are exactly 0 where footfall is 0.6 or more, crown 0.7 or more, keepclear 0.5 or more. ORDER in each material chain: slot A (before the water layer): soot, run-off, foot, steps, ground film, rust (water darkens by the surface's porosity, so white goes grey when wet); wetness; joints; slot B (after, so they stay dull): cracks and chips; slot C: moss, algae, lichen; rubbish last; 3D growth separate. RULES THE KIT KEEPS: never edit a mesh or a material slot; amount 0 gives exactly the input; no Bevel, AO or Pointiness nodes (edges come from masks made once from geometry); marks sized in plate dots so they read at the painter's size, fading to the layer's average tone, never to clean; per-object numbers are custom properties (wk_seed, wk_role_id, wk_zmin) so a material shared by two kinds of object is weathered only where the set says.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED by the kit's checks on the street: no layer names a place (lint 0 hits, re-run here: CLEAN); both settings files validate (re-run here in Blender 5.2.2); joints still pass 21 of 22 lightings (20 counting every dot); plate brightness moves 1-1.6 percent; plants 195 to 157 after the fix round; drawing time 2.1 times then 1.4 times; the courtyard took the kit from a settings file and a look alone, no code change, and turned visibly mossy. RE-CHECK VERDICT: at film size the kit adds little a viewer can see except rust and a few weeds; the walls are nearly black and seen edge-on so soot, run-off and damp vanish.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Three things the courtyard could not do by settings (fixed in the kit_patched copy): moss on a roof whose materials sit inside geometry nodes, wall sheets facing the garden (explicit front), per-material dials; further fixes are in garden/final/stage/kit (the newest copy: roles.py and reader.py changed, plus preset garden_kept.json). Four copies exist (kits/weathering, garden/ours/kit_orig, kit_patched, final/stage/kit); start from the newest and fold back. The kit's harness reaches the rented machine through a fixed path to the old always-on client (harness/remote.py CLIENT). Street-only parts: integrate/legacy_* (wetness, joints, rubbish pinned copies), street_weathering.py, masks/packs/pit_village_street, harness/baseline (frozen numbers). harness/.remote_state.json is a hash cache of uploaded files (no ids) but should not be copied. Layers can read wk_ numbers of geometry instances and turn eaves mint green: keep tile shapes as object instances. An Attribute node on an object with no such property reads 0, so a missing wk_<layer>_amount silently switches the layer off on that object (run kit.report()). Not handled: lichen in the street, graffiti, road lines, anything modern.

techniques.name: B9. Grime, soot, run-off and damp: how much is too much, dark walls, and what survives painting
techniques.what_it_is: Numbers for how big, how faint and how much dirt reads, measured on the pit village plates and the painter's repaints.
techniques.why_it_matters: Dirt that is too fine vanishes; too much turns the place into dark mush.
techniques.how_to_do_it: RULES (plate 1536x2730, painter sees about half): marks (chips, specks, moss dots, weed tufts, rust specks) width 5 dots or more and contrast 0.08 or more come back about 80 percent of the time (8 dots needs 0.05, 12 needs 0.04, 3 needs 0.12); lines (cracks, drips, joints) 3 dots at 0.11, 5 at 0.08, 8 at 0.055, 12 at 0.04; patches (soot masses, damp, moss patches) 15 dots or wider at 0.04 or more (0.06 to be safe), they return about 1.3 times stronger; nothing under 0.03 and narrower than 8 dots survives; keep the darkest part of anything you want seen at 0.10-0.12 or more with its surround at 0.18 or more (painted 0.10 arrives as 0.015-0.03, 0.08 as black); do not plant dark detail in the far third of a road, the painter makes its own. Dark grime on about a quarter of a surface and a darkening of about a third (to 65 percent) reads as dirty but legible; 45 percent of the area at half brightness is mush. Order of importance: big tonal masses, colour accents, a few clean cracks and joints, grit and chips near the camera, weeds as tufts, anything finer skip. Very dark walls cannot take dark grime: use pale or coloured grime (salts, lichen, rust runs, moss). Where it goes: soot on tops and sheltered sides, run-off below sills, ledges, eaves and pipe joints, pale run-off and rust-coloured streaks under iron, damp bands and splash at wall feet, whitened steps, dirt rings round fires and props.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED on five plate and painting pairs (17,942 marks full size, 8,624 wet): a fit called GOOD predicted that 95 percent of specks and 75 percent of lines came back (called LOST: 21 and 16 percent), fair for specks, 10-15 points optimistic for lines. Mush measures (kit versus before, per class): M1 at most 25 percent of the class darkened by a third; M2 share under 0.10 rises by at most 8 points (3 on walls); M3 mean brightness drops at most 12 percent; M4 spread kept at 85 percent; M5 brightness bands 5-10, 10-20, 20-40 m stay between 0.80 and 1.00. 87 percent of 3,320 small wall marks (0.03 or more) are in the lost group, and that is fine. Painter weakens colour (red and orange saturation 0.46 to 0.21 in one pair) and moves dark olive and yellow-brown to grey-teal or pale.
techniques.traps_and_failures: The first kit round turned the street's plate walls 23 percent darker (line 12); pale panels on red brick and cold blue-white doorsteps had to be calmed; walls seen edge-on hid stains; first mismeasure said 95-100 percent kept for everything (counted any dark thing nearby); no plate had moss or weeds when the survival numbers were made, so colour and weed survival were inferred. These numbers are for painted plates; for a direct render use the value and detail checks (B17).

techniques.name: B10. Weeds, moss, lichen and litter: rules for where they grow, and designed shapes
techniques.what_it_is: Growth and rubbish as habitat rules (damp, shade, edges, shelter) with hard keep-out zones, drawn as a few designed shapes.
techniques.why_it_matters: The person asked for weeds and moss; the first checkers found lime-bright weeds in puddles and weeds mid-slab, and one claim of 9.8 percent moss on planks was really 0.6 percent.
techniques.how_to_do_it: WHERE: moss on damp plus shade (wall feet, drips, water edge, low ground, sheltered stone, plank ends and gaps near water and posts); weeds at joints, kerb feet, gutter edges, stone cracks and the gravel edge; NEVER on the road crown, wheel or foot lanes, doorsteps, round a fire, on raked gravel; 5 cm clear of litter pieces (baked distance picture) and out of puddles (baked picture of puddles from above); nothing doubles growth a scan already carries (existing_growth mask). SHAPES (garden, designed): grass tufts of 5-9 simple blades, at least 8 different tuft meshes, scale range 3 to 1, heights 12-70 cm, clumps of 2-5, at least 3 tints, seed heads on 15-28 percent, 20 percent with dry straw tips, 10 percent with a reddish tint, flowers few (at least 20 but under 0.3 percent of the picture); moss as soft domes 15-50 cm with a light top and darker underside, size varied 0.6-1.5 and the count cut by about a third in a bank, some flat; moss caps: ONE soft rounded cap per big rock with a lighter top edge, a thin green rim at the waterline and a darker wet band below; moss on timber only at gaps, plank ends, post feet; roof moss 4-10 percent in valleys, eave edge and ridge, lichen 1-3 percent as pale flecks; keep dead-grass tufts few (they are the lightest thing on a dark road). LITTER: a rubbish mask from the set's real shape (gutters, wall feet, doorsteps, pipe and post feet, inside corners, rings round props, never the road middle), broken into patches, heavier at the kerb than the pavement (about 8 to 1), drives painted muck plus about 6,400 to 58,753 small 3D pieces; pieces near the camera capped in size; flat irregular lumps not faceted gems, short curved straw not matchsticks. Trees and a forest: the maple as 5-8 layered pads of same-size leaves on a bent trunk with visible branches (silhouette area within 10 percent of before), the pine as 5 flat cloud discs on a curved trunk with plated bark, leaves instanced with geometry nodes (56,000 real-size leaves in layers); scatter with stable ids and a keep-clear width round paths.
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED: street plants 195 in view of the main camera before, 157 after puddle and litter rules; without the litter clearance 79 percent of weeds stood within 5 cm of litter (limit 3 percent); 37 percent of plants stood in puddles before the baked puddle picture; first checker measured 0.6 percent olive on the left plank run (claimed 9.8), later 6.6 percent green by colour count (cannot separate moss from green planks); roof moss, lichen and drip-stain counts were judged, not measured, by the direction step. Keep dials: cushions_amount 0.3, dead_grass_share 0.08, weed_cover 0.02, wallgrowth moss_amount 0.05 (a green band at every wall foot otherwise).
techniques.traps_and_failures: First lawn colour under the new tufts stayed the old smeared scan; moss cushion banks still read as a heap of like domes; flat moss strings looked like floating; geometry-nodes multi-input sockets read their links in reverse, so seed heads were on 4 percent of tufts instead of 28 (found by counting realised triangles: 23,489 against 33,080 expected); lichen first looked like small white flowers; star-shaped saturated leaves; the weathering kit's splash, crack and growth layers gave stripes on rocks and a moss sticker on a lantern until toned down on stones.

techniques.name: B11. Damage and age on timber, roof, wall and stone (designed numbers)
techniques.what_it_is: Numbers the direction step set for wear that reads as designed. They were chosen by judgement from concept images (kind: judged or invented), then checked.
techniques.why_it_matters: They give a model concrete targets for 'wear, damage, replaced boards, cracks, chips'.
techniques.how_to_do_it: PLANKS: width 9-17 cm, thickness 4.5-7 cm varied plank to plank, gap 5-14 mm, bow up to 6 mm, cup up to 4 mm, twist up to 1.5 degrees, rounded worn top edges 6-12 mm, 3 mm underside bevel, chipped corners on 10-15 percent, end checks (small real wedge splits) on 15-20 percent, 6-9 percent replaced planks (lighter, nail heads not pegs), end grain darker, a walking line lighter by 0.02-0.06 luminance and dished 1-2 mm, no two planks exact copies, at least 25 round pegs and 6 iron cramps on a bridge; moss and mould 4-12 percent of plank area concentrated near posts, rocks, water and in shade (walking line at most half the average); post feet dark and wet to the waterline with a green band; deck boards 1.2-2.4 m with staggered butt joints (no two joints within 40 cm), 3.5 cm nosing; posts chamfered 1.5 cm with 2-3 real drying checks, dark end grain, soot on rafter tails. ROOF TILES: tone standard deviation at least 0.02, at least 6 chipped, 3 slipped (2-5 cm, 2-4 degrees), 1 missing with dark underlay, ridge-end caps and eave-end discs, 6-10 dark drip stains under eave ends. WALLS: at least 4 hairline cracks as single dark lines and 2 plaster-loss patches per long wall, splash band at the base, 3 chipped cap tiles. STONES: 1-2 chips and one crack on a few rocks, lantern with 2 cracks and a chipped cap corner, moss in joints and on top.

techniques.name: B12. Construction that makes sense: every plank on a support, every support on the ground, and the checks that prove it
techniques.what_it_is: The garden bridge 'made no sense': boxes overlapped, nothing was fixed to anything. It was rebuilt bottom-up and checked by script.
techniques.why_it_matters: The person said the logic must make sense 'even for an artistic style'; the same fault (floating parts) is common in generated places.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Stack from the ground: flat footing stones on the bed, posts (square 14 cm, 1.5 cm chamfer), cross beams (bearers) pegged to the posts, two stringers per run (three at turns) on the bearers, planks across, pegs, a few iron cramps (flat strap, two nail heads) across joints; no span between supports over 1.4 m; at each turn a square landing and one diagonal breaker board; end and landing posts rise 10-20 cm as bollards, no railing. For houses and sheds the same bottom-up thinking: sill on stone, posts on sill, beams on posts, rafters on beams, roof on rafters, floor and door threshold so a doorway looks onto something. CHECKS (acceptance tests as code): contact graph with parts touching within 5 mm and overlapping at least 4 cm: every part connected to ground; every plank on at least 2 stringers, every stringer on 2 bearers or a sill, every bearer on 2 posts, every post on a footing standing on the bed within 1 cm; nothing floats (minimum distance to any support under 5 mm); walkability: rays straight down every 5 cm along the route hit a plank top, steps between neighbours at most 2 cm, slope at most 1:20; seated check for pegs and cramps (some vertex inside the wood or within 1 mm); a ground-seating ray (place_prop style, cast from below after view_layer.update). Remove bare gaps: coplanar faces 1-2 cm apart (model_lint same-plane and floors checks).
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED by the checker on the saved scene: 59 planks, none with fewer than 2 supports (26 have 2, 19 have 3, 12 have 4, 2 have 6); all 18 posts on a footing or pier with about 17 square decimetres of contact; footings: 5 flat on the bed within 2 mm, 4 sunk 6-20 cm into the bank, 3 hang over the bank by 2.5-13.5 cm; all 100 pegs have vertices inside wood; cramps: 24 small parts, 14 not inside wood, for 6 of 8 straps one nail head hovers 13.7-18.3 mm above the lower plank (the strap crosses from the thicker breaker board). Scene inspection before the job found: a veranda step floating 23 cm, bridge posts 2-7 cm short, wall caps floating 6.5 cm, a lantern glow buried in stone, 77 deck faces fighting a plinth. Scenario's delivery gate on the street found 73 inside-out closed parts.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Builders reported pegs as seated; the checker found the cramps were not. The four corner rails were held only by the beams they cross. Two footing stones overhung the bank. An engine house had no floor. Always run the check on the saved scene, not on the builder's own list of parts.

techniques.name: B13. Cheap geometry that reads, and what to spend triangles on
techniques.what_it_is: Rules for edges, real geometry and vertex colours that make a model stop reading as a CG box.
techniques.why_it_matters: A model with flat boxes and razor corners looks cheap even with a good texture.
techniques.how_to_do_it: (1) Bevel 0.8-1.5 cm on walls, copings, sills (catches a 2-4 px highlight), 6 mm on small trims, 0.6-1.2 cm on planks; bevel with harden_normals=True plus a Weighted Normal modifier after it, smooth shading; bevel after the boolean cut, never before. (2) Real geometry only where it is at least 1 cm proud and in focus (voussoirs, copings, window reveals, sill drips, setts nearest the camera), below that a normal map. On screen size: pixels = metres x focal pixels / distance (film lens 1649 px). (3) Join parts that share a material and never move (232 parts to 19). (4) Vertex colours give free large-scale variation: darken wall feet and under cornices, soot under eaves, dirty paths, break tiling (give every mesh of a material the attribute, white = 1, or meshes render black in three.js). (5) Bake edge wear and cavity dirt only if you must: Pointiness is Cycles-only (bake as Emit); untested here. (6) Budget a place by drawing time: garden builders were allowed at most 1.5 million added triangles each, a final under 90 s on a 4090 and 12 GB card memory (the pine alone is 194,000 vertices, the gravel court 112,000); the film route budgets by seconds a frame (0.9 s held, 4.3 s sliding).
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED: a box is 12 triangles, 44 with 1 bevel segment, 108 with 2 (MCP notes); the FOUNDRY painterly library made a render 223 s against 33 s (7 times slower) and nothing looked painted; it was rejected (log 34).
techniques.traps_and_failures: Bevel without harden_normals on flat-shaded parts shows facets, not highlights; without a bevel the big walls have razor corners; model_kit.py today does the first (A6). A geometry-nodes modifier must end in Realize Instances or applying it fails.

techniques.name: B14. Building a place in parts with owners (the stage pattern and the workflow it suggests)
techniques.what_it_is: The garden character job and the mine scene both split a place into parts built at the same time by separate helpers, then combined.
techniques.why_it_matters: It is the way to build a village in parts with fresh checkers (request item 4).
techniques.how_to_do_it: GARDEN PATTERN: each part is a stage_NAME.py with apply(options) that works on the open starting scene and is idempotent (it first removes what it created before; everything it creates carries garden_owner and garden_role custom properties, a g6_made mark and sits in its own collection 'G6 name'); materials it creates are named 'G6 name / what'; never rename or delete another's object; never edit a shared material or node group in place, copy it ('G6 name / old name'); replacement objects must be linked into the same receiver collections as the originals or they go dark; frozen things listed (cameras, lights, world, render settings, the pond outline, the route within 0.15 m, deck width 1.05 m, water level); contracts written between owners (the bed stays within 0.1 m of its height inside 1.2 m of the bridge because footings stand on it); each builder gets an ordered step list so stopping early leaves a coherent result, a time box (about 2.5 hours), a size limit (60 MB, big files on the store) and a poly budget; a final step runs the stages in order (any order must work) and draws finals; each stage can be skipped. MINE PATTERN: one shared plan file (LAYOUT in metres, +X right, +Y away, +Z up), one ground_height(x, y) every part seats things on, each module defines build(collection_name) returning {objects, notes}, creates no cameras, world or lights unless told, thousands of shapes in ONE MeshBuilder object per material group, under about 300k triangles per part before displacement, a report JSON of object count, triangles, displacement users, build seconds and known flaws. WORKFLOW SHAPE for the plugin: Plan (style note, place facts, layout, ownership table, acceptance tests) -> Build parts in parallel -> Combine in order and fingerprint -> two fresh checkers (B15) -> one fixer per owner in parallel -> combine and redraw -> fresh re-check -> report; the existing workflows are the model: build-pages.js (parallel builders then one consistency reviewer), critique-film.js (critics then a skeptic that dedupes and ranks), check-fixes.js (independent checkers compare each finding with the new pictures and the code and look for new problems), test-script-with-newcomers.js (test, fix confirmed items only, verify, last fix); each is meta {name, description, whenToUse, phases}, args checks, JSON schemas, phase(), parallel(), agent(prompt, {label, phase, schema, effort}).
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED: ownership after the fix round: 141 existing objects changed and 188 added, all on the owners' lists (0 outside), all 188 new objects carry owner and role and sit in G6 collections, lights, light links, world, render settings and cameras identical, 0 changed node groups. Stage times on a card: wood 2.7 s, roof 20.5 s. Mine: six helpers 2 h 41 min.
techniques.traps_and_failures: Builders could not write report.md (the tool refused: subagents must return findings as text), so reports came back as structured output; one fixer for everything was replaced by four in parallel; the saved file drops unused data (58 unused materials and 1 node group were lost, so 'nothing vanished' was false); 48 leftover preview cameras were left in the scene (delete or hide before handing over); a helper's message to the concept helper woke a second copy that made 8 extra paid calls.

techniques.name: B15. Fresh checkers that re-measure the builders' claims
techniques.what_it_is: After the builders, fresh helpers checked the garden twice: an art check, then a construction, normal-map and money check; after the fix round a re-check.
techniques.why_it_matters: Builders' own reports were wrong in important places; the person's rule is that a place must be judged by someone who has not seen the work.
techniques.how_to_do_it: Give each checker: the person's words, the style note, the acceptance list, the scene, the pictures; tell them to recompute, not read the builders' numbers; ask for yes or no on 'art style kept', 'more character', 'construction makes sense', a list of problems each with the cheapest fix, claims checked with 'holds' and evidence, what they tested and what not, and who they are not blind to (say if they saw the list). Checker jobs: re-open the saved scene and trace structure; wiring and direction of every normal map; ownership against the start scene; the fal request history against the ledger and prices; a grep for personal details and the key folder; their own re-measure of value range, detail energy, squint (two formulas) and palette; about 25 crops at 100 percent. After fixes a different fresh checker compares each old finding with new pictures and looks for new faults (fixes make new faults). Limit rounds: one fix round was enough here; decide what counts before the check (two silhouette yardsticks gave opposite answers).
techniques.measured_results: MEASURED. Claims that did NOT hold: moss and mould 9.8 percent of planks (0.6 percent measured, then 'plausible, not measured'); 'nothing vanished' (58 materials dropped on save); 'all pegs and cramps seated' (14 of 24 cramp parts not in wood); 'plank normal fails +0.061' (their test plane was wrong, true +0.55); 'a reviewer names 12 of 16 features' (7-11, then 9-13). Claims that held: value range, detail energy, budget (29 paid calls equal fal's history of 29 requests, none after 02:12), ownership, normal wiring (85 materials, 0 problems). Problems found by the first art check: pale clean planks, one knot on most planks, lantern moss like a sticker, pond not reading at normal size, a darker heavier maple, bean-bag moss cushions, hairy pine, features invisible at 1200 px, smeared lawn.
techniques.traps_and_failures: A checker's first sheet maker crashed on a float64 buffer so metrics were rerun; one checker's work was lost in a container restart and re-run; a squint test missed (0.883 hero and 0.873 veranda against 0.92) and every fixer missed it too, so decide in advance whether a miss is accepted by the person; no blind reviewer test was ever run.
